1b:Tb64,```text
[HYDROGRAPHIC DIVIDE: Aravallis act as Great Continental Divide ➔ State has only 1.16% surface water & 1.72% groundwater]
                                         │
[TRIPARTITE OUTFLOW REGIMES]:
 1. INLAND DRAINAGE (~60.2% area - LARGEST): Ephemeral streams ending in desert sands/playas (Ghaggar, Kantli, Sabi, Ruparel)
 2. BAY OF BENGAL (~22.4% area): Dendritic, perennial canyons, largest volume (Chambal, Banas, Banganga, Gambhir)
 3. ARABIAN SEA (~17.4% area): Western slopes to Kutch/Khambhat (Luni, Mahi, Sabarmati, West Banas)
                                         │
[ARABIAN SEA DETAILS]:
 • Luni (495 km, Nag Pahar): Sweet till Balotra ➔ Saline after; Jojari (ONLY right-bank, non-Aravalli tributary); Jawai (Amrit Sarovar)
 • Mahi (576 km, Amjhoru MP): Inverted 'U' shape; Crosses Tropic of Cancer 2x; Baneshwar Triveni Sangam (Som+Mahi+Jakham); 81m Jakham Dam
 • Sabarmati (Padarana, Udaipur): Lifeline of Gujarat (only 44 km in Raj); Wakal, Sei tunnel to Jawai Dam
 • West Banas (Naya Sanwara, Sirohi): Enters Little Rann of Kutch near Deesa
                                         │
[BAY OF BENGAL DETAILS]:
 • Chambal (965 km, Janapav MP): Perennial; 241 km MP-Raj border; Chulia Falls (18 m); Utkhat Bhumi badlands (Dang ki Rani Karauli);
   4 Dams: Gandhi Sagar (MP, 115 MW), Rana Pratap Sagar (Chittor, 172 MW - largest storage), Jawahar Sagar (99 MW), Kota Barrage (0 MW)
 • Banas (480 km, Khamnor Rajsamand): Longest river ENTIRELY inside Raj; Bisalpur Dam (lifeline of Jaipur); 
   3 Triveni Sangams: Bigod (Banas+Bedach+Menal), Rajmahal (Banas+Khari+Dai), Rameswaram (Banas+Chambal+Seep); Ayad turns Bedach at Udaisagar
 • Banganga (Bairat): Rundhit Sarita (severed river); Jamwa Ramgarh Dam
 • Gambhir (Karauli): Panchana Dam (largest earthen/clay dam, 5 rivulets) feeds Keoladeo via Ajan Dam
                                         │
[INLAND DRAINAGE DETAILS]:
 • Ghaggar (Shivalik HP, 465 km): Saraswati/Dead River; Enters Tibbi; Bed = Nali; Flood in Pak = Hakra; Kalibangan on bank; Talwara lowest lake
 • Kantli (Khandela, Sikar, 100 km): Longest purely internal river; Torawati basin; Ganeshwar copper culture & Sunari iron furnaces
 • Sabi (Sewar, Kotputli): Drains to Haryana (Najafgarh); Jodhpura PGW site
 • Ruparel (Udainath, Alwar): Moti Jheel Dam ("Lifeline of Bharatpur") ➔ Sujan Ganga Canal to Lohagarh moat
                                         │
[LAKES TAXONOMY]:
 • Saline: Sambhar (8.7% India's salt, Ramsar 1990, Mendha brings max salt), Pachpadra (98% NaCl, Kharwals, Moroli bush), Didwana (industrial Na₂SO₄)
 • Freshwater: Jaisamand/Dhebar (Salumbar, 7 islands: Baba ka Bhagra & Pyari), Rajsamand (Raj Prashasti 25 black marble slabs by Ranchhod Bhatt), 
   Pichhola (Banjara built, Jag Mandir inspired Taj Mahal), Fateh Sagar (Connaught Dam, USO Solar Observatory), Nakki (highest 1200 m, freezes)
```

| **Freshwater Lake**| **Rajsamand Lake** | Rajsamand (Gomati river) | Man-made reservoir | • Built for famine relief (1662–76); *Nauchowki ki Pal*.<br>• **Raj Prashasti**: World's largest stone inscription (25 slabs, 1,106 verses). |

---1d:Ta4c,1. **Jojari River Uniqueness**:
   - The **ONLY right-bank tributary of the Luni**.
   - The **ONLY Luni tributary that does not originate from the Aravallis** (originates in the flat plains of Pondlu, Nagaur).
2. **Balotra Salinity Transition**:
   - Luni water is fresh/sweet from Nag Pahar all the way to **Balotra (200+ km)**.
   - It turns brackish/saline downstream of Balotra due to subterranean halite soils, capillary leaching, and dyeing effluents.
3. **Longest River Distinctions**:
   - Longest river *flowing through* Rajasthan: **Chambal (965 km)**.
   - Longest river *flowing entirely and exclusively within Rajasthan*: **Banas (480 km)**.
   - Longest purely *inland* river within Rajasthan: **Kantli (100 km)**.
4. **Mahi Tropic of Cancer & Power Sharing**:
   - Mahi cuts the Tropic of Cancer ($23^\circ 30'\text{ N}$) **twice** (inverted 'U' course).
   - In Mahi Bajaj Sagar, capital is shared 45:55 between Rajasthan and Gujarat, but **100% of the 140 MW power is reserved exclusively for Rajasthan**!
5. **Dam Superlatives**:
   - Tallest Dam in Rajasthan: **Jakham Dam (81 metres)** in Pratapgarh.
   - Longest Dam in Rajasthan: **Mahi Bajaj Sagar Dam (3,109 metres)** in Banswara.
   - Largest Dam by Water Storage: **Rana Pratap Sagar Dam** in Rawatbhata (Chittorgarh).
   - Largest Earthen/Mud Dam: **Panchana Dam** (Karauli, fed by 5 rivulets).
6. **Kota Barrage Produces Zero Power**:
   - Of the 4 Chambal dams, **Kota Barrage produces 0 MW of electricity**; it is purely an irrigation diversion structure.
   - **Gandhi Sagar Dam is NOT in Rajasthan** (located in Mandsaur, MP).
7. **The Ayad to Bedach Name Change**:
   - Originates from Gogunda as **Ayad** (nourishing ancient Ahar civilization).
   - Enters **Udaisagar Lake**; downstream of Udaisagar Lake, it is rechristened as **Bedach**.
8. **Rundhit Sarita (Severed River)**:
   - **Banganga** originates at Bairat and historically reached Yamuna, but now terminates in the Bharatpur wetlands before reaching its master stream — classified as a *Rundhit Sarita*.
9. **Salt Grades: Pachpadra vs Didwana**:
   - **Pachpadra**: 98% pure NaCl, supreme edible grade.
   - **Didwana**: High sodium sulphate ($Na_2SO_4$), strictly **non-edible industrial grade** for leather and dye industries.
10. **Updated Districts (50-District Lens)**:
    - **Jaisamand Lake** is now in **Salumbar district** (NOT Udaipur).
    - **Pachpadra Lake** is now in **Balotra district** (NOT Barmer).
    - **Didwana Lake** is now in **Didwana-Kuchaman district** (NOT Nagaur).
    - **Bairat / Banganga origin** is now in **Kotputli-Behror district** (NOT Jaipur).

---1e:T8b8,### Card 1
- **Q**: What are the three Triveni Sangams associated with the Banas River system?
- **A**: 
  1. **Bigod (Bhilwara)**: Banas + Bedach + Menal.
  2. **Rajmahal (Tonk/Kekri border)**: Banas + Khari + Dai.
  3. **Rameswaram Ghat (Sawai Madhopur)**: Banas + Chambal + Seep.

### Card 2
- **Q**: What makes the Jojari River unique in the hydrology of Western Rajasthan?
- **A**: It is the only tributary of the Luni River that joins from the right bank, the only one that originates from the non-Aravalli plains (Pondlu, Nagaur), and the only one flowing in a north-to-southwest trajectory.

### Card 3
- **Q**: Name the 4 cascading dams of the Chambal Valley Multipurpose Project, their sequence, and their power capacities.
- **A**: 
  1. **Gandhi Sagar Dam** (Mandsaur, MP; 1960; 115 MW).
  2. **Kota Barrage** (Kota, Rajasthan; 1960; 0 MW — pure irrigation).
  3. **Rana Pratap Sagar Dam** (Rawatbhata, Chittorgarh; 1970; 172 MW — largest storage reservoir in Rajasthan).
  4. **Jawahar Sagar Dam** (Kota/Bundi; 1972; 99 MW — peak load pick-up dam).

### Card 4
- **Q**: What is the Raj Prashasti, where is it located, and what records does it contain?
- **A**: The world's largest stone inscription, engraved on 25 polished black marble slabs on the *Nauchowki ki Pal* of **Rajsamand Lake**. Composed by Ranchhod Bhatt Telang in 24 cantos and 1,106 Sanskrit verses, it chronicles Mewar's history from Bappa Rawal to Maharana Raj Singh, including the 1615 Mughal-Mewar Treaty and dam construction expenses.

### Card 5
- **Q**: Compare the salt harvesting methods and chemical nature of Sambhar, Pachpadra, and Didwana lakes.
- **A**: 
  - **Sambhar**: 8.7% of India's salt; harvested via *Kyār* pans and *Reshta* wind crusts by Sambhar Salts Ltd.; edible.
  - **Pachpadra**: 98% pure $NaCl$; highest culinary purity in India; harvested by traditional Kharwal caste using branches of the *Moroli* bush.
  - **Didwana**: High in Sodium Sulphate ($Na_2SO_4$); non-edible industrial brine harvested in pits called *Dêval*; used for leather tanning and chemicals (Rajasthan State Chemical Works).

[CONTROLLING FACTORS: Subtropical latitude (23°03'N to 30°12'N) ➔ Tropic of Cancer in Banswara/Dungarpur ➔ Aravalli SW-NE strike ➔ Continentality]
                                    │
[MONSOON DYNAMICS: SW Monsoon Arabian Sea Branch (Runs parallel to Aravallis = No orographic barrier = Rain deficit)
                   vs Bay of Bengal Branch (Purvaiya enters from SE/East, sheds moisture on Hadoti & Mewar, sheds little beyond Aravallis)]
                                    │
[WEATHER PHENOMENA: Loo (Hot dry summer advection wind) ➔ Baboolya (Summer convective dust devil) 
                    ➔ Mahawat (Mediterranean Western Disturbances in Dec–Jan = "Golden Drops" for Rabi crops)]
                                    │
[GENERAL CLIMATIC ZONES (5 Zones based on Rainfall & Isohyets)]:
 Arid (<20 cm, Thar) ➔ Semi-Arid (20–40 cm, Bagar) ➔ Sub-Humid (40–60 cm, Aravallis) ➔ Humid (60–80 cm, Eastern Plains) ➔ Very Humid (>80 cm, Hadoti & Mt. Abu)
                                    │
[KÖPPEN SYSTEM (Rainfall + Temp + Veg)]: 
 BWhw (Arid Desert, Xerophytes, Rep: Phalodi/Bikaner) ➔ BShw (Semi-arid Steppe, LARGEST Köppen zone, Rep: Nagaur/Sikar)
 ➔ Cwg (Monsoon Dry Winter, Ganga-type, Rep: Jaipur/Tonk) ➔ Aw (Tropical Savanna, Deciduous, Rep: Banswara/Jhalawar)
                                    │
[THORNTHWAITE SYSTEM (P-E & T-E Indices)]:
 EA'd (Tropical Desert) ➔ DB'w (Semi-arid North/Ganganagar) ➔ DA'w (Semi-arid Mesothermal, LARGEST Thornthwaite zone) ➔ CA'w (Sub-humid South/Hadoti)
                                    │
[10 ICAR AGRO-CLIMATIC ZONES]:
 I-A (Arid NW) ➔ I-B (Irrigated NW) ➔ I-C (Hyper-Arid Irrigated: LARGEST ZONE) 
 ➔ II-A (Transitional Inland) ➔ II-B (Luni Transitional) 
 ➔ III-A (Semi-Arid East) ➔ III-B (Flood Prone East) 
 ➔ IV-A (Sub-Humid Aravalli) ➔ IV-B (Humid Southern: SMALLEST ZONE) ➔ V (Humid SE Hadoti)
```

---20:Td7c,### A. Tripartite Scheme Comparison (General vs Köppen vs Thornthwaite)

| Zone Category | General Scheme (Rainfall) | Köppen Code & Diagnostic Rep. District | Thornthwaite Code & Zone Name | Key Diagnostic Features & Flora |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Arid / Pure Desert** | Arid Zone (<20 cm) | **BWhw** (Rep: Jaisalmer, Phalodi, Bikaner) | **EA'd** (Tropical Arid / Desert) | Extreme heat, xerophytic thorn bushes, scrub (*Phog*, *Kair*, *Khejri*), <20 cm rain. |
| **Semi-Arid / Steppe** | Semi-Arid Zone (20–40 cm) | **BShw** (**LARGEST**; Rep: Nagaur, Sikar, Jodhpur) | **DA'w** (**LARGEST**; Semi-arid Mesothermal) | Steppe grasslands, thorny scrub, high variability, 20–40 cm rain. |
| **Northern Irrigated** | Semi-Arid North | Covered under BShw / BWhw | **DB'w** (Semi-arid Microthermal; Rep: Ganganagar, Hanumangarh) | Canal irrigation dominance, moderate winter temperature. |
| **Sub-Humid / Plains** | Sub-Humid Zone (40–60 cm) | **Cwg** (Rep: Jaipur, Dausa, Alwar, Tonk) | Grouped in DA'w / CA'w | Dhok (*Anogeissus pendula*) forests, mixed deciduous, 50–70 cm rain. |
| **Humid / Savanna** | Very Humid Zone (>80 cm) | **Aw** (Rep: Banswara, Dungarpur, Jhalawar, Mt. Abu) | **CA'w** (Sub-humid / Tropical; Rep: Banswara, Jhalawar, Kota) | Savanna grassland, teak (*Tectona grandis*), bamboo, heavy rainfall (>80–100 cm). |

### B. The 10 ICAR Agro-Climatic Zones of Rajasthan

| Zone Code | Official Name | Representative HQ / Research Stn. | Districts Included (50-District Lens) | Distinctive Agricultural Signature |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| **V** | Humid South-Eastern Plain | Ummedganj (Kota) | Kota, Baran, Bundi, Jhalawar | Chambal command; Black Vertisols; Soyabean, Mustard, Coriander (*Dhaniya*), Garlic, Mandarin Orange. |

---21:Tb05,1. **Why Arabian Sea Monsoon Fails in Western Rajasthan**:
   - The Aravalli mountain axis lies **parallel (SW to NE)** to the incoming Arabian Sea monsoon winds.
   - Hence, winds blow unhindered toward the Himalayas without encountering an orographic barrier to trigger condensation.
2. **Mahawat Causation Trap**:
   - Mahawat is caused by **Mediterranean Western Disturbances (Temperate Cyclones)** brought by the Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream in winter (December–January).
   - It is **NOT** caused by the retreating monsoon or northeast monsoon!
   - Invaluable for **Rabi crops** (Wheat, Mustard, Gram) — termed *"Golden Drops"* (*Mavath*).
3. **Largest Köppen Zone vs Largest Thornthwaite Zone**:
   - Köppen's largest zone by area in Rajasthan: **BShw** (Semi-arid Steppe).
   - Thornthwaite's largest zone by area in Rajasthan: **DA'w** (Semi-arid Mesothermal).
4. **Agro-Climatic Extremes**:
   - **Largest Zone**: **Zone I-C** (Hyper-Arid Partially Irrigated Plain: Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Churu).
   - **Smallest Zone**: **Zone IV-B** (Humid Southern Plain: Banswara, Dungarpur, Pratapgarh, Salumbar).
5. **Rainfall Superlatives (Place vs District)**:
   - **Wettest Place**: **Mount Abu** (~150 cm).
   - **Wettest District**: **Jhalawar** (~100 cm).
   - **Driest Place**: **Sam** (Jaisalmer, <5 cm).
   - **Driest District**: **Jaisalmer** (~10 cm).
6. **Diurnal vs Annual Temperature Range Trap**:
   - **Highest Diurnal Range** (day vs night variance): **Jaisalmer** (coarse sandy soil radiates heat rapidly).
   - **Highest Annual Range** (summer extreme vs winter freeze): **Churu** (records both >48°C and <0°C).
7. **Purvaiya Direction**:
   - *Purvaiya* refers to moisture-bearing easterly winds originating from the **Bay of Bengal branch** entering Rajasthan through Hadoti and the Eastern Plains.
8. **Isohyet Markers**:
   - **50 cm Isohyet**: Separates Western Arid/Semi-Arid plains from the Eastern Plains (runs along the eastern slope of Aravallis).
   - **25 cm Isohyet**: Bisects the desert into Pure Arid Marusthali (<25 cm) and Semi-Arid Bagar (25–50 cm).
   - **10 cm Isohyet**: Represents the westernmost international border fringe of Jaisalmer.
9. **Baboolya vs Loo**:
   - **Loo**: Intense, dry, scorching westerly advection winds blowing during afternoon hours in May–June.
   - **Baboolya**: Intense localized cyclonic whirlwind / convective dust devil created by steep localized pressure differentials.
10. **Tropic of Cancer in Rajasthan**:
    - Passes through southernmost Rajasthan at **23°30' N** latitude for **26 km**.
    - Bisects **Banswara** (passes through Kushalgarh) and touches the southern border of **Dungarpur** (Chikhli village).
    - Sun rays fall perpendicularly on Banswara on June 21st, while Sriganganagar receives the most slanting rays.

---22:T9f9,### Card 1
- **Q**: What are the four Köppen climate codes used for Rajasthan, and which single letter is the primary discriminator?
- **A**: 
  - **BWhw**: Tropical desert arid climate (Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Phalodi).
  - **BShw**: Semi-arid steppe climate (**largest** zone; Jodhpur, Nagaur, Shekhawati).
  - **Cwg**: Sub-humid monsoon dry-winter climate (Eastern plains: Jaipur, Alwar, Sawai Madhopur).
  - **Aw**: Tropical wet & dry savanna climate (Banswara, Dungarpur, Jhalawar, Mount Abu).
  - Primary discriminators: **B** (dry/arid), **C** (warm temperate mesothermal), **A** (megathermal tropical), with **W** (desert) and **S** (steppe).

### Card 2
- **Q**: Explain the meteorological origin and agricultural significance of *Mahawat*.
- **A**: Winter precipitation occurring in December–January caused by temperate cyclonic storms originating over the Mediterranean Sea and transported into NW India by the Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream. Known as "Golden Drops" because it acts as natural elixir for Rabi crops, especially wheat, barley, gram, and mustard.

### Card 3
- **Q**: Which is the largest and which is the smallest Agro-Climatic Zone of Rajasthan under ICAR classification?
- **A**: 
  - **Largest**: **Zone I-C (Hyper-Arid Partially Irrigated Zone)** comprising Bikaner, Jaisalmer, and Churu.
  - **Smallest**: **Zone IV-B (Humid Southern Plain Zone)** comprising Dungarpur, Banswara, Pratapgarh, and Salumbar.

### Card 4
- **Q**: Why does Jhalawar receive the highest district rainfall while Mount Abu receives the highest point rainfall?
- **A**: Mount Abu receives ~150 cm because its high altitude (1,220+ m) forces direct orographic lifting of moisture from the Arabian Sea monsoon branch. Jhalawar receives ~100 cm over the longest rainy spell (40 days) because it sits directly in the entry gateway of the Bay of Bengal monsoon (*Purvaiya*) and receives the tail-end showers of both Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal systems.

### Card 5
- **Q**: Distinguish between the temperature profiles of Jaisalmer and Churu.
- **A**: Jaisalmer has the highest **diurnal** temperature range (greatest fluctuation between day and night due to rapid heating and cooling of porous quartz sand dunes). Churu has the highest **annual** temperature range (greatest divergence between summer heat >48°C and winter sub-zero temperatures <-1°C due to continental interior position, lack of vegetative cover, and calcrete subsoil layers).

---25:T882,1. **IGNP Headworks vs Storage Dam**:
   - IGNP originates at the **Harike Barrage** (diversion weir at the confluence of Satluj and Beas in Punjab).
   - It does **NOT originate at Bhakra Dam** (Bhakra is an upstream storage reservoir on the Satluj).
2. **Zero Irrigation from Rajasthan Feeder**:
   - The first **204 km** of the canal (Rajasthan Feeder) permits **ZERO direct irrigation**; it serves purely as a sealed transit conduit.
   - Irrigation commences strictly at **Masitawali Head (Hanumangarh)**.
3. **The Rawatsar Branch Anomaly**:
   - Of the 9 IGNP branches, **8 branches are on the Right (Western) Bank**, but **Rawatsar Branch is the ONLY branch on the Left Bank**.
   - All 7 lift canals are exclusively on the Left Bank.
4. **IGNP Tail Point Specifics**:
   - Terminal point of the Main Canal: **Mohangarh (Jaisalmer)**.
   - Absolute tail-end of the extended canal command (Baba Ramdev Sub-Branch): **Ghadra Road (Barmer)**.
5. **Narmada Canal Mandatory Micro-Irrigation**:
   - Pressurized drip and sprinkler irrigation is **statutorily mandatory for 100% of the command area**.
   - Traditional flood irrigation is illegal in the Narmada command.
6. **Gang Canal Construction Material**:
   - Built in 1927 with **hydraulic lime-mortar concrete and kankar masonry (*चूना-कंकड़*)**, NOT Portland cement!
7. **The Cause of the Sem Problem**:
   - Waterlogging (*Sem*) in Badopal (Hanumangarh) is caused by an **impermeable subterranean gypsum/calcrete hardpan** at 5–15 m depth, NOT just surplus canal water.
8. **Jhalra Does NOT Harvest Direct Runoff**:
   - A **Jhalra** collects **subterranean seepage (*अंतःस्रवण जल*)** from an adjacent higher lake or tank, NOT surface rainwater runoff directly.
9. **The Tripartite Water Taxonomy**:
   - *Palār Paani*: Direct rainwater runoff.
   - *Pātāl Paani*: Deep groundwater (wells/tube-wells).
   - *Rejāṇi Paani*: Trapped subterranean moisture above the gypsum band, tapped by Kuis.
10. **Modified PKC-ERCP Funding Pattern**:
    - Designated a **National Project** on **28 January 2024** with a **90% Central Government grant : 10% State funding ratio**.

---26:T8f7,### Card 1
- **Q**: What is the structural difference between an IGNP Branch and an IGNP Lift Canal?
- **A**: 
  - **Branches (शाखाएं)**: Flow westward (Right Bank) by natural **gravity** because the terrain slopes downward (exception: Rawatsar Branch on Left Bank).
  - **Lift Canals (लिफ्ट नहरें)**: Flow eastward (Left Bank); water must be **mechanically lifted by 30 to 60 metres** using electric turbine pumps because the terrain rises toward the Aravalli foothills.

### Card 2
- **Q**: Trace the history, dimensions, and entry point of the Rajasthan Feeder canal.
- **A**: Originates at Harike Barrage (Punjab) at the confluence of Satluj and Beas. Total length: 204 km (170 km in Punjab/Haryana, 34 km in Rajasthan). Enters Rajasthan at Kharakhera village (Hanumangarh) and terminates at Masitawali Head. Zero irrigation is allowed along its length.

### Card 3
- **Q**: What is a Khadin, who developed it, and how does it facilitate crop cultivation without irrigation?
- **A**: Developed in 15th-century Jaisalmer by Paliwal Brahmins. An earthen bund (*Dhora*) impounds monsoon runoff in a valley between gravel mounds. After soaking for 2–3 months and depositing fertile silt, the standing water is released or recedes. The retained subsoil moisture is sufficient to mature a high-yield winter Rabi crop (Wheat, Gram, Mustard) without any subsequent irrigation.

### Card 4
- **Q**: Name the oldest and longest IGNP lift canal, its old name, and its popular title.
- **A**: **Kanwarsain Lift Canal** (formerly *Bikaner-Lunkaransar Lift Canal*). Irrigates Bikaner and Sriganganagar; acclaimed as the **"Lifeline of Bikaner"**.

### Card 5
- **Q**: What are the key terms of the Modified PKC-ERCP Link agreement signed on 28 January 2024?
- **A**: Tripartite MoU between Ministry of Jal Shakti, Rajasthan, and Madhya Pradesh integrating the Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal (PKC) link with ERCP. Declared a National Project with 90% Central funding : 10% State funding, providing drinking water to 21 eastern districts up to 2051, new irrigation to 2.8 lakh hectares, and recharging 1,487 traditional water bodies.

---29:T980b,### Part I: Prehistoric Sites, Epigraphy & Medieval Rajput Dynasties
* **Chapter 01: Prehistoric Civilizations, Archaeological Sites & Epigraphic Heritage**
  * Paleolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic sites in Rajasthan: Bagor (Kothari river, Mesolithic animal husbandry proof), Tilwara (Luni basin).
  * Chalcolithic & Bronze Age Civilizations:
    * Ahar-Banas Culture (Dhulkot, Tambavati Nagari, terracotta bulls, black-and-red ware, baking ovens).
    * Ganeshwar (Kantli river, Sikar/Neem Ka Thana, Mother of Copper Cultures, 99% pure copper tools).
    * Kalibangan (Ghaggar river, Hanumangarh, ploughed field, fire altars, grid plan, earthquake evidence).
    * Balathal (Vallabhnagar, Udaipur, woven cloth, copper knives), Gilund (Rajsamand).
  * Iron Age & Historic Civilizations: Bairat (Viratnagar, Ashokan Bhabru edict, Buddhist chaityas, Greek coins), Sunari, Rairh (Tatanagar of Rajasthan), Nagari (Madhyamika), Nagar (Karkot Nagar).
  * Epigraphic Heritage & Inscriptions: Ghosundi Inscription (early Vaishnavism / Bhagavat cult), Bijolia Inscription (Chauhan genealogy, Gotra, ancient place names: Jabalipura, Shakambhari, Mandalgarh), Ranakpur Prashasti, Kumbhalgarh Prashasti, Kiradu Inscriptions.
* **Chapter 02: Early Medieval Dynasties: Gurjara-Pratiharas & Chauhans**
  * Gurjara-Pratiharas: Origin theories, Mandore branch (Harishchandra, Rajjil, Nagabhata I), Bhinmal-Kannauj branch (Vatsaraja and the Tripartite Struggle, Nagabhata II, Mihir Bhoja, Mahendrapala I - court poet Rajasekhara, Mahipala); Administrative titles and temple patronage.
  * Chauhans of Shakambhari & Ajmer: Vasudeva (551 CE, Sambhar salt lake creation), Ajayraja (Ajmer foundation 1113 CE, Ajaymeru fort), Arnoraja (Ana Sagar lake), Vigraharaja IV / Bisaldeo (Harkeli drama, Sanskrit college / Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra, golden age), Prithviraja III (Battles of Tarain 1191 & 1192 CE, digvijaya policy, Chand Bardai).
  * Chauhans of Ranthambore: Govindaraja (1194 CE), Hammiradeva (1282–1301 CE, "Hammir Hatth", resistance against Jalaluddin & Alauddin Khalji, 1301 CE siege, first Jauhar of Rajasthan).
  * Chauhans of Jalore: Kirtipala (Kitu ek mahan Rajput), Kanhadadeva (1308 Siwana siege / Sataldeo, 1311 Jalore siege / Alauddin Khalji, Padmanabha's *Kanhadade Prabandha*).
* **Chapter 03: The Guhils & Sisodias of Mewar**
  * Guhil foundations: Guhaditya (566 CE), Bappa Rawal (734 CE, captured Chittor from Man Mori, Nagda capital, Eklingji temple), Jaitra Singh (Battle of Bhutala 1227 CE against Iltutmish, shifted capital to Chittor).
  * Rawal Ratan Singh & 1303 CE Chittor Siege (Alauddin Khalji, Rani Padmini's Jauhar, Khizr Khan).
  * Rana Hammir (1326 CE, Rana branch/Sisodia foundation, "Vishama Ghati Panchanan").
  * Maharana Kumbha (1433–1468 CE): Battles of Sarangpur (1437 CE), Treaty of Champaner (1456 CE), construction of 32 of 84 forts (Shyamaldas's *Vir Vinod*), Vijay Stambha (architects: Jaita, Napa, Poma, Punja), literary works (*Sangitaraja*, *Sangitamimamsa*, *Rasikapriya* commentary).
  * Maharana Sanga (1509–1528 CE): Unification of Rajput confederacy, battles of Khatoli, Dholpur, Gagron, Bayana (Feb 1527), and Battle of Khanwa (March 1527, Babur, cannonry, tulghuma tactics, wounded warrior).
  * Maharana Pratap (1572–1597 CE): Coronation at Gogunda, Mughal diplomatic missions (Jalal Khan, Man Singh, Bhagwan Das, Todar Mal), Battle of Haldighati (June 1576, commanders, Hakim Khan Sur, Jhala Manna, Chetak), Guerrilla warfare, Battle of Dewair (1582, "Marathon of Mewar"), Chavand capital, architectural & artistic renaissance.
  * Maharana Amar Singh I (Mughal-Mewar Treaty 1615 CE) & Maharana Raj Singh (Battle of Debari, Rajsamand Lake, Charumati episode, patron of Srinathji temple Nathdwara).
* **Chapter 04: The Rathores of Marwar & Bikaner**
  * Marwar: Rao Siha (founder), Rao Chunda (Mandore capital), Rao Jodha (1459 CE Jodhpur foundation, Mehrangarh fort), Rao Maldeo (1531–1562 CE, "Hashmat Vala Raja", battle of Paheba, battle of Giri-Sumel 1544 against Sher Shah Suri).
  * Rao Chandrasen (1562–1581 CE, "The Forgotten Hero", "Pratap of Marwar", Nagaur Court 1570 boycott, Bhadrajun & Siwana resistance).
  * Mota Raja Udai Singh, Maharaja Jaswant Singh I (Battle of Dharmat 1658, court scholars, *Bhasha Bhushan*), Durgadas Rathore and the 30-Year Rathore-Mughal War for Maharaja Ajit Singh.
  * Bikaner: Rao Bika (1465/1488 CE Bikaner foundation), Rao Jaitasi (Battle of Rati-Ghati against Kamran), Rai Singh ("Karna of Rajputana", Junagarh fort, Prithviraj Rathore and *Veli Krishan Rukmani Ri*), Anup Singh (Anup Sanskrit Library).
* **Chapter 05: The Kachhwahas of Amber-Jaipur & Allied Dynasties**
  * Kachhwahas of Amber: Dulherai (1137 CE), Bharmal (1562 Sambhar alliance with Akbar), Bhagwan Das, Man Singh I (Mughal mansabdar of 7000, Bengal/Bihar/Kabul campaigns, Shila Devi temple, Amer palaces).
  * Mirza Raja Jai Singh (served 3 Mughal emperors, Treaty of Purandar 1665 with Shivaji, Bihari Lal's *Bihari Satsai*).
  * Sawai Jai Singh II (1700–1743 CE): Foundation of Jaipur (1727 CE, Vidyadhar Bhattacharya), Jantar Mantar observatories (Jaipur, Delhi, Mathura, Ujjain, Varanasi), Ashvamedha Yajna, Hurda Conference (1734 CE).
  * Sawai Pratap Singh (Hawa Mahal 1799, Ustad Lal Chand, Gandharva Baisi), Sawai Ram Singh II (Pink City coloring, Maharaja College).
  * Allied Dynasties: Bhatis of Jaisalmer (Jaisal 1156 CE, Sonar Kila, 2.5 Sākas), Hadas of Bundi and Kota (Rao Deva, Surjan Hada, Shatrushal, Zalim Singh Jhala), Jats of Bharatpur (Badan Singh, Maharaja Suraj Mal - "Plato of the Jat Tribe", Lohagarh Fort).

### Part II: Colonial Impact, Resistance & Modern Awakening
* **Chapter 06: British Treaties of 1818 & The 1857 Revolution in Rajasthan**
  * Subordinate Alliance Treaties of 1818: Causes (Maratha-Pindari devastation, succession disputes), Lord Hastings & Charles Metcalfe, treaty provisions, states sequence (Karauli 1st, Sirohi last 1823), Political Agents.
  * 1857 Revolution: 6 British Cantonments (Naseerabad, Neemuch, Deoli, Beawar, Erinpura, Kherwara - note Beawar & Kherwara did not participate), Naseerabad outbreak (28 May 1857, 15th Bengal Native Infantry), Neemuch outbreak (3 June 1857, Mohammad Ali Beg), Erinpura & "Chalo Dilli, Maro Firangi" (21 August 1857).
  * Auwa's Resistance: Thakur Kushal Singh, Battle of Bithoda (8 Sept 1857), Battle of Chelawas / "Battle of Black and White" (18 Sept 1857, Monk Mason killed), Brigadier Holmes' attack on Auwa (Jan 1858), Sugali Mata idol.
  * Kotah Revolt: Mass rebellion without military cantonment, Jaidayal & Mehrab Khan, execution of Major Burton, captivity of Maharao Ram Singh II.
* **Chapter 07: Peasant & Agrarian Movements**
  * Bijolia Peasant Movement (1897–1941, Mewar): 84 types of taxes (Lāg-Bāg), Chanwari Tax (Rao Krishna Singh, 1903), Talwar Bandhai Tax (Rao Prithvi Singh, 1906); Phase 1 (1897–1915, Sadhu Sitaram Das, Nanji-Thakari Patel); Phase 2 (1916–1923, Vijay Singh Pathik / Bhoop Singh, Uparmal Panch Board 1917, *Pratap* newspaper by Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi); Phase 3 (1923–1941, Manikya Lal Verma, Jamnalal Bajaj, agreement with Sir T. Raghavachari).
  * Bengu Peasant Movement (1921–1925): Ramnarayan Chaudhary, Rupa Ji and Kripa Ji Dhakar martyrdom (Govindpura firing by Trench).
  * Bundi (Barad) Peasant Movement: Nanak Ji Bhil martyrdom (Dabi firing 1923, Jhanda Geet).
  * Nimuchana Massacre (Alwar, 14 May 1925): Wild boar problem and tax hike, Gandhi described as "Dyerism Double Distilled".
  * Shekhawati Peasant Movement: Panchpana landlords, Katrathal Women's Conference (1934, Kishori Devi, 10,000 peasant women).
* **Chapter 08: Tribal Awakening Movements**
  * Bhagat Movement: Govind Guru (Banjara family, Vedsa village), establishment of Samp Sabha (1883), 10 rules, Mangarh Dham Massacre (17 Nov 1913, Mewar Bhil Corps firing, 1500 Bhils martyred, "Jallianwala Bagh of Rajasthan").
  * Eki Movement (Matrikundiya, Rashmi, Chittor 1921): Motilal Tejawat ("Bavji"), 21-point demand charter ("Mewar Ki Pukar"), Neemra firing (1922).
  * Meena Movement: Criminal Tribes Act (1871) and Jairam Pesha Act (1930), daily police roll-call requirement, Meena Kshatriya Sabha (1933), Muni Magan Sagar's Meena Mahasabha (1944 Neem Ka Thana), abolition of Jairam Pesha (1952).
* **Chapter 09: Prajamandal Movements & Modern Awakening**
  * Foundation and chronological matrix: Marwar Prajamandal (1934, Jai Narayan Vyas, Bhanwarlal Saraf), Mewar Prajamandal (1938, Manikya Lal Verma, Balwant Singh Mehta), Jaipur Prajamandal (1931 Kapur Chand Patni / 1936 Jamnalal Bajaj), Bikaner Prajamandal (1936 Magharam Vaidya in Calcutta), Kota Prajamandal (1939 Nayanuram Sharma), Sirohi (Gokulbhai Bhatt).
  * Gentlemen's Agreement (1942, Jaipur): Mirza Ismail and Hiralal Shastri, non-participation in Quit India Movement; dissent and Azad Morcha (Baba Harish Chandra).
  * Women's Role: Anjana Devi Chaudhary, Ratna Shastri, Narayani Devi Verma, Kalibai (Rastapal sacrifice 1947), Nagendra Bala.
  * Role of Press: *Tyagbhoomi*, *Aagiwan*, *Tarun Rajasthan*, *Naveen Rajasthan*, *Rajasthan Kesari*.
* **Chapter 10: The Unification of Rajasthan (1948–1956)**
  * The 7 Stages Complete Matrix:
    1. Matsya Union (18 March 1948): Alwar, Bharatpur, Dholpur, Karauli + Neemrana; Capital: Alwar; Rajpramukh: Udaybhan Singh (Dholpur); PM: Shobharam Kumawat; Named by K.M. Munshi.
    2. Former Rajasthan / Rajasthan Union (25 March 1948): 9 states (Banswara, Bundi, Dungarpur, Jhalawar, Kota, Pratapgarh, Shahpura, Tonk, Kishangarh) + Kushalgarh; Capital: Kota; Rajpramukh: Bhim Singh (Kota); PM: Gokul Lal Asawa.
    3. United Rajasthan (18 April 1948): Rajasthan Union + Udaipur (Mewar); Capital: Udaipur; Rajpramukh: Bhupal Singh; PM: Manikya Lal Verma; Inaugurated by Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru.
    4. Greater Rajasthan (30 March 1948 - Rajasthan Day): United Rajasthan + Jaipur, Jodhpur, Bikaner, Jaisalmer; Capital: Jaipur; Maharajpramukh: Bhupal Singh; Rajpramukh: Man Singh II; PM: Hiralal Shastri; Patel Committee (P. Satyanarayan Rao Committee) recommendations on high court, capital, education.
    5. United Greater Rajasthan (15 May 1949): Greater Rajasthan + Matsya Union; Dr. Shankar Rao Deo Committee recommendations.
    6. Rajasthan Union (26 January 1950): Inclusion of Sirohi (excluding Delwara & Abu); Name officially became "Rajasthan".
    7. Reorganized Rajasthan (1 November 1956): Fazal Ali State Reorganization Commission; Inclusion of Abu-Delwara, Ajmer-Merwara, Sunel Tappa of MP; Sironj sub-district transferred to MP; Abolition of Rajpramukh post, first Governor: Gurmukh Nihal Singh.

### Part III: Art, Architecture, Performing Arts & Cultural Heritage
* **Chapter 11: Fort Architecture of Rajasthan**
  * Classification (Kautilya & Shukraniti: Giri, Jal, Dhanvan, Vana, Sainya, Parikha, Paridha).
  * UNESCO 6 Hill Forts of Rajasthan (Inscribed 2013: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron, Amber, Jaisalmer).
  * Architectural Anatomy & Bastions:
    * Chittorgarh: Largest living fort, 7 gates (Padan Pol to Ram Pol), Vijay Stambha, Kirti Stambha, 3 Sākas (1303, 1535, 1568).
    * Kumbhalgarh: 36 km wall (second longest in world), Katargarh (Eye of Mewar), birthplace of Maharana Pratap.
    * Gagron: Water fort (Jal Durg) at confluence of Ahu and Kali Sindh, Achaldas Khichi ri Vachanika, Jauhar 1423.
    * Mehrangarh: Mayuradhwaja Durg, Chintamani, Chamunda Mata temple, cannons (Kilkila, Shambhuban, Gajni Khan).
    * Junagarh: "Zameen Ka Geona", Suraj Pol, Anup Mahal, Karan Mahal.
* **Chapter 12: Palaces, Havelis, Baoris, Chhatris & Temples**
  * Havelis: Patwon ki Haveli (5-storey stone carving), Salim Singh ki Haveli (Jahaz Mahal), Nathmal ki Haveli (architect brothers Hathi and Lalu); Shekhawati Havelis (fresco wall paintings, gold leaf work).
  * Baoris (Stepwells): Chand Baori (Abhaneri, 3,500 steps, Harshat Mata temple), Raniji ki Baori (Bundi, "City of Stepwells"), Neemrana Baori.
  * Chhatris (Cenotaphs): 84-Pillared Chhatri (Bundi), Moosi Maharani Chhatri (Alwar), Bada Bagh (Jaisalmer), Gaitore (Jaipur kings), Jaswant Thada ("Taj Mahal of Marwar").
  * Temple Architecture: Gurjara-Pratihara / Maha-Maru style (Osian temples: Sachiya Mata, Surya temple; Kiradu temples: "Khajuraho of Rajasthan"; Harshat Mata Abhaneri); Jain Temples (Dilwara 5 temples: Vimal Vasahi, Luna Vasahi; Ranakpur: 1444 pillars, Dharanashah, architect Depaka).
* **Chapter 13: Schools of Rajasthani Painting**
  * Classification (Anand Coomaraswamy's *Rajput Painting* 1916).
  * Mewar School: Udaipur sub-style (Sahibdin, Manohar, *Arsha Ramayana*), Nathdwara sub-style (Pichhwai painting on cloth, women artists: Kamala & Ilaichi), Chavand sub-style (Nasiruddin, *Dhak* ragamala).
  * Marwar School: Jodhpur style (yellow/red palette, spiral clouds), Kishangarh style (Golden Age under Savant Singh / Nagari Das, master painter Nihal Chand, *Bani Thani* - "Indian Mona Lisa"), Bikaner style (Usta and Mathewarn art, Muslim artists, signatures on paintings).
  * Dhundhar School: Amer style, Jaipur style (Suratkhana, large portraits, Sahibram, Mohammad Shah), Alwar style (elephant tusk paintings, miniature courtesan portraits), Shekhawati fresco paintings.
  * Hadoti School: Bundi style (bird and animal representation, lush vegetation, *Chitrashala* by Ummed Singh), Kota style (hunting scenes with women hunting, Vallabh sect influence).
* **Chapter 14: Folk Performing Arts**
  * Folk Dances:
    * Professional & Commercial: Terah Taali (Kamad sect women for Ramdevji, 13 cymbals/manjiras, Mangi Bai), Bhawai (balance brass pots on head, Dayaram, Rup Singh), Kalbelia (UNESCO 2010, Gulabo Bai, Pungi instrument), Chari dance (Gujjar women, brass pot with burning cottonseeds, Falqu Bai).
    * Tribal Dances: Bhil dances (Gair, Neja, Yudh, Dwichakri, Ghumra); Garasia dances (Valar - without instrument, Lur, Mandal, Moria, Walo); Sahariya dances (Shikari, Chhail); Kanjod dances (Chakri, Dhakad).
    * Regional: Ghoomar (State dance, "Soul of Rajasthani dance"), Agni dance (Jasnathi sect at Katariyasar, dance on burning embers shouting "Fateh-Fateh"), Dhol dance (Jalore, Thākna style, sponsored by Jai Narayan Vyas), Bam dance (Bharatpur-Alwar, big drum Bam), Kacchi Ghodi (Shekhawati wooden horse dance).
  * Folk Theatre (Khyal): Turra-Kalangi (Tukangir & Shah Ali, Shiva-Shakti dialogue, non-scripted, Chanderi origin), Kuchamani Khyal (Lachhiram), Shekhawati Khyal (Nanu Ram, Duliyarana), Tamasha (Jaipur, Banshidhar Bhatt, Phoolji Bhatt), Rammat (Bikaner-Jaisalmer, Patta culture, Maharaj Tej Kavi's *Swatantra Bavani* gifted to Gandhi), Gavari / Rai (Bhil mythological drama of Shiva & Bhasmasur, 40 days in Bhadrapada).
  * Musical Instruments:
    * Tata (Stringed): Sarangi (King of instruments), Rawanhattha (coconut shell, played during Pabuji ki Phad), Kamayacha (Manganiyars), Jantar (played with Devnarayanji ki Phad), Tandura / Ektara.
    * Sushira (Wind): Algoza (State instrument, twin flutes), Pungi, Shehnai, Bankiya, Bhungal, Mashak.
    * Avanaddha (Membranophone): Mridang / Pakhawaj, Dhol, Chang, Khanjari, Daph, Damru, Mandal.
    * Ghana (Idiophone): Manjira, Khartal (Siddique Khan Manganiyar), Thali, Chimta, Jhalar.
* **Chapter 15: Folk Deities, Saints & Religious Movements**
  * The Panchpir:
    1. Pabu Ji: Born Kolumand (Phalodi), camel protector (brought camels/sandhis to Marwar), Rebaris worship him, Pabuji ki Phad (longest phad, Rawanhattha, Nayak Bhopas), Pabuji ra Pavade (Mathe instrument), died fighting Jind Rao Khichi for Deval Charni's cows.
    2. Ramdev Ji: Born Runducha/Pokhran, Tanwar Rajput, Runicha fair (Bhadrapada Shukla 2 to 11), Samadhi at Ramdevra, founded Kamadiya sect, authored *Chaubis Vaniya*, Terah Taali dance, communal harmony, white horse (Leela).
    3. Goga Ji: Born Dadrewa (Churu), snake protector deity, fought Mahmud of Ghazni ("Jahir Peer"), Top: Dhurmedi (Nohar, Hanumangarh, built like mosque by Firoz Shah Tughlaq with Bismillah inscribed), Shirshmedi (Dadrewa), Goga Navami.
    4. Harbhuji: Sankhla Rajput, vehicle is cart (Chhakada Gadi), blessed Rao Jodha with Katari to regain Mandore, temple at Bengti (Phalodi).
    5. Mehaji Manglia: Temple at Bapini (Jodhpur/Phalodi), horse: Kirad Kabra, Janmashtami fair.
  * Other Folk Deities: Tejaji (Born Karnal, Nagaur, cow protector, snakebite at Sursura, fair at Parbatsar), Devnarayan Ji (Gurjar deity, incarnation of Vishnu, Phad read with Jantar, neem leaves offering), Mallinath Ji (Tilwara, Barmer cattle fair), Veer Kallaji (Four-armed deity of 1568 Chittor battle).
  * Lok Deviyan: Karni Mata (Deshnok, white rats / Kabas), Shila Devi (Amer, brought from Jasore by Man Singh I), Jeen Mata (Rewasa, Sikar, longest song / Chirja), Tanot Mata (Soldiers' goddess, Jaisalmer), Sheetla Mata (Chaksu, donkey vehicle, cold food / Basoda).
  * Saints & Panths: Jambhoji (1451 Pipasar, founded Bishnoi sect with 29 rules at Samrathal Dhora, animal/tree protection), Jasnathji (Katariyasar, 36 rules, Gorakhnath disciple), Dadu Dayal ("Rajasthan's Kabir", Naraina/Jaipur headquarters, 52 pillars/disciples, Sundardas, Rajjabji), Mirabai (Rathore of Merta, married Bhojraj of Mewar, Bhakti poetry), Saint Mavji (Baneshwar Dham founder, Chopra texts).
* **Chapter 16: Fairs, Festivals, Customs, Ornaments, Costumes & Literature**
  * Fairs & Festivals: Pushkar Fair (Kartik Purnima), Gangaur (Chaitra Shukla 3, Shiva-Parvati worship, 18 days), Teej (Shravan Shukla 3 - Hariyali Teej in Jaipur; Kajli Teej in Bundi - Bhadrapada Krishna 3), Sheetla Ashtami (Chaitra Krishna 8), Baneshwar Fair (Tribal Kumbh, Som-Mahi-Anas confluence, Magh Purnima).
  * Customs & Sanskars: 16 Sanskars; Marriage customs (Bindoli, Samela, Toran, Barāt, Dapa, Natra); Mourning rituals (Mosar/Nukta, Badhar).
  * Traditional Ornaments (Head: Rakhdi, Borla, Sheeshfool; Neck: Timaniya, Champakali, Hansli, Thussi; Nose: Nath, Besri; Hand: Chuda, Hathphool, Damna; Foot: Pajeb, Jhanjhar, Kadla).
  * Rajasthani Literature & Dialects: Dingal (Western Rajasthani bardic poetry) vs. Pingal (Eastern Rajasthani mixed with Braj); Major works: *Prithviraj Raso* (Chand Bardai), *Vansh Bhaskar* (Suryamal Misran), *Kanhadade Prabandha* (Padmanabha), *Batān ri Phulwari* (Vijaydan Detha), *Dharti Dhoran Ri* & *Pāthal aur Peethal* (Kanhaiyalal Sethia); 5 Major Dialects: Marwari, Dhundhari, Haroti, Mewati, Malvi.
* **Chapter 17: Traditional Handicrafts & GI Tags of Rajasthan**
  * Crafts: Thewa Art (Gold foil on colored glass, Pratapgarh, Soni family, Padma Shri awards), Blue Pottery (Jaipur, glazed pottery introduced from Turko-Persia by Man Singh I / patronized by Ram Singh II, Kripal Singh Shekhawat), Usta Art (Camel hide gold embossing, Bikaner, Hisamuddin Usta), Tarkashi (Silver wire inlay, Nathdwara).
  * Textiles & Printing: Sanganeri Print (Natural dyes on white base), Bagru Print (Dabu resist print, red & black), Akola Print (Dabu print of Chittor), Bandhej / Tie & Dye (Jaipur, Jodhpur), Lehariya and Mothada, Kota Doria (Masuria weaving).
  * All GI Tags of Rajasthan (Pokhran Pottery, Blue Pottery, Sanganeri, Bagru, Kota Doria, Thewa, Kathputli, Bikaner Usta, Kashidakari, Nathdwara Pichhwai).

### Part IV: Morphotectonic Divisions, Drainage & Environment
* **Chapter 18: Morphotectonic Divisions of Rajasthan**
  * 4 Master Divisions:
    1. Western Sandy Plain (61.11% area, 40% population, arid & semi-arid): Great Desert (Marusthali), Sand dune typology (Barkhan / crescent dunes, Seif, Longitudinal, Transverse), Reg, Hamada, Semi-Arid Transitional Plain (Rajasthan Bagar): Luni Basin (Godwar), Shekhawati Internal Drainage, Nagauri Upland (Kobar Patti / Fluorosis belt), Ghaggar Plain.
    2. Aravalli Mountain Region (9% area, 10% population, oldest fold mountains, pre-Cambrian): North Aravalli (Raghunathgarh 1055m, Babai, Bairat), Central Aravalli (Taragarh, Goramji 934m, Moramji), South Aravalli (Abu block, Guru Shikhar 1722m, Ser 1597m, Dilwara 1442m, Jarga 1431m, Achalgarh 1380m, Kumbhalgarh 1224m); Major Passes (Ghats): Desuri, Hathi, Someshwar, Jhilwa.
    3. Eastern Plains (23% area, 39% population, fertile alluvium): Banas Basin (Mewar Plain & Malpura-Karauli Plain), Chhappan Basin / Mahi Plain (56 villages/streams between Banswara-Pratapgarh), Chambal Basin (Badland topography / Bīhad / Ravines).
    4. South-Eastern Hadoti Plateau (6.89% area, 11% population, Deccan lava & Vindhyan scarpland): Vindhyan Scarpland (Sandstone), Deccan Lava Plateau (Black regur soil), Shahbad Upland (horseshoe hill), Mukundara Hills.
* **Chapter 19: Drainage Systems of Rajasthan**
  * Hydrographic Divide: Aravalli Range acting as the Great Indian Water Divide (50 cm isohyet).
  * Three Drainage Classifications:
    1. Arabian Sea Drainage (17%): Luni River (Origin: Nag Pahar Ajmer, sweet water till Balotra, tributaries: Sukri, Bandi, Jawai, Guhiya, Lilri, Jojari - only right-bank tributary not from Aravalli), Mahi River (Origin: Amjhoru MP, crosses Tropic of Cancer twice, "Ganga of Kanthal", tributaries: Som, Jakham, Anas), Sabarmati, West Banas.
    2. Bay of Bengal Drainage (23%): Chambal River (Origin: Janapav MP, only perennial river, waterfalls: Chulia 18m, dams: Gandhi Sagar MP, Rana Pratap Sagar Chittorgarh, Jawahar Sagar, Kota Barrage), Banas River ("Varnasha" / Hope of Forest, Origin: Khamnor hills Rajsamand, confluence at Rameswaram Ghat Sawai Madhopur, tributaries: Berach, Bedach, Kothari, Khari, Morel), Gambhir, Banganga (Arjun ki Ganga).
    3. Inland Drainage System (60% - largest): Ghaggar River ("Saraswati / Dead River", Origin: Shivalik HP, enters Tibbi Hanumangarh, flood reaches Fort Abbas Pakistan), Kantli River (Origin: Khandela Sikar, inland flow in Torawati), Sabi (Origin: Sewar hills, enters Haryana), Ruparel (Origin: Udainath hills Alwar), Mendha, Rupangarh.
  * Lakes: Salt Lakes (Sambhar - 8.7% of India's salt, Didwana, Pachpadra - 98% NaCl, Lunkaransar); Freshwater Lakes (Jaisamand / Dhebar Lake - largest artificial lake, 7 islands: Babaka Bhagra, Pyari; Rajsamand - Raj Prashasti in 25 marble slabs by Ranchhod Bhatt; Pichhola - Jag Niwas & Jag Mandir, Natni ka Chabutra; Fateh Sagar; Nakki Lake - highest lake, toad rock, nun rock).
* **Chapter 20: Water Infrastructure & Major Canals**
  * Indira Gandhi Canal Project (IGNP): Origin: Harike Barrage (confluence of Satluj & Beas), Feeder canal (204 km: 170 km in Punjab/Haryana, 34 km in Rajasthan), Main canal (445 km till Mohangarh Jaisalmer, tail at Ghadra Road Barmer); 7 Lift Canals (Bikaner-Lunkaransar/Kanwarsain, Gandheli-Sahawa, Gajner, Kolayat, Phalodi, Pokhran, Jodhpur) and 9 Branches; Benefits and problems (waterlogging, Sem problem, salinity).
  * Eastern Rajasthan Canal Project (ERCP / Modified PKC Link): Interlinking Parbati, Kalisindh, and Chambal to address drinking/irrigation water across 21 eastern districts.
  * Narmada Canal Project: Origin: Sardar Sarovar Dam Gujarat, enters Silu (Sanchore/Jalore), total 458 km, first project in India where **drip/sprinkler irrigation is mandatory**.
  * Bisalpur Dam: On Banas river in Tonk, lifeline drinking water for Jaipur, Ajmer, Tonk.
  * Traditional Water Harvesting Systems: Tanka, Khadin (Paliwal Brahmins of Jaisalmer), Baori, Jhalra, Nadi, Kui/Beri, Tobha, Paar system.
* **Chapter 21: Climate, Agro-Climatic Zones & Soils**
  * Climate Attributes: Extreme continental climate, erratic rainfall (10 cm in Jaisalmer to 100 cm in Jhalawar - wettest district; Mount Abu - wettest place 150 cm); Isohyets: 25 cm separates Marusthali from Bagar, 50 cm divides Western arid from Eastern humid.
  * Climatological Classifications:
    * Koeppen: BWhw (Arid hot desert), BShw (Semi-arid steppe), Cwg (Sub-humid monsoon with dry winter), Aw (Tropical wet & dry - Hadoti, Banswara).
    * Thornthwaite (CA'w, DA'w, DB'w, EA'd) and Trewartha.
  * The 10 Agro-Climatic Zones of Rajasthan: I-A (Arid Western), I-B (Irrigated North-Western Plain), I-C (Hyper Arid Partially Irrigated), II-A (Internal Drainage Dry Zone), II-B (Transitional Plain of Luni Basin), III-A (Semi-Arid Eastern Plain), III-B (Flood Prone Eastern Plain), IV-A (Sub-Humid Southern Plain & Aravalli Hills), IV-B (Humid Southern Plain), V (Humid South-Eastern Plain).
  * Soils: ICAR classification (Desert soils, Red-yellow, Black/Regur, Alluvial, Brown); Modern USDA Taxonomy: Aridisols (Western arid), Entisols (All across desert), Alfisols (Eastern plains), Inceptisols (Aravalli & sub-humid), Vertisols (Black clayey Hadoti plateau).
* **Chapter 22: Forest Cover, Wildlife & Biodiversity Conservation**
  * Forest Profile (ISFR 2023 Analysis): Total Recorded Forest Area (RFA: 32,863 sq km ~ 9.60% of state); Legal Classification: Reserved Forests (37%), Protected Forests (56%), Unclassed Forests (7%); Actual Forest Cover (16,654 sq km ~ 4.87%); Top forest districts (Udaipur, Alwar, Pratapgarh); Lowest (Churu, Hanumangarh).
  * State Symbols: State Tree: Khejri (*Prosopis cineraria*, Kalpvriksha, 1983); State Flower: Rohida (*Tecomella undulata*, 1983); State Animal (Wild): Chinkara (*Gazella bennettii*, 1981); State Animal (Domestic): Camel (2014); State Bird: Godawan / Great Indian Bustard (*Ardeotis nigriceps*, 1981, Critically Endangered).
  * Protected Area Network:
    * National Parks (3): Ranthambore (1980), Keoladeo Ghana (1981, UNESCO World Heritage, Ramsar Site), Mukundara Hills (2012).
    * Tiger Reserves (5): Ranthambore (1973), Sariska (1978), Mukundara Hills (2013), Ramgarh Vishdhari (Bundi, 2022 - 52nd in India), Dholpur-Karauli (2023 - 54th in India).
    * Ramsar Wetland Sites (2): Keoladeo Ghana (1981) and Sambhar Lake (1990).
    * Conservation Reserves: Bisalpur, Joda Beed, Gogelao, Beed Jhunjhunu, Mansa Mata, Rotu, Jawai Bandh (Leopards), Shahbad Jungle, Hamirgadh.
* **Chapter 23: Mineral Wealth, Hydrocarbons & Renewable Energy**
  * Mineral Profile ("Museum of Minerals"): Rajasthan produces 81 varieties (57 commercially exploited); Monopoly / Sole Producer in India: Lead & Zinc (Zawar, Rampura Agucha - world's richest zinc mine, Rajpura Dariba), Wollastonite (100%), Jasper (100%), Selenite (100%), Garnet (Tamra/Raktmani), Calcite, Gypsum (Jamsar Bikaner).
  * Non-Metallic & Building Stones: Makrana Marble (White calcitic), Yellow Sandstone (Jaisalmer), Red Sandstone (Dholpur/Karauli), Kota Stone, Granite (Jalore - Granite City).
  * Hydrocarbon Architecture: 4 Petroliferous Basins across 14 districts:
    1. Barmer-Sanchore Basin (Mangala - first commercial oil field 2004, Bhagyam, Aishwarya, Saraswati, Raageshwari).
    2. Jaisalmer Basin (Natural gas: Tanot, Dandewala, Gamnewala, Manhera Tibba).
    3. Bikaner-Nagaur Basin (Heavy oil: Poonam, Baghewala).
    4. Rajasthan Shelf / Vindhyan Basin (Kota, Jhalawar, Baran).
    * Pachpadra Oil Refinery (HPCL Rajasthan Refinery Ltd - HRRL: 74:26 JV, 9 MMTPA capacity, BS-VI petrochemical complex).
  * Renewable Energy Leadership:
    * Solar Energy: Rajasthan ranks #1 in India; Bhadla Solar Park (Phalodi, 2245 MW - world's largest contiguous solar park), Fatehgarh, Nokh; State Solar Policy targets.
    * Wind Energy: Jaisalmer ("Wind City"), Pratapgarh, Phalodi.

### 1. The Lower Paleolithic Epoch (Handaxe-Cleaver Horizon)
* **First Discovery**: In 1870, **C.A. Hackett** discovered the first Acheulian Paleolithic stone handaxe (*कुठार*) in Rajasthan from **Jaipur** and **Indragarh** (Bundi district). Subsequent discoveries were made by Seton-Karr in Jhalawar.
* **Western Arid Corridor (Didwana & Jayal Formations)**: Excavations led by **Dr. V.N. Misra** and S.N. Rajaguru established the *Jayal-Didwana Acheulian sequence* in Nagaur. The calcareous conglomerate gravel beds at 16R (Didwana) proved human habitation dating back over 390,000 years.
* **Mewar & Hadoti River Terraces**: Abundant Lower Paleolithic handaxes and cleavers made of local quartzite were recovered along the Berach, Gambhiri, Wagan, Bamani, and Chambal river valleys (Chittorgarh, Kota, Jhalawar).

### 2. The Middle & Upper Paleolithic Transitions
* **Middle Paleolithic (Nevasian Flake Industry)**: Dominated by fine-grained chert, jasper, and agate flakes rather than crude quartzite. Major concentrations lie along the Luni valley (Pali, Barmer, Jodhpur) and Pushkar lakes (Budha Pushkar, Hokra).
* **Upper Paleolithic (Blade-Burin Horizon)**: Characterized by parallel-sided blade production and burins. The sand dunes of Budha Pushkar and Didwana document early arid hunter-gatherer adaptation.

### 3. The Mesolithic Master-Sites: Bagor & Tilwara

#### A. Bagor Civilization (Maha Satiyan Mound)
* **Geographical Locator**: Situated on the **Kothari River**, approximately 25 km west of Bhilwara.
* **Excavation Leadership**: Excavated between **1967 and 1970** jointly by **Dr. V.N. Misra** (Deccan College, Pune) and **Dr. L.S. Leshnik** (Heidelberg University, Germany).
* **Stratigraphy & Material Culture (Three Phases)**:
  * **Phase I (c. 5000–2800 BCE - Pure Mesolithic)**:
    * Characterized by millions of tiny, geometrically crafted **microliths** (triangles, lunates, trapezes, bladelets) made of quartz and chert.
    * Stone-paved floors with stone boundary alignments serving as living huts.
    * **Faunal Evidence of Animal Husbandry**: Along with Adamgarh (Hoshangabad, MP), Bagor provides the **earliest undisputed scientific evidence of animal domestication in the Indian subcontinent** (bones of sheep, goats, and humped cattle showing butcher cut-marks).
  * **Phase II (c. 2800–600 BCE - Copper Contact)**: Appearance of copper tools (3 arrowheads, a spearhead, awls) alongside stone microliths, indicating trade contacts with the Ahar-Banas chalcolithic cultures; introduction of handmade pottery.
  * **Phase III (c. 600 BCE–200 CE - Iron Age)**: Iron tools, wheel-thrown pottery, and extended burials.
* **Burial Practices**: Dead bodies buried inside living floors; oriented strictly **East-West** in Phase I with legs bent, and **West-East** in Phase II with elaborate grave goods (pots, copper tools, ornaments).

#### B. Tilwara (Luni River Basin)
* **Geographical Locator**: Situated on the banks of the **Luni River** in **Balotra district** (historically Barmer district).
* **Excavator**: Excavated in **1967–68** by **Dr. V.N. Misra**.
* **Material Findings**: Microlithic industry similar to Bagor; circular living huts with packed clay floors; ash layers containing burnt bones of domesticated cattle, sheep, and wild game; circular fire-hearths with coarse handmade pottery.

### I. The Ahar-Banas Culture (The Copper Smelting Metropolis)

```text
[CHRONOLOGY: c. 2100 BCE – 1500 BCE | GEOGRAPHY: Berach/Banas Valley, South-East Rajasthan]
```

#### 1. Historical & Epigraphic Nomenclature
* **Ancient Inscriptional Designation**: In ancient Sanskrit records, the settlement is designated as **Tambavati Nagari** (ताम्रवती नगरी — The City of Copper) due to its specialized copper-smelting industry.
* **Medieval Inscriptional Name**: In 10th and 11th-century epigraphs of the Guhila rulers, it is designated as **Aghatpur** (आघाटपुर) or **Aghat Durg** (आघाट दुर्ग).
* **Local Regional Name**: Modern villagers call the high archaeological mound **Dhulkot** (धूलकोट — The Mound of Dust/Ashes), measuring approximately 500 meters in length and 15 meters in height.

#### 2. Excavation History & Field Archaeologists
1. **1953**: First preliminary scientific exploration by **Akshay Kirti Vyas** (A.K. Vyas).
2. **1954–1956**: Systematic trenching and classification conducted under **Ratan Chandra Agrawala** (R.C. Agrawala) of the Rajasthan Department of Archaeology.
3. **1961–1962**: Large-scale stratigraphic horizontal excavations led jointly by **Prof. H.D. Sankalia** (Deccan College, Pune), **Dr. V.N. Misra**, and **P.C. Seshedri**.

#### 3. Distinctive Material Culture & Architectural Anatomy
* **Domestic Architecture**: Houses were rectangular, spacious, built on stone slab foundations with sun-dried mud bricks and river pebbles; roofed with bamboo mats plastered with black soil; reinforced with internal reed screens.
* **Joint Family & Communal Living**: Excavations revealed multi-room houses; one single room contained **six distinct clay hearths (चूल्हे)**, demonstrating either a joint family structure or a communal kitchen setup for copper smiths.
* **The Black-and-Red Ware (BRW) Ceramic Tradition**:
  * The pottery was manufactured using inverted firing technique, yielding a jet-black interior and rim with a reddish-brown exterior.
  * Surface decorated with geometric white pigment paintings (dots, chevrons, wavy lines, concentric circles).
  * Unique domestic storage jars called **Gore** and **Kothar** (गोरे एवं कोठे) designed to preserve grains from humidity and pests.
* **Metallurgical Supremacy**:
  * Abundance of copper axes, celts, bangles, rings, and knives.
  * Discovery of **clay crucibles and terracotta tuyeres** containing copper slag (*तांबा गलाने की भट्ठियां*), proving local smelting of ore extracted from the nearby Aravalli deposits (Khetri, Delwara, Debari).
* **Religious & Ritual Paraphernalia**:
  * **The Banasian Bull (बनासियन बुल)**: Hand-modeled terracotta bull figurines characterized by stylized humps and elongated horns; unbaked or baked; believed to represent a fertility or religious cult.
  * **Terracotta Seals with Foreign Iconography**: A circular terracotta seal with a central figure of **Apollo** holding an arrow with a quiver on his back, flanked by a deer, indicating trans-regional cultural and commercial exchange.
  * **Subsistence**: Clear evidence of **rice** (chaff impressions on pottery), wheat, barley, and jowar; bones of humped cattle, water buffalo, sheep, goats, pigs, and deer.

The Ahar culture spans across more than 90 identified settlements in the Mewar plains. Four satellite sites are critically tested by RPSC:

### III. Ganeshwar Civilization (The Mother of Copper Age Cultures)

```text
[CHRONOLOGY: c. 2800 BCE – 2000 BCE | GEOGRAPHY: Kantli Basin, Neem Ka Thana (Aravalli Foothills)]
```

#### 1. Morphotectonic Locator & Excavation
* **Geographical Situation**: Located along the seasonal **Kantli River** at Ganeshwar in **Neem Ka Thana district** (historically Sikar district), nestled near the copper-rich zones of Khetri, Kho-Dariba, and Singhana.
* **Excavation Leadership**: Discovered in **1977** and excavated under **R.C. Agrawala** and **Vijay Kumar** (1978–1979) by the Rajasthan Department of Archaeology.

#### 2. Epistemic Status & Historical Stature
* **Pivotal Titles**:
  1. **"ताम्रयुगीन संस्कृतियों की जननी"** (*The Mother of Copper Age Cultures*).
  2. **"पुरातत्व का पुष्कर"** (*The Pushkar of Archaeology*).
  3. **"ताम्र-संचयी संस्कृति"** (*The Copper Accumulating Culture*).
* **Chronological Precedence**: Radio-carbon dates place Ganeshwar between **2800 BCE and 2200 BCE**, proving that Ganeshwar predates both Mature Harappa and Ahar, serving as the foundational metallurgical source from which copper metallurgy diffused.

#### 3. Metallurgical Super-Abundance
* **Artifact Typology**: Over **5,000 copper implements** were recovered, including:
  * Hundreds of copper fishhooks (*मछली पकड़ने के कांटे*), pointing to perennial stream flow in ancient Kantli and dietary reliance on fish.
  * Arrowheads (*तीर के फलक*), celts (*कुल्हाड़ियां*), spearheads (*भाले*), chisels (*छेनी*), razors, and bangles.
* **Chemical Purity**: Spectroscopic chemical analysis revealed that the copper implements contain **up to 99% pure copper**, with negligible or zero tin/lead alloying.
* **Economic Linkages**: Ganeshwar functioned as the primary industrial metallurgical quarry, supplying refined copper ingots and tools to Kalibangan, Harappa, and Mohenjo-daro across the ancient Hakra-Saraswati trade corridor.

#### 4. Ceramic Assemblage (Ochre Colored Pottery)
* Yielded large quantities of **Kripashvarni Mridbhand** (कपिशवर्णी मृद्भाण्ड / Ochre Colored Pottery - OCP).
* Thin-walled, slipped, orange-to-red ware, decorated with incised linear patterns and geometric motifs.

---

### IV. Kalibangan: The Bronze Age Harappan Metropolis

```text
[CHRONOLOGY: Pre-Harappan: c. 2900–2700 BCE | Mature Harappan: c. 2700–1900 BCE | GEOGRAPHY: Ghaggar Basin, Hanumangarh]
```

#### 1. Nomenclature & Discovery Sequence
* **Etymology**: The Punjabi word *Kalibangan* literally translates to **"Black Bangles"** (काली चूड़ियां), derived from the dense scatter of terracotta and faience black bangles observed on the surface mounds.
* **Discovery Milestones**:
  1. **Luigi Pio Tessitori (1916–1919)**: The Italian Indologist explored Kalibangan while collecting bardic chronicles; he identified the mounds as prehistoric but could not establish their Harappan identity before his death in Bikaner in 1919.
  2. **Amlananda Ghosh (A. Ghosh, 1952–1953)**: Conducted systematic archaeological reconnaissance along the dry bed of the Ghaggar-Saraswati; correctly identified the Harappan affiliation of Kalibangan and discovered dozens of allied Sothi sites.
  3. **Comprehensive Horizontal Excavations (1961–1969)**: Conducted under the directorship of **B.B. Lal**, **B.K. Thapar**, **M.D. Khare**, **K.M. Srivastava**, and **S.P. Jain**.

#### 2. Stratigraphic Horizons: Two Distinct Epochs

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        THE KALIBANGAN STRATIGRAPHY                     │
├───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PERIOD I: PRE-HARAPPAN (SOTHI)   │ PERIOD II: MATURE HARAPPAN         │
├───────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ • c. 2900 BCE – 2700 BCE          │ • c. 2700 BCE – 1900 BCE           │
│ • Fortified rhomboid settlement   │ • Dual fortified citadel & city    │
│ • World's earliest ploughed field │ • Standard Harappan grid layout    │
│ • Evidence of early earthquake    │ • 7 Fire altars on mud platforms   │
│ • Mud bricks in ratio 3:2:1       │ • Standard Harappan bricks: 4:2:1  │
└───────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### 3. Canonical Features of Period I (Pre-Harappan / Early Harappan)
* **The World's Earliest Ploughed Agricultural Field (विश्व का प्राचीनतम जुता हुआ खेत)**:
  * Located south-east of the fortified mound outside the city walls.
  * Shows a grid of intersecting furrows (*दोहरे परकोटेदार हल के निशान*): closely spaced parallel furrows in one direction crossed at right angles by widely spaced furrows.
  * **Agronomic Significance**: Proves dual cropping in a single season—chana (gram) planted in narrower furrows and sarson (mustard) in wider furrows, an identical practice still followed in northern Rajasthan.
* **Earliest Evidence of an Earthquake**: Stratigraphic cleavage fractures, collapsed mud-brick walls, and fissured ground strata prove that an earthquake around 2700 BCE brought an end to Period I.
* **Brick Ratio**: Unbaked mud bricks strictly following the **$3:2:1$** dimensional ratio ($30 \times 20 \times 10\text{ cm}$).

#### 4. Canonical Features of Period II (Mature Harappan Metropolis)
* **Settlement Morphology**:
  * Unlike Mohenjo-daro and Harappa where only the Western Citadel was fortified, **at Kalibangan both the Western Citadel (गढ़ी क्षेत्र) and the Eastern Lower Town (नगर क्षेत्र) were independently fortified** with massive mud-brick defensive walls.
  * Streets oriented along cardinal axes (North-South and East-West), forming a classic **Grid / Chessboard / Oxford Pattern**.
  * Brick ratio shifted to the standardized Harappan **$4:2:1$** ratio ($30 \times 15 \times 7.5\text{ cm}$ and $40 \times 20 \times 10\text{ cm}$).
* **Religious Architecture & Fire Altars (अग्निकुंड / हवन कुंड)**:
  * On the southern mud-brick platform of the Citadel stood a row of **seven rectangular clay Fire Altars (7 अग्निवेदियां)**.
  * Altars contained central terracotta cylinders (*stambha*), charcoal, ash, and terracotta cakes (*पिंड*), alongside cattle bones, confirming community fire rituals and animal sacrifice.
* **Public Sanitation & Drainage Systems**:
  * Unlike Mohenjo-daro's street drains of baked bricks, Kalibangan houses used **wooden drainage pipes (लकड़ी की नाली)** carved from scooped tree trunks to channel water into domestic soakage jars (*कच्चे घड़े*).
  * Houses constructed predominantly of **sun-dried mud bricks**; burnt bricks were reserved strictly for wells, bathing floors, and drains.
* **Surgical & Medical Archaeology (Trepanning)**:
  * Discovery of a child's cranium with **six surgically trepanned holes (कपाल छेदन / शल्य चिकित्सा)** and signs of bone healing, providing the earliest global proof of brain surgery / hydrocephalus treatment.
* **Seals & Inscriptions**:
  * Discovery of a **cylindrical clay seal** bearing Mesopotamian motifs, proving direct overseas or overland maritime trade connections.
  * Terracotta seals inscribed with the Harappan boustrophedon script (*भावचित्रात्मक लिपि*, written right to left, then left to right).
* **Mortuary Archaeology (Three Burial Rites)**:
  1. *Extended Inhumation (पूर्ण शवाधान)*: Corpse placed supine in a rectangular pit, head oriented North, accompanied by pottery.
  2. *Pot Burial / Fractional Burial (आंशिक शवाधान)*: Bones placed inside a round clay urn.
  3. *Symbolic / Memorial Burial (प्रतीकात्मक शवाधान)*: Rectangular pit containing grave pottery and personal items but **zero human skeletal remains**, erected as a cenotaph for individuals dying far from home.

### 1. Bairat (Ancient Viratnagar)
* **Geographical & Historical Context**: Located at the base of the Aravalli hills in **Kotputli-Behror district** along the Banganga river. Ancient capital of the **Matsya Janapada**; legendary refuge of the Pandavas during their final year of incognito exile (*अज्ञातवास*).
* **Principal Excavators**:
  * **Dayaram Sahni (1936–1937)**: Excavated Bijak ki Pahadi and Bhimsen ki Dungri.
  * **Nilratan Banerjee & Kailash Nath Dixit (1962–1963)**: Stratigraphic confirmation of NBPW, Buddhist chaityas, and Maurya-Greek continuity.
* **Key Mounds**: **Bijak ki Pahadi** (बीजक की पहाड़ी), **Bhimsen ki Dungri** (भीम की डूंगरी), **Moti Dungri**, and **Ganesh Dungri**.
* **Epigraphic Discoveries (The Ashokan Edicts)**:
  * **The Bhabru Rock Edict (भाब्रू शिलालेख)**: Discovered on Bijak ki Pahadi in **1837 by Captain Burt**. Written in Brahmi script and Prakrit language, it is preserved today in the **Asiatic Society Museum, Kolkata**. In it, Ashoka explicitly terms himself *Piyadasi Raja Magadhe* (प्रियदसी राजा मगधे) and confesses his personal faith in the **Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha (त्रिरत्न)**.
  * **Minor Rock Edict I**: Located at Bhimsen ki Dungri, confirming Bairat as a provincial administrative seat of the Mauryan empire.
* **The Buddhist Circular Chaitya Shrine**:
  * On Bijak ki Pahadi, excavations revealed a **circular brick-and-timber Chaitya shrine (गोल बौद्ध मंदिर)**, supported by 26 octagonal wooden pillars and encircled by a circumambulatory path (*प्रदक्षिणा पथ*).
  * Scientifically recognized as the **oldest surviving free-standing circular temple architecture in India**.
* **Numismatic Discovery (The Cloth-Wrapped Coin Hoard)**:
  * Excavation recovered a terracotta jar containing **36 silver coins wrapped in a piece of woven cotton fabric**:
    * **8 Punch-Marked Silver Coins** (Dharana/Karshapana) of the Mauryan imperial series.
    * **28 Indo-Greek / Bactrian Silver Coins**, including **16 coins belonging to King Menander (Milinda)**, proving Indo-Greek commercial and political control over north-eastern Rajasthan in the 2nd century BCE.
* **Hiuen Tsang's Testimony (634 CE)**: The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Xuanzang visited Bairat (*Po-li-ye-to-lo*), noting 8 Buddhist monasteries, and recorded that the city was devastated by the Huna conqueror **Mihirakula**.

### 2. Rairh (The Tatanagar of Ancient Rajasthan)
* **Locator & Excavators**: Situated on the banks of the Dhil river in Niwai tehsil of **Tonk district**. Excavated between **1938 and 1940 by K.N. Puri** and **Dayaram Sahni**.
* **Numismatic Super-Hoard**: Unearthed **3,075 silver Punch-Marked coins (Dharana)**, representing the largest single ancient coin hoard discovered in India.
* **Industrial Metallurgical Scale**: Large-scale iron smelting complexes, tongs, anvils, and iron weapons; hence termed **"राजस्थान का टाटानगर"** (*Tatanagar of Rajasthan*).
* **Malava Antiquities**: Hundreds of coins inscribed with *Malavanam Jayah* (मालवानां जयः).

### 3. Nagari (Ancient Madhyamika)
* **Locator & Excavator**: Located on the Berach river in **Chittorgarh district**. Excavated in **1915–1916 by Dr. D.R. Bhandarkar**.
* **Janapada Stature**: Capital of the **Sibi Janapada (शिवि जनपद)**; coins bearing the Brahmi legend *Majhimikaya Sibijanapadasa* (मझिमिकाया शिबिजानपदस) were discovered here.
* **Hathibada Enclosure (हाथीबाड़ा प्राकार)**: Massive cyclopean stone enclosure wall dedicated to the Vaishnava Bhagavata shrine of Sankarshana and Vasudeva.

### 4. Other Significant Historic Sites
* **Nagar (Karkot Nagar, Tonk)**: Capital of the Malava republic; yielded thousands of Malava copper coins, Mahishasuramardini terracotta plaques, and seals.
* **Sunari (Neem Ka Thana)**: Located on Kantli river; ancient iron-smelting blast furnaces operated with blow-pipe bellows (*धौंकनी से चलने वाली भट्ठियां*); fine NBPW bowls.
* **Jodhpura (Kotputli-Behror)**: Located on Sabi river; continuous sequence from OCP through Black-and-Red Ware, Painted Grey Ware (PGW), to NBPW; iron smelting ovens.
* **Rangmahal (Hanumangarh)**: Excavated in **1952–1954 by Swedish archaeologist Hanna Rydh**; yielded distinctive Kushana-Gupta painted red pottery with tall sprinkler bottles (*टोंटीदार घड़े*) and terracotta plaques of Gandhara-Mathura synthesis.
* **Naliasar (Sambhar, Jaipur Rural)**: Kushana, Yaudheya, and Gupta coins; bronze figurines.

---2d:T3161,Inscriptions (*अभिलेख*) and Prashastis (*प्रशस्तियां*) constitute the primary lithic evidence for reconstructing the political, dynastic, socio-economic, and religious history of Rajasthan.

### Detailed Analysis of Major Inscriptions

#### 1. Barli Inscription (443 BCE)
* **Discovery Location**: Found embedded in the pillar of Bhilot Mata temple at **Barli** near Ajmer; discovered by **G.H. Ojha** (Gauri Shankar Hirachand Ojha); now preserved in the Government Museum, Ajmer.
* **Historical Significance**: The **oldest surviving inscription in Rajasthan** (and second oldest in India after Piprahwa). Engraved in early Brahmi script; predates Ashoka; references the 84th year of Mahavira Nirvana, providing crucial evidence of early Jain diffusion in central Rajasthan.

#### 2. Ghosundi Inscription (2nd Century BCE)
* **Location**: Found on a boundary wall at **Ghosundi** village near Nagari (Chittorgarh); discovered and read by **Dr. D.R. Bhandarkar**.
* **Language & Script**: Sanskrit language written in Brahmi script.
* **Canonical Historical Value**:
  * The **earliest epigraphic record in Rajasthan documenting the worship of the Bhagavata (Vaishnava) cult**.
  * Records that King **Sarvatata** (सर्वतात) of the Gajayana gotra, son of a woman of the Parashara gotra, performed the **Ashvamedha sacrifice (अश्वमेध यज्ञ)** and constructed a stone boundary wall (*पूजा-शिला-प्राकार*) dedicated to **Sankarshana (Balarama)** and **Vasudeva (Krishna)**.

#### 3. Samoli Inscription (646 CE)
* **Location**: Samoli village, Bhomat region of Udaipur.
* **Ruler**: Reign of Guhila ruler **Siladitya** (शिलादित्य).
* **Crucial Historical Proofs**:
  * Mentions the flourishing of the **Jawar silver and zinc mines (जावर माइन्स)** by a merchant community head named Jaitak.
  * Records the establishment of the temple of **Aranyavasini Devi** (अरण्यवासिनी देवी / Forest Goddess).
  * Demonstrates that the Guhilas of Mewar maintained monetized urban settlements in the forested tribal pockets of southern Rajasthan as early as the 7th century.

#### 4. The Mandore & Ghatiyala Inscriptions of the Gurjara-Pratiharas
* **Mandore Inscription of Bauka (837 CE)**: Traces the origin of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty to the Brahmana ancestor **Harishchandra** (Rohilliddhi) and his Kshatriya wife **Bhadra**, explaining the dual Brahmana-Kshatriya lineages.
* **Ghatiyala Inscription of Kakkuka (861 CE, Jodhpur)**:
  * Composed by Pratihara ruler **Kakkuka**; engraved on a pillar near a Jain temple.
  * Mentions that Kakkuka defeated the turbulent **Abhira (अभीर)** bandits who had terrorized traders.
  * Records the establishment of a flourishing public market (*हट्ट*) with free shops for Jain merchants, symbolizing civic rehabilitation.

#### 5. Bijolia Inscription (1170 CE)

```text
[DATE: Phalguna Vadi 3, Vikram Samvat 1226 (1170 CE) | TEMPLE: Parshvanath Temple, Bijolia (Bhilwara)]
```

* **Composer & Scribe**: Composed by the Jain scholar **Gunabhadra** (गुणभद्र); engraved on rock by the mason **Govinda** (गोविन्द); commissioned during the reign of Chauhan ruler **Someshwara** by the Jain Shravaka **Lolaka**.
* **Five Pillars of Historical Revelations**:
  1. **Chauhan Lineage**: Explicitly states that the Chauhans of Shakambhari are **Vatsa-Gotriya Brahmanas** (वत्सगोत्रीय ब्राह्मण), tracing their origin to the sage Vatsa at Ahichchhatrapura.
  2. **Dynastic Genesis**: Mentions **Vasudeva Chauhan** as the founder of the dynasty in **551 CE**, who created the sacred **Sambhar Salt Lake** (*शाकम्भरी झील*).
  3. **Conquests of Vigraharaja IV**: Records that Vigraharaja IV (Bisaldeo) captured **Dhilli** (Delhi) from the Tomaras.
  4. **Ancient Toponymic Registry (प्राचीन भौगोलिक नाम)**: Supplies the ancient names of historical Rajasthani cities:
     * *Jabalipura* (जाबालिपुर) $\rightarrow$ Jalore
     * *Shakambhari* (शाकम्भरी) $\rightarrow$ Sambhar
     * *Mandalgarh* (मंडलकर) $\rightarrow$ Mandalgarh
     * *Vindhyavalli* (विंध्यवल्ली) $\rightarrow$ Bijolia
     * *Nagadraha* (नागद्रह) $\rightarrow$ Nagda
     * *Sripatha* (श्रीपथ) $\rightarrow$ Bayana
     * *Kanthikapuri* (कांठिकापुरी) $\rightarrow$ Kankroli
  5. **Land Grants**: Details administrative land donations designated as *Dohali* (डोहली) given to temples.

#### 6. Chirwa Inscription (1273 CE)
* **Location**: Chirwa village, north of Udaipur; engraved on a temple gate during the reign of Guhila ruler **Samarsimha**.
* **Historical Highlights**: Provides genealogical achievements of Mewar rulers **Jaitra Singh**, **Tejasimha**, and **Samarsimha**; describes Jaitra Singh’s destruction of the Sultanate forces of **Iltutmish** at the **Battle of Bhutala** (भूताला का युद्ध); mentions administrative posts such as *Talaraksha* (नगर रक्षक/Police Chief) and early instances of the Sati rite among Rajput nobility.

#### 7. Kumbhalgarh Prashasti (1460 CE)
* **Location**: Originally carved on five large slabs placed inside the Mamadev (Kumbha Swami) temple at **Kumbhalgarh Fort** (now preserved in Udaipur Museum); begun by court scholar **Atri** and completed by his son **Kanhavyas** (or Maheshwar).
* **Canonical Value for RPSC**:
  * Traces Guhila ancestry from Bappa Rawal; asserts that Bappa received royal sovereignty through the blessing of sage **Harit Rashi** (हारीत ऋषि).
  * Officially confers the supreme war epithet **"विषम घाटी पंचानन"** (*Vishama Ghati Panchanan* — Lion in the perilous pass of warfare) upon **Rana Hammir** for his resurgence of Mewar after the 1303 disaster.
  * Records detailed accounts of Maharana Kumbha’s military victories over Malwa, Gujarat, and Nagaur.

#### 8. Ranakpur Prashasti (1439 CE)
* **Location**: Engraved on a pillar in the Chaumukha Jain temple of **Ranakpur** (Pali district).
* **Composer & Architect**: Composed under the patronage of the Porwad Jain minister **Dharanashah**; the master sculptor-architect was **Depaka** (देपा/दीपक).
* **Historical Anomaly Resolved**: Uniquely treats **Bappa Rawal** and **Kalbhoj** as two distinct individuals (which modern historians like G.H. Ojha corrected, proving Kalbhoj was Bappa Rawal’s personal name and Bappa was his title).
* Details Maharana Kumbha’s capture of Sarangpur, Narana, Ajmer, and Mandore.

#### 9. Kirti Stambha Prashasti (1460 CE)
* **Location**: Engraved on the top floors of the 9-storey **Vijay Stambha** (Tower of Victory) at Chittorgarh.
* **Composers**: Begun by Maharana Kumbha’s court poet **Atri** (अत्रि); completed after Atri's death by his son **Kavi Mahesh** (कवि महेश).
* **Literary Catalogue of Kumbha**:
  * Records the full titles of Maharana Kumbha: *Abhinav Bharatacharya*, *Hindu Suratan*, *Rano Raso*, *Hal Guru*, *Dan Guru*, *Chail Guru*.
  * Documents the scholarly treatises authored by Kumbha himself, specifically: **Sangitaraja** (संगीतराज, in 5 Ratnakosas), **Sangitamimamsa** (संगीतमीमांसा), **Sudha Prabandha** (सूड प्रबंध), and his commentaries on Jayadeva’s *Gitagovinda* (**Rasikapriya**) and Sarangadeva's *Sangitaratnakara*.

#### 10. Raj Prashasti (1676 CE)
* **Location**: Carved on **25 black marble slabs** embedded in the niches of the *Nau-Chauki Pal* (नौचौकी पाल) embankment of **Rajsamand Lake** (Rajsamand district).
* **Composer**: Composed in classical Sanskrit verse by **Ranchhod Bhatt Tailang** (रणछोड़ भट्ट तैलंग) under the patronage of **Maharana Raj Singh I**.
* **Global Distinction**: Recognized as the **largest stone-slab Sanskrit inscription in the world** (25 slabs containing 24 cantos).
* **Historical Contents**: Comprehensive history of Mewar from Bappa Rawal to Raj Singh; complete text and terms of the **Mughal-Mewar Treaty of 1615** (Amar Singh I - Jahangir); detailed technical records of the severe famine relief construction of the Rajsamand Dam.

[CRITICAL ALERT: RECENT RPSC RAS PRELIMS & MAINS LINGUISTIC / FACTUAL TRAPS]
```

1. **The Modern District Reorganization Trap**:
   * *Ganeshwar* is no longer in Sikar; it is situated in **Neem Ka Thana district**.
   * *Bairat* is no longer in Jaipur; it is located in **Kotputli-Behror district**.
   * *Tilwara* is no longer in Barmer; it is in the newly formed **Balotra district**.
   * *Sunari* is in **Neem Ka Thana district** (previously Jhunjhunu border).
2. **The "Ploughed Field" Excavation Trap**: Do not confuse Amlananda Ghosh (who discovered the site in 1952) with the discovery of the ploughed field. The ploughed field was scientifically identified in Period I excavations under **B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar**.
3. **The Copper Purity Trap**: If RPSC asks which site yielded implements made of **nearly 100% (99%) pure copper**, the answer is strictly **Ganeshwar**, NOT Ahar. Ahar had copper smelting furnaces, but Ganeshwar yielded the ultra-pure tool hoards.
4. **The Kiln-Fired Bricks in Chalcolithic Trap**: Chalcolithic cultures almost universally used sun-dried mud bricks. The **sole exception in the Ahar-Banas complex that used burnt/fired bricks** is **Gilund** (Rajsamand), NOT Ahar itself.
5. **The Animal Husbandry Chronology Trap**: The earliest evidence of animal husbandry in Rajasthan is at **Bagor** (Mesolithic, Kothari river), NOT Kalibangan or Ahar.
6. **The Leprosy Skeleton Trap**: The earliest human skeleton exhibiting leprosy in India was excavated at **Balathal** (Udaipur), dated to c. 2000 BCE by Dr. V.N. Misra.
7. **The Double-Burial Trap**: Do not confuse Kalibangan with Lothal. Lothal had "twin burials" (male-female in one grave). Kalibangan had **three forms of burials** (extended, urn/fractional, and symbolic/memorial without skeleton).
8. **The Drainage Material Trap**: Kalibangan did NOT have baked brick street sewers like Mohenjo-daro. It used **scooped wooden drain pipes (लकड़ी की नाली)** and domestic soakage jars.
9. **The Inscriptional Authorship Trap**:
   * *Kirti Stambha Prashasti* was begun by **Atri** and completed by his son **Mahesh**.
   * *Bijolia Inscription* was composed by **Gunabhadra** and engraved by **Govinda**.
   * *Raj Prashasti* was composed by **Ranchhod Bhatt Tailang**.
10. **The "Vishama Ghati Panchanan" Source Trap**: Rana Hammir is conferred this famous title in the **Kumbhalgarh Prashasti** (and Rasikapriya commentary), NOT the Kirti Stambha Prashasti.
11. **The Bhabru Edict Current Location Trap**: Discovered by Captain Burt in 1837 at Bairat, the Bhabru edict is currently housed in the **Asiatic Society Museum, Kolkata**, NOT in Jaipur or Delhi.
12. **The "Vatsa-Gotra" Chauhan Inscription**: The claim that Chauhans were Vatsa-gotriya Brahmanas is made in the **Bijolia Inscription (1170 CE)**, which refuted the Agnikula origin myth for that period.
13. **The Earliest Vaishnavism Inscription**: RPSC frequently asks for the earliest record of the Bhagavata cult in Rajasthan; it is the **Ghosundi Inscription (2nd Century BCE)**, NOT the Nagari or Bijolia inscription.
14. **The Bappa Rawal vs. Kalbhoj Epigraphic Ambiguity**: The **Ranakpur Prashasti (1439 CE)** erroneously lists Bappa Rawal and Kalbhoj as two separate kings.
15. **The Banasian Bull Material**: The Banasian Bull is made of **terracotta (clay)**, NOT bronze or copper.
16. **The Tatanagar Epithet Trap**: The title "Tatanagar of Rajasthan" belongs to **Rairh (Tonk)** due to its massive hoard of 3,075 punch-marked silver coins and iron tools, NOT Khetri.
17. **The Swedish Expedition Site**: The foreign expedition led by Dr. Hanna Rydh in 1952–54 excavated **Rangmahal** (Hanumangarh), NOT Kalibangan.
18. **The Indo-Greek Coins at Bairat**: Total coins recovered in the cloth jar = 36 (8 punch-marked + 28 Indo-Greek, out of which **16 were of King Menander**).
19. **The First Paleolithic Tool Finder**: **C.A. Hackett (1870)** found the first handaxe in Jaipur and Indragarh, NOT D.R. Bhandarkar or A. Ghosh.
20. **The Sothi Culture Connection**: A. Ghosh classified the pre-Harappan ceramic horizon at Kalibangan as **"Sothi Culture"** (named after Sothi in Bikaner), calling it Proto-Harappan.
21. **The Fire Altars Count**: Exactly **seven rectangular fire altars** were found in a row on the mud-brick platform of the Western Citadel at Kalibangan.
22. **The Samoli Inscription Economic Link**: Proves the operational status of the **Jawar silver-zinc mines** in 646 CE under Guhila Siladitya.
23. **The Kakkuka Market Establishment**: The **Ghatiyala Inscription (861 CE)** describes the clearing of robbers and the building of a merchant *Hatta* by Pratihara King Kakkuka.
24. **The Cotton Fabric Archaeological Sites**: Two sites in Rajasthan yielded ancient woven cotton fabric: **Bairat** (wrapping 36 coins) and **Balathal** (Chalcolithic woven textile).
25. **The Barli Inscription Script**: Written in early **Brahmi script** (pre-Ashokan), NOT Kharosthi or Nagari.

(A) 1, 2, and 3 only  
(B) 1, 3, and 4 only

*Answer*: **(B)**
