#### The Shila Devi Legend (Jessore, Bengal)
During the Bengal expedition (1604 CE), Man Singh defeated **Raja Kedar Rai of Jessore** (now Bangladesh). 
- Kedar Rai was believed to be invincible due to the divine presence of an ancient black-stone idol of Goddess Durga.
- Man Singh recovered the sacred idol from the oceanbed/palace and brought it triumphantly to Amer.
- He consecrated the goddess within Amer Fort as **Shila Devi (शीला देवी)**, designating her as the supreme **Ishta Devi (इष्ट देवी — Chosen Personal Deity)** of the Jaipur royal family (whereas Jamway Mata remained the dynastic Kuldevi).

---

### 4.3 Cultural, Architectural & Literary Renaissance under Man Singh I

#### Monumental Architecture
1. **Amer Palaces (आमेर महल)**: Initiated the construction of the grand Rajput-Mughal palaces in 1592 CE, including the Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas, and foundational ramparts.
2. **Jagat Shiromani Temple (जगत शिरोमणि मंदिर, Amer)**:
   - Commissioned by Man Singh’s chief queen, **Rani Kanakavati (रानी कनकवती)**, in memory of their beloved eldest son, Crown Prince **Jagat Singh**, who died in Bengal.
   - Known as the *Meera Temple of Amer*; enshrines the sacred black-stone idol of Lord Krishna which was originally worshipped by **Meera Bai** at Chittorgarh, brought to Amer by Man Singh during military campaigns.
3. **Govind Devji Temple (Vrindavan, UP)**:
   - Constructed the monumental 7-storey red-sandstone temple of Radha-Govind Devji at Vrindavan in 1590 CE (the upper storeys were later dismantled during Aurangzeb’s iconoclastic campaign).
4. **Baikunthpur Temple (Bihar)** & **Man Mandir Ghat / Observatory at Varanasi**.

#### Court Scholars & Treatises
Man Singh was an extraordinary patron of Sanskrit and Dingal scholarship:
- **Pundarik Vitthal (पुंडरीक विट्ठल)**: Master musicologist who authored foundational musicological classics:
  1. *Ragamala* (रागमञ्जरी)
  2. *Raga Manjari*
  3. *Raga Chandrodaya*
  4. *Nartan Nirnaya* (नर्तन निर्णय)
- **Kripa Ram**: Authored *Kavya Kalpadrum*.
- **Murari Dan**: Authored *Maan Prakash* (chronicle of Man Singh's life).
- **Dalpat Raj**: Authored *Pawan Paschisi* and *Patra Prashasti*.
- **Death**: Passed away on 6 July 1614 CE at **Elichpur (Maharashtra)** while commanding Mughal forces in the Deccan.

### 5.3 Cultural & Architectural Patronage

#### Mahakavi Bihari Lal & The Bihari Satsai
- When Mirza Raja Jai Singh married a young princess and neglected royal administration, remaining locked inside his palace chambers, court poet **Bihari Lal (बिहारी लाल)** sent him a single subtle Dingal-Braj couplet via a maidservant:
  > *"नहिं पराग नहिं मधुर मधु, नहिं विकास यहि काल।*  
  > *अली कली ही सौं बंध्यो, आगे कौन हवाल॥"*  
  > *(There is neither pollen nor sweet nectar here, nor has the flower bloomed. If the bee is already enslaved by the bud, what will happen in the future?)*
- Jai Singh emerged immediately from his chambers and resumed governance.
- He rewarded Bihari Lal with **one gold mohur (Ashrafi) for every couplet** composed.
- Bihari composed the world-renowned masterwork **Bihari Satsai (बिहारी सतसई)**, containing **713 Dohas** in exquisite Braj Bhasha.
- Other Scholars: **Ram Kavi** authored *Jai Singh Charitra*.

#### Architecture
- Constructed **Jaigarh Fort (जयगढ़ दुर्ग)** atop the Cheel ka Teela (Hill of Eagles) in Amer, designed as the invincible military armory and treasury of the kingdom.
- Built the **Sheesh Mahal (Glass Palace)**, **Jai Mandir**, and **Diwan-i-Aam** within Amer Fort.
- Constructed the Jai Singh Pura settlements in Delhi, Agra, and Aurangabad.
- **Death**: Passed away on 28 August 1667 CE at **Burhanpur (Madhya Pradesh)**, allegedly poisoned on Aurangzeb’s secret instigation.

---53:T340f,### 6.1 Accession & The Imperial Epithet "Sawai"
Ascended the throne in 1700 CE at the age of 12. Originally named **Vijay Singh**.
- **The Bestowal of "Sawai"**: Impressed by his sharp intellect and fearless repartee at the Deccan court, Mughal Emperor **Aurangzeb** proclaimed that the young prince was a quarter (*Sawai* / सवाया — 1.25) ahead of his illustrious ancestor Mirza Raja Jai Singh in wisdom. Aurangzeb renamed him **Jai Singh** and granted the hereditary title **Sawai (सवाई)**, while his younger brother was renamed Vijay Singh.
- **Service Across 7 Mughal Emperors**: Reigned across the tenures of seven Mughal monarchs: Aurangzeb, Bahadur Shah I, Jahandar Shah, Farrukhsiyar, Rafi-ud-Darajat, Rafi-ud-Daulah, and Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela'.

#### City Palaces & Govind Devji
- **City Palace (Chandra Mahal)**: Constructed as the sovereign residence, rising 7 storeys (Sukh Niwas, Ranga Mandir, Pitam Niwas, Chhatra Niwas, Shri Niwas, Mukut Mandir).

Sawai Jai Singh II declared that the true sovereign King of Jaipur was **Lord Govind Devji**, and that he and all subsequent Kachhwaha rulers would govern only as His humble prime ministers / trustees (**Diwans**).

### 6.3 The Scientific Renaissance: Five Astronomical Observatories (Jantar Mantar)
Sawai Jai Singh was deeply dissatisfied with the inaccuracies in contemporary Islamic (*Zij-i-Ulugh Beg*) and European astronomical tables. He constructed five monumental stone observatories (**Jantar Mantar / जंतर-मंतर** — from *Yantra Mantra* / Instruments and Formulas):

```
                    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │       THE 5 JANTAR MANTAR OBSERVATORIES SEQUENCE       │
                    └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                                │
    ┌─────────────────┬─────────────────┼─────────────────┬─────────────────┐
    │                 │                 │                 │                 │

#### Key Astronomical Instruments at Jaipur
1. **Brihat Samrat Yantra (बृहत् सम्राट यंत्र)**: The world’s largest stone sundial (standing 27 meters / 90 feet tall), capable of measuring local solar time to an astonishing accuracy of **two seconds**.
2. **Jai Prakash Yantra (जयप्रकाश यंत्र)**: Inverted hemispherical bowls mapped to celestial coordinates; invented by Sawai Jai Singh himself.
3. **Ram Yantra (राम यंत्र)**: Cylindrical open-air structure used to measure azimuth and celestial altitude.
4. **Digamsha Yantra & Misra Yantra**.

#### Scientific Publications & Astronomical Catalogues
- **Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi (ज़िज-ए-मोहम्मदशाही, 1733 CE)**: Compiled astronomical tables dedicated to Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah.
- **Yantra Raj (यंत्रराज)**: Authored Sanskrit treatise on astronomical instrumentation.
- Court Astrologer **Jagannath Samrat** translated Ptolemy's *Almagest* into Sanskrit as **Siddhanta Samrat** and Euclid's *Elements* as **Rekhaganita**.
- Court Scholar **Kewalram** translated logarithmic tables into Sanskrit as *Vibhag Sarni*.

---

### 6.4 The Vedic Renaissance & The Last Ashvamedha Yajna (1740 CE)
Sawai Jai Singh revived ancient Vedic ritualism across northern India:
- Performed the sacred Vedic rites: **Rajasuya**, **Vajapeya**, **Purushamedha**, and the legendary **Ashvamedha Yajna (अश्वमेध यज्ञ, 1740 CE)**.
- **The Last Hindu King to Perform Ashvamedha**: Celebrated as the last monarch in Indian history to complete the Ashvamedha Yajna.
- **The Sacrificial Horse Episode**: The royal sacrificial horse let loose across the realm was boldly intercepted and challenged by **Deep Singh Kumbhani (दीपसिंह कुंभाणी)**, a proud Rajput vassal, resulting in a fierce skirmish.
- **Chief Ritual Priest**: The rituals were presided over by **Pundarik Ratnakar (पुंडरीक रत्नाकर)**, who authored the Sanskrit chronicle *Jai Singh Kalpadrum*.

---

### 6.5 Geopolitics, The Hurda Conference & Maratha Clashes

#### The Hurda Conference (17 July 1734 CE / हुरड़ा सम्मेलन)
To counter the devastating invasions and extortionate taxes (*Chauth* and *Sardeshmukhi*) extracted by the Marathas under Peshwa Baji Rao I, Sawai Jai Singh organized a grand pan-Rajput sovereign conference at **Hurda (हुरड़ा, modern Shahpura district / erstwhile Bhilwara)** on 17 July 1734.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        THE HURDA CONFERENCE COMPOSITION (1734 CE)                      │
├──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ President of Conference  │ Maharana Jagat Singh II of Mewar (Presided over session)    │
│ Chief Architect & Planner│ Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber-Jaipur                          │
│ Participating Sovereigns │ • Maharaja Abhai Singh (Marwar / Jodhpur)                   │
│                          │ • Bakht Singh (Nagaur)                                      │
│                          │ • Maharao Durjan Sal (Kota)                                 │
│                          │ • Maharaja Zorawar Singh (Bikaner)                          │
│                          │ • Rao Dalel Singh (Bundi)                                   │
│                          │ • Gopal Singh (Karauli)                                     │
├──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Core Pact Clauses:                                                                     │
│ 1. Mutual Defense: The enemy of one Rajput house shall be regarded as the enemy of all.│
│ 2. United Monsoon Encampment: All armies shall assemble at Rampura post-monsoon to     │
│    launch a joint offensive against the Marathas.                                      │
│ 3. Extradition: No state shall harbor traitors or rebels from another Rajput kingdom.  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Historical Failure: Collapsed completely due to deep-seated personal mutual jealousies,│
│ dispute over supreme military leadership, and absence of collective commitment.       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Major Clashes with Marathas & Regional Battles
- **Battle of Pilsud (1715 CE)**: Jai Singh defeated Maratha armies in Malwa.
- **Battle of Mandsaur (1733 CE)**: Besieged by Malhar Rao Holkar; Jai Singh was compelled to pay 6 lakh rupees in cash and assign 28 Parganas.
- **Battle of Gangwana (1741 CE)**: Fought a ferocious battle against **Bakht Singh of Nagaur** (who charged with only 5,000 Rathores against Jai Singh's 50,000 troops); Jai Singh sustained immense casualties despite holding the field.
- **Death**: Sawai Jai Singh passed away on 21 September 1743 CE at Jaipur.

---54:T2734,### 7.1 Ishwari Singh vs Madho Singh I — The Fratricidal Succession War

#### The Roots of Discord: The Devari Pact of 1708 CE
When Sawai Jai Singh II signed the **Devari Pact (1708)**, he agreed to marry Mewari Princess **Chandra Kunwari** (daughter of Maharana Amar Singh II) on the binding condition that her male issue would inherit the Jaipur throne regardless of seniority. 
- However, when Jai Singh died in 1743, his eldest son **Ishwari Singh** was crowned.
- Chandra Kunwari’s son, **Madho Singh I**, claimed the throne with the military backing of his maternal uncle, Maharana Jagat Singh II of Mewar, and Maratha general Malhar Rao Holkar.

```
                    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

#### Madho Singh I (1750–1768 CE)
- Ascended the throne following Ishwari Singh's tragic demise.
- **Jaipur Massacre of Marathas (January 1751 CE)**: Enraged by Maratha arrogance and endless financial extortion, the citizens and soldiers of Jaipur shut the city gates and massacred approximately **5,000 Marathas** trapped inside the walled city in a single day.
- **Battle of Kakor (1759 CE)**: Defeated Malhar Rao Holkar.
- **Battle of Bhatwara (1761 CE)**: Fought against Shatrushal Hada of Kota over control of Ranthambore; Kota’s brilliant faujdar **Zalim Singh Jhala** emerged victorious.
- **Urban Foundations**: Founded the fortified city of **Sawai Madhopur (1763 CE)** and constructed the Moti Doongri Palaces in Jaipur.

---

### 7.2 Sawai Pratap Singh (1778–1803 CE) — The Cultural Zenith

#### The War with Mahadji Scindia: Battle of Tunga (1787 CE)
- Maratha general **Mahadji Scindia** marched upon Jaipur demanding arrears of tribute.
- **Battle of Tunga (तुंगा का युद्ध, 28 July 1787 CE)**:
  - Fought near Bassi (Jaipur). Sawai Pratap Singh allied with **Maharaja Vijay Singh of Jodhpur**.
  - The united Rajput cavalry charged Scindia’s French-trained infantry and heavy artillery, routing the Marathas and forcing Scindia to retreat from Rajasthan.

#### The Construction of Hawa Mahal (1799 CE)
The crown architectural achievement of Jaipur’s cultural history:
- **Construction Year**: 1799 CE.
- **Chief Architect**: **Ustad Lal Chand (उस्ताद लालचंद)**.
- **Inspiration & Shape**: Dedicated to Lord Krishna and Radha; designed in the magnificent contour of **Lord Krishna's Crown (मुकुट)**.
- **Anatomy & Windows**: Built without foundational pillars directly from the street ramparts; features **5 storeys** and **953 exquisitely carved jharokhas (latticed windows)** designed to allow royal women (*Pardanashin Ranis*) to observe street processions and festivals (Teej, Gangaur) while remaining completely invisible to the outside world, enjoying natural air-conditioning via the Venturi effect.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          THE 5 STOREYS OF HAWA MAHAL (TOP TO BOTTOM)                   │
├─────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 5th Storey (Top)    │ Hawa Mandir (हवा मंदिर) — Namesake of the entire monument        │
│ 4th Storey          │ Prakash Mandir (प्रकाश मंदिर)                                    │
│ 3rd Storey          │ Vichitra Mandir (विचित्र मंदिर)                                  │
│ 2nd Storey          │ Ratan Mandir (रतन मंदिर)                                        │
│ 1st Storey (Base)   │ Sharad Mandir (शरद मंदिर)                                        │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Cultural Court: Gandharva Baisi & Brijnidhi
- **Gandharva Baisi (गंधर्व बाईसी / प्रताप बाईसी)**: Sawai Pratap Singh maintained an extraordinary royal academy consisting of **22 scholars, 22 classical musicians, 22 poets, 22 astrologers, and 22 physicians**, patronized inside the *Gunijan Khana*.
- **Literary Authorship**: Pratap Singh was a master poet of Braj Bhasha, writing under the pen-name **"Brijnidhi" (बृजनिधि)**. His collected poetical works are compiled in *Brijnidhi Granthawali*.
- Organized a monumental **Music Conference (Sangeet Sammelan)** under the presidency of **Devarshi Brijpal Bhatt**, which compiled the definitive musicological encyclopedia: **Radha Govind Sangeet Sar (राधा गोविंद संगीत सार)**.

---

### 7.3 Subsequent Rulers of Jaipur

#### Sawai Jagat Singh II (1803–1818 CE) — "The Rasiya Raja"
- Ruled during a period of administrative chaos and moral decadence; notorious for his infatuation with concubine **Ras-Kapur (रसकपूर)**, whom he minted on state coins and placed on royal elephants.
- Engaged in the catastrophic **Battle of Gingoli (1807 CE)** against Maharaja Man Singh of Jodhpur over the marriage alliance with Princess Krishna Kumari of Mewar.
- Signed the Treaty of Subordinate Alliance with the British East India Company on **2 April 1818**.

#### Sawai Ram Singh II (1835–1880 CE) — The Modern Maker of Jaipur
- Reigned during the 1857 Revolution; assisted the British with his royal army (rewarded with the pargana of Kotputli and the imperial title **"Sitar-e-Hind"**).
- **The "Pink City" Painting (1876 CE)**:
  - In 1876 CE, to celebrate the state visit of **Albert Edward, Prince of Wales** (later King Edward VII), Sawai Ram Singh II ordered the entire walled city of Jaipur painted in warm **terracotta pink (गेरुआ रंग)**, symbolizing hospitable welcome. British journalist and traveller Lord Robert subsequently coined the term **"The Pink City"**.
- **Modern Institutional Foundations**:
  1. **Maharaja College (1844 CE)**: Premier modern higher education center.
  2. **Madarsa-i-Hunari (1857 CE)**: School of Arts and Crafts, later renamed *Rajasthan School of Arts*.
  3. **Albert Hall Museum (1876 CE)**: Foundation stone laid by Prince Albert; designed in dazzling Indo-Saracenic style by British architect **Sir Samuel Swinton Jacob**.
  4. **Ramniwas Garden** & State Photography Studio (Ram Singh was himself an accomplished photographer).
- **Social Reforms**: Outlawed Sati, female infanticide, and human slavery across Jaipur state.

#### Sawai Man Singh II (1922–1949 CE)
- The last de facto ruling Maharaja of Jaipur; celebrated international polo player; married **Maharani Gayatri Devi** (named one of the world's most beautiful women by *Vogue*, later MP for Jaipur).
- Appointed the **First and Only Rajpramukh of Greater Rajasthan (30 March 1949 to 31 October 1956)** upon the integration of the princely states.

### 8.1 The Bhatis of Jaisalmer & The Celebrated 2.5 Sākas
- **Lineage**: Claim descent from Lord Krishna's Yadav lineage (**Chandravanshi Kshatriyas**); title **"Chhatrapati Yadavpati"** and **"Uttar Bhad Kivad Bhati"** (The Northern Gateway Shield of India against invaders from Multan and Sindh).
- **Founding of Jaisalmer (1156 CE)**: **Maharawal Jaisal** shifted the capital from Lodhurva to the yellow-sandstone **Trikuta Hill (त्रिकूट पहाड़ी)**, constructing the world-renowned **Sonar Kila (स्वर्ण दुर्ग / Jaisalmer Fort)**.
- **The 2.5 Sākas of Jaisalmer (जैसलमेर के ढाई साके)**:
  1. **First Sāka (c. 1299 / 1312 CE)**:
     - Ruler: **Rawal Moolraj I** (and Kunwar Ratan Singh).
     - Invader: Sultan **Alauddin Khalji** (following Bhati plunder of imperial treasure horses).
     - Full Sāka: Royal queens performed fire Jauhar; Moolraj fell in Kesariya combat.
  2. **Second Sāka (c. 1370 CE)**:
     - Ruler: **Rawal Duda** (and Kunwar Tilaksi).
     - Invader: Sultan **Firoz Shah Tughlaq**.
     - Full Sāka: Complete Jauhar and Kesariya; fort occupied by Delhi garrison for years.
  3. **The Half Sāka (Ardha Sāka / अर्ध साका, 1550 CE)**:
     - Ruler: **Rawal Lunkaran Bhati**.
     - Invader: Afghan chieftain **Amir Ali of Kandahar** (who sought shelter as a refugee and deceitfully infiltrated armed soldiers concealed in women’s palanquins / *Dolas*).
     - **Why Half Sāka?**: Taken by total surprise without time to prepare a sacred pyre, the Rajputs slaughtered their own womenfolk with swords to preserve their honor before charging the enemy (**Kesariya was executed**). In the ferocious battle that ensued, Rawal Lunkaran and his men **completely annihilated Amir Ali and emerged victorious!** Because victory was won and no traditional fire Jauhar occurred, it is canonized as an **Ardha Sāka**.

---

### 8.2 The Hadas of Bundi and Kota (Chauhan Branch)
- **Founding of Bundi (1241 CE)**: **Rao Deva Hada** conquered the Bandu valley from Meena chieftain Jaita, founding the sovereign state of Bundi.
- **Taragarh Fort (Bundi, 1354 CE)**: Constructed by **Rao Bar Singh Hada** atop a steep crag (named *Taragarh* because it appears like a star from the plains).
- **Surjan Hada (1569 CE)**: Heroically defended Ranthambore Fort against Akbar until Rao Bhagwan Das and Man Singh negotiated an honorable peace treaty. Surjan Hada surrendered Ranthambore and received imperial governorship of Varanasi.
- **Bundi Fresco Renaissance (Chitrashala)**:
  - Bundi is celebrated worldwide for the exquisite wall frescoes (*Bhitti Chitra*) of the **Chitrashala (रंगशाला)** inside Garh Palace, constructed under **Maharao Umed Singh** (depicting Radha-Krishna lila, rains, and lush flora/fauna).
- **The Partition of Kota (1631 CE)**:
  - In 1631 CE, Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan rewarded **Madho Singh Hada** (son of Bundi ruler Rao Ratan Singh) for his military valor by carving **Kota** out of Bundi as an independent sovereign princely state.
- **Zalim Singh Jhala (जालिम सिंह झाला) — The "Bismarck of Rajasthan"**:
  - The brilliant Faujdar, Prime Minister, and de facto ruler of Kota during the chaotic late-18th and early-19th centuries.
  - Skilfully maneuvered between Marathas, Pindaris, and the British East India Company.
  - In the 1817 British Subsidiary Treaty, he inserted a secret supplementary clause reserving hereditary administration for his family.
  - Ultimately, in **1838 CE**, the British partitioned Kota to create the independent princely state of **Jhalawar (झालावाड़)** for Zalim Singh's grandson, **Madan Singh Jhala** (the last princely state created in Rajasthan).

---

### 8.3 The Jats of Bharatpur (Sinsinwar Dynasty)
- **Peasant Rebellion Against Mughal Tyranny**:
  - **Gokula (1669 CE)**: Led Tilpat peasant revolt against Aurangzeb’s religious bigotry.
  - **Rajaram (1688 CE)**: Sinsinwar Jat leader who desecrated Emperor Akbar’s tomb at Sikandra (Agra), excavated Akbar’s bones, and consigned them to fire in accordance with Hindu funeral rites.
  - **Churaman (1695–1721 CE)**: Built the mud fortress of Thun, organized regular Jat cavalry.
- **Badan Singh (1722–1756 CE)**:
  - Formally established the royal house of Bharatpur. Sawai Jai Singh II recognized him as Raja, conferring the title **"Brajraj" (ब्रजराज)** and the estate of Deeg.
  - Constructed the magnificent water palaces of **Deeg (डीग के जलमहल)**, Kumher, and Vair.

#### Maharaja Suraj Mal (1756–1763 CE) — "The Plato of the Jat Tribe"
The most formidable, intellectually brilliant, and militarily unconquered monarch of the Jat dynasty:

#### Historiographical Epithets Conferred on Suraj Mal
1. **The Plato of the Jat Tribe (जाटों का प्लेटो)**: Bestowed by modern European and Indian historians for his statecraft, clear judicial intellect, and administrative acumen.
2. **The Ulysses of the Jats / Jat Aflatun (जाटों का अफलातून)**.

#### Maharaja Jawahar Singh & The Ashtadhatu Gates (1765 CE)
- Invaded Delhi in 1765 CE, besieged the Red Fort, and extracted imperial tribute.
- **The Historic Ashtadhatu Gates (अष्टधातु के किवाड़)**:
  - Removed the colossal eight-metal gates of Delhi's Red Fort.
  - **The Historical Provenance**: These monumental gates originally belonged to **Chittorgarh Fort**, looted by Sultan Alauddin Khalji in 1303 CE and brought to Delhi. Jawahar Singh triumphantly retrieved them and installed them permanently at the northern entrance of **Lohagarh Fort** in Bharatpur!

#### Maharaja Ranjit Singh & The Epic Defense of Lohagarh (1805 CE)
- During the Second Anglo-Maratha War, Maratha general **Jaswant Rao Holkar** sought sanctuary in Bharatpur after being pursued by British Commander-in-Chief **Lord Lake**.
- Honoring the sacred Rajput-Jat tradition of asylum (*Sharanagat Raksha*), Ranjit Singh flatly refused to surrender Holkar.
- **The Siege of Lohagarh (1805 CE)**: Lord Lake besieged Lohagarh Fort with heavy British siege artillery, launching **five successive assaults**. The thick mud ramparts absorbed the exploding iron cannonballs harmlessly. Lake lost over 3,000 British soldiers and commanders, withdrew in humiliation, and concluded a treaty with Ranjit Singh. Hence, the fort earned its eternal title: **"Lohagarh — The Invincible Iron Fort"**.

---57:T17bf,1. **Trap 1: The Kuldevi vs Ishta Devi of the Kachhwahas**:

2. **Trap 2: The First Capital of the Kachhwahas**:
   - *Trap*: Assuming Amer was the first capital.
   - *Fact*: **Dausa** was the first capital (founded 1137 CE by Dulherai); Amer was acquired 70 years later in **1207 CE by Kakil Dev**.

   - *Trap*: Calling Mariam-uz-Zamani "Jodha Bai".
   - *Fact*: Mariam-uz-Zamani was **Harkha Bai** (daughter of Bharmal of **Amber**). *Jodha Bai* (Mani Bai / Jagat Gosain) was the daughter of Mota Raja Udai Singh of **Jodhpur**!

   - *Trap*: Attributing Barah Kothri to Sawai Jai Singh II.
   - *Fact*: Founded by **Prithviraj Kachhwaha (1503–1527 CE)** for his 12 sons.

   - *Trap*: Believing Mirza Raja Jai Singh or Jaswant Singh held 7,000 mansab under Akbar.
   - *Fact*: Only **Mirza Raja Man Singh I** and Akbar's foster-brother **Mirza Aziz Koka** held the supreme mansab of **7,000 Jat and 6,000 Sawar** under Akbar.

---58:T2620,### 11.1 Section A: 2-Mark High-Density Formulations (15–20 Words)

#### Q1: What is the historical significance of the Sambhar Alliance (1562 CE)?
**Answer**: Contracted between **Raja Bharmal** and **Akbar**, it was the first matrimonial alliance between a Rajput ruler and the Mughals, inaugurating mutual military-political cooperation.

#### Q2: What was the "Barah Kothri" administrative system?
**Answer**: Instituted by **Prithviraj Kachhwaha** (Amer), partitioning the kingdom of Dhundhar into twelve autonomous noble estates for his twelve sons to prevent succession warfare.

#### Q3: State two key clauses of the Treaty of Purandar (1665 CE).
**Answer**: Concluded between **Mirza Raja Jai Singh** and **Chhatrapati Shivaji**: (1) Shivaji surrendered 23 of 35 forts to the Mughals; (2) Prince Sambhaji received 5,000 Mansab.

#### Q4: Why was the 1550 CE conflict in Jaisalmer designated as an "Ardha Sāka"?
**Answer**: Rawal Lunkaran and warriors performed Kesariya against Amir Ali of Kandahar and won the battle; hence, traditional female fire Jauhar was not performed.

#### Q5: What was the primary objective and outcome of the Hurda Conference (1734 CE)?
**Answer**: Organized by **Sawai Jai Singh II** to forge a pan-Rajput military coalition against Maratha incursions. It collapsed due to internal noble rivalries.

#### Q6: Why is Maharaja Suraj Mal termed the "Plato of the Jat Tribe"?
**Answer**: Conferred by historians in recognition of his extraordinary statesmanship, cool intellect, unyielding military defense, and administrative sagacity.

#### Q7: Who was Gandharva Baisi?
**Answer**: The royal cultural academy of **Sawai Pratap Singh** (Jaipur), comprising 22 scholars, 22 classical musicians, 22 poets, 22 astrologers, and 22 physicians patronized inside *Gunijan Khana*.

### 11.2 Section B: 5-Mark Analytical Blueprints (50 Words)

#### Q8: Analyze the military and administrative stature of Mirza Raja Man Singh I under Emperor Akbar.
**Answer**:
Mirza Raja Man Singh I (1589–1614 CE) was the pre-eminent Hindu general of the Mughal Empire:
- **Unrivalled Mansab**: Held the premier rank of 7,000 Jat and 6,000 Sawar, alongside royal titles *"Farzand"* and *"Mirza Raja"*.
- **Imperial Conquests**: Commanded the Battle of Haldighati (1576); governed Kabul, Bihar, and Bengal (three tenures); annexed Orissa (1592) and crushed eastern Afghan insurgencies.
- **Cultural Imprint**: Constructed Amer Palaces, Jagat Shiromani Temple, and consecrated the historic Shila Devi idol in Amer Fort.

#### Q9: Outline the urban and architectural planning principles of Jaipur city (1727 CE).
**Answer**:
Founded on 18 November 1727 CE by Sawai Jai Singh II with Bengali architect Vidyadhar Bhattacharya:
- **Classical Alignment**: Synthesized ancient Vastu Shastra, Shilpa Shastra, and European gridiron layouts.
- **Nine Chowkris**: Divided the walled city into 9 rectangular sectors (*Nau Chowkris*), reflecting the nine celestial planets (*Nav-Graha*).
- **Geometric Grid**: Built wide straight avenues (111 feet wide) intersecting at exact right angles (*Chaupars*), enclosed within defensive city walls featuring 7 majestic gateways.

#### Q10: Explain the defense architecture that rendered Lohagarh Fort (Bharatpur) impregnable.
**Answer**:
Constructed in 1733 CE by Maharaja Suraj Mal, Lohagarh Fort represented an unbreachable defensive marvel:
- **Double Mud Ramparts**: Surrounded by thick, outer mud walls behind stone masonry which harmlessly absorbed explosive iron artillery cannonballs without shattering.
- **Sujan Ganga Moat**: Encircled by a deep, wide water trench fed by the Ruparel and Banganga rivers, preventing subterranean mining and sapping.
- **Military Record**: Successfully repulsed five massive siege assaults by British Commander-in-Chief Lord Lake in 1805 CE.

#### Q12: Trace the evolution of the Kachhwaha dynasty's relationship with imperial powers from Raja Bharmal's 1562 alliance to the 1818 British Subsidiary Treaty.
**Answer**:
The geopolitical orientation of the Kachhwahas evolved across four transformative epochs between 1562 and 1818 CE:

1. **The Foundation of Strategic Subservience (Bharmal to Bhagwan Das, 1562–1589)**:
   - Bharmal pioneered the 1562 Sambhar matrimonial accord with Akbar, trading regional isolation for imperial patronage (*Amir-ul-Umara*).
   - Ensured dynastic survival against hostile Mewat governors, embedding Amber's nobility into the administrative core of the Mughal Empire.

2. **The Era of Imperial Hegemony (Man Singh I to Mirza Raja Jai Singh, 1589–1667)**:
   - Kachhwahas served as supreme field marshals of the empire. Man Singh conquered Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, attaining 7,000 mansab.
   - Mirza Raja Jai Singh served three emperors across 46 years, orchestrating the historic Treaty of Purandar (1665) against Shivaji Maharaj, establishing Amber as the premier power in Rajasthan.

3. **Autonomous Renaissance & Maratha Vulnerability (Sawai Jai Singh II to Pratap Singh, 1700–1803)**:
   - Sawai Jai Singh II exploited Mughal decline to construct Jaipur (1727) and revive sovereign Vedic rites.
   - The collapse of imperial Delhi exposed Dhundhar to devastating Maratha incursions. Despite victories at Rajmahal (1747) and Tunga (1787), internal succession wars (Ishwari vs Madho Singh) and crippling Holkar-Scindia extortion exhausted the state's treasury.

4. **The British Subsidiary Alliance (Sawai Jagat Singh II, 1818)**:
   - Devastated by Pindari marauders and Maratha tribute demands, Sawai Jagat Singh II signed the Treaty of Subordinate Alliance with the British on 2 April 1818, terminating sovereign military autonomy in exchange for British crown protection.

#### The Diplomatic Architecture: Lord Hastings & Charles Metcalfe
- **Imperial Architect**: The British Governor-General, **The Marquess of Hastings (Lord Hastings, 1813–1823)**, reversed the non-intervention (*Laissez-faire*) policy of Lord Barlow and Sir George Barlow, inaugurating the doctrine of **Subordinate Cooperation (अधीनस्थ पृथक्करण की नीति)**.
- **Principal Diplomatic Negotiator**: **Sir Charles Metcalfe (चार्ल्स मेटकॉफ)**, the British Resident at Delhi, was entrusted with the diplomatic portfolio to negotiate, draft, and finalize subsidiary treaties with the Rajput states. He was assisted by **Captain James Tod** (Mewar, Kota, Bundi) and **John Malcolm** (Malwa and southern Rajputana).

---

### 1.2 Core Treaty Provisions & Institutional Framework
The standard bilateral treaties signed between the British East India Company and the Rajput princely houses contained uniform institutional covenants:
1. **Surrender of External Sovereignty**: Princely states surrendered the right to maintain independent foreign relations, wage war, or enter into diplomatic correspondence with any other Indian or foreign power.
2. **British Protection & Garrisoning**: The East India Company guaranteed territorial integrity and military defense against external aggression and internal rebellions.
3. **The Tribute (*Khiraj* / खिराज)**: Princely states agreed to pay an annual tribute (*Khiraj*) to the British, calculated initially as the tribute previously extracted by the Marathas.
   - **Exemption Exceptions**: **Jaisalmer, Bikaner, and Alwar** paid **zero Khiraj** because they had never been subjugated to Maratha tribute demands.
4. **Non-Interference Clause (Article 3/9)**: The Company pledged not to interfere in the internal civil administration of the princely states (a clause routinely violated through appointed Political Agents).
5. **Appointment of Political Agents**: A British Political Agent (PA) was stationed at key royal courts to oversee British interests and monitor state finances.

---

#### Crucial Examination Invariants Regarding the Treaties
1. **The Supplementary Treaty of Kota (February 1818)**: Metcalfe added a secret supplementary clause declaring that while Ummed Singh's progeny would inherit the throne (*Rajya*), the executive administrative authority (*Diwani / Faujdari*) would remain hereditary to **Faujdar Zalim Singh Jhala** and his descendants, leading directly to future civil war (Battle of Mangrol 1821) and the ultimate creation of **Jhalawar State (1838 CE)**.
2. **The Sirohi Delay (1823 CE)**: Sirohi was the final state to sign in 1823 because Maharaja Man Singh of Jodhpur falsely claimed that Sirohi was an internal feudal dependency (*Pargana*) of Marwar. British investigations under Col. Tod disproved this claim, granting Sirohi sovereign treaty status on 11 September 1823.
3. **Creation of Tonk Princely State (November 1817)**: The British detached Tonk from Indore (Holkar) and established it as an independent Muslim princely state under **Nawab Amir Khan Pindari** in November 1817 to neutralize the Pindari threat.

  - Agent to the Governor-General for Rajputana (Mount Abu / Ajmer): **George Patrick Lawrence (जॉर्ज पैट्रिक लॉरेंस)**.
  - Subordinate **Political Agents (PAs)** stationed at princely capitals:

---5a:T1384,### 2.1 Causes of Discontent in Rajasthan
1. **Economic Exploitation**: Crippling *Khiraj* payments drained state treasuries, forcing princes to levy heavy cess (*Lāg-Bāg*) and land revenue (*Bhog*) upon peasants and Jagirdars.
2. **Erosion of Feudal Privileges**: British interference disrupted the centuries-old relationship between Rajput rulers and their hereditary Jagirdars (*Samants*), disenfranchising the nobility.
3. **Interference in Religious & Social Customs**: Abolition of Sati, banning of Samadhi and female infanticide, combined with fears of religious conversion fueled by rumors of bone-dust mixed in flour and greased cartridges (*Enfield Rifle*).
4. **Disbandment of Native Armies**: The British disbanded traditional state armies, establishing British-officered local corps (e.g., Mewar Bhil Corps, Jodhpur Legion, Shekhawati Brigade) financed directly from state treasuries.

---

### 2.2 The Six British Military Cantonments in Rajasthan
During May 1857, approximately 5,000 native Indian soldiers served in British regiments across Rajasthan, supervised by around 30 British officers. **Not a single British European soldier or regiment was stationed in Rajasthan** (the nearest European troops were in Agra and Deesa, Gujarat).

#### Detailed Breakdown of Cantonments

| Cantonment | Modern District Location | Stationed Native Regiment | Outbreak Date | Participated in Revolt? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: |
| **Naseerabad (नसीराबाद)** | Ajmer | 15th & 30th Bengal Native Infantry, Bombay Lancers | 28 May 1857 | **YES (Epicenter)** |
| **Neemuch (नीमच)** | Erstwhile Rajputana Agency (Now MP border) | 1st Bengal Cavalry, Artillery, 72nd N.I. | 3 June 1857 | **YES** |
| **Erinpura (एरिनपुरा)** | Pali (near Sirohi border) | Jodhpur Legion (जोधपुर लीजन) | 21 August 1857 | **YES** |
| **Deoli (देवली)** | Tonk | Mahidpur Regiment & Kota Contingent cavalry | 5 June 1857 | **YES** |
| **Beawar (ब्यावर)** | Beawar (erstwhile Ajmer) | Mer Regiment / Merwara Battalion (मेर रेजीमेंट) | — | **NO (Remained loyal)** |
| **Kherwara (खेरवाड़ा)**| Udaipur | Mewar Bhil Corps (मेवाड़ भील कोर — MBC) | — | **NO (Remained passive)** |

> **Key Takeaway**: **Beawar and Kherwara** cantonments did NOT take part in the 1857 Revolution!

---5b:T3fc7,### 3.1 The Naseerabad Outbreak (28 May 1857) — The First Spark
- **Trigger**: Following the Meerut outbreak, AGG George Patrick Lawrence grew suspicious of the **15th Bengal Native Infantry (BNI)** stationed in Ajmer (which protected the imperial magazine and treasury) and disarmed/transferred them to Naseerabad. This insult, combined with the presence of greased cartridges and armed patrols of the loyal Bombay Lancers, triggered the revolt.
- **The Strike**: On the afternoon of **28 May 1857**, soldiers of the 15th BNI mutinied, seizing the artillery battery. They were joined by the **30th Bengal Native Infantry**.
- **British Casualties**:
  - **Major Spottiswoode** and **Colonel Newbery** were killed on the spot.
  - **Lt. Lock** and **Captain Hardy** were wounded.
  - British officers, women, and children evacuated under escort of Bombay Lancers towards Beawar.
- **March to Delhi**: After ransacking the cantonment, burning bungalows, and seizing state funds, the sepoys marched directly to Delhi to reinforce the Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar.

---

### 3.2 The Neemuch Outbreak (3 June 1857) & The Rungaram Episode
- **The Loyalty Oath Confrontation (2 June 1857)**: British commander **Colonel Abbott** assembled the garrison on 2 June and administered a solemn oath of loyalty on the Quran and Gita. An Indian officer, **Mohammad Ali Beg (मोहम्मद अली बेग)**, boldly stood up and challenged Abbott:
  > *"Did you British remain loyal to your oath when you deceitfully annexed Awadh? Why then should Indians be bound to oaths of loyalty to you?"*
- **The Outbreak (3 June 1857)**: At 11:00 PM on 3 June, led by **Mohammad Ali Beg** and Subedar **Hira Singh**, the Neemuch garrison revolted, fired artillery, and burned British bungalows.
- **The Doongla Shelter & Rungaram**:
  - Approximately 40 British officers, women, and children fled Neemuch under Captain Showers.
  - They reached **Doongla village (डूंगला, Chittorgarh)**, where a noble peasant farmer named **Rungaram (रूंगाराम)** provided them shelter and food despite grave personal risk.
- **Maharana Swaroop Singh's Sanctuary at Jag Mandir**:
  - Mewar's **Maharana Swaroop Singh**, guided by Political Agent Major Showers, dispatched Mewari troops to rescue the refugees.
  - Swaroop Singh accommodated them safely within the **Jag Mandir Palace (जग मंदिर)** in Pichhola Lake, Udaipur, appointing **Gokulchand Mehta** to oversee their hospitality and security.

---

### 3.3 The Erinpura Outbreak & The Jodhpur Legion (21 August 1857)
- **The Mount Abu Trigger**: In August 1857, a contingent of 90 soldiers of the **Jodhpur Legion** was stationed at Mount Abu for training.
- **The Attack at Mount Abu (21 August 1857)**: Led by **Motiram**, **Sheetaldas**, and **Tilakram**, the sepoys attacked the British barracks at Mount Abu, wounding AGG Lawrence’s son, Captain Arthur Lawrence.
- **The Assembly at Erinpura**: The mutineers marched to the main cantonment at Erinpura on 23 August, where the entire garrison mutinied, looting the treasury and armory.
- **The Historic War Cry**: Indian Christian officer **Subedar Moti Khan**, **Subedar Sheetaldas**, and **Dafedar Abdul Ali** hoisted the flag of freedom, leading the march towards Delhi with the iconic battle cry:
  > *"चलो दिल्ली, मारो फिरंगी!"*  
  > *(March to Delhi, Slay the Foreigner!)*

---

### 3.4 Auwa's Epic Resistance: Thakur Kushal Singh Champawat

```

#### The Battle of Bithoda (8 September 1857 / बिथोड़ा का युद्ध)
- **Combatants**: Thakur Kushal Singh and allied revolutionaries vs the joint army of **Jodhpur Maharaja Takht Singh** (commanded by Faujdar **Onad Singh / Anar Singh**) and British artillery under **Captain Heathcote**.
- **Outcome**: The revolutionaries crushed the royalist-British forces:
  - Faujdar **Onad Singh was killed** on the battlefield; Rajmata's horse was captured.
  - Captain Heathcote fled for his life.
  - Huge quantities of artillery, guns, and ammunition fell into the hands of the Auwa patriots.

#### The Battle of Chelawas (18 September 1857 / चेलावास का युद्ध) — "The Battle of Black and White"
Ten days after Bithoda, AGG George Patrick Lawrence marched personally from Ajmer with an elite imperial army, joined by the Political Agent of Jodhpur, **Mock Mason (मॉक मेसन)**.
- **The Nomenclature**: Known across Rajasthani folklore as the **"Battle of Black and White" (गोरों-कालों का युद्ध)** due to the direct confrontation between European British troops ("Gora") and native Indian patriots ("Kala").
- **Climax & Severed Head of Mock Mason**:
  - The revolutionaries routed Lawrence’s army; Lawrence fled towards Beawar.
  - Political Agent **Mock Mason was killed** outside Auwa.
  - The revolutionaries **severed Mock Mason's head**, paraded it through the village with beating drums, and **hung it defiantly on the main monumental gate of Auwa Fort**!

```
                    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │          THE BATTLE OF CHELAWAS (18 SEPT 1857)         │
                    │               "GORON-KALON KA YUDDHA"                  │
                    └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                                │
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                                             │

│   and Jodhpur PA Mock Mason.         │                     │ • Severed head hung on Auwa Fort Gate.           │

└──────────────────────────────────────┘                     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### The Celebrated Bardic Folk Songs of Auwa
The defiance of Auwa inspired timeless Dingal and Marwari patriotic folk ballads:
> *"ढोल बाजे, चंग बाजे, भलो बाजे बांकियो।*  
> *एजेंट ने मार कर, आउवा के दरवाजे पर टांकियो॥"*  
*(Drums echo, changs resound, and the clarion pipe plays gloriously! Slaying the British Agent, they nailed him to the gate of Auwa!)*

#### The Fall of Auwa (January 1858) & Major Taylor Commission
- **British Counter-Attack**: In January 1858, British Commander-in-Chief **Brigadier Holmes** surrounded Auwa with a colossal army and siege artillery.
- **Evacuation**: Sensing that artillery would pulverize the fort, Kushal Singh handed over defense to his younger brother **Prithvi Singh of Lambiya** and slipped out safely under cover of heavy rain and fog.
- **Sanctuary**: Sheltered by **Rawat Jodh Singh** of Kothariya (Mewar) and **Rawat Kesari Singh** of Salumber.
- **Sack of Auwa (24 January 1858)**: Holmes captured Auwa, blew up its ramparts, seized the sacred idol of **Sugali Mata**, and took it to Ajmer.
- **The Major Taylor Commission (1860 CE)**:
  - Kushal Singh surrendered before British authorities at Neemuch in August 1860.
  - The British constituted the **Major Taylor Commission** to investigate his role in the murder of Mock Mason.
  - The Commission **acquitted Kushal Singh** of murder charges, ruling that Mock Mason was killed in open military engagement, not through premeditated assassination.
  - Kushal Singh passed away peacefully at Udaipur in 1864 CE.

---

### 3.5 The Kota Mass Uprising (15 October 1857) — The Democratic Revolution
The rebellion at Kota stands distinct in Indian history: it was **not** initiated by regular military cantonment sepoys, but by **local state troops, common citizens, and administrative officials**, establishing an independent civil administration for nearly six months!

```
                    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │        THE KOTA POPULAR UPRISING (OCTOBER 1857)        │
                    └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                                │
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                                             │
┌────────┴─────────────────────────────┐                     ┌─────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
│  Leaders & Mobilization              │                     │  The Siege & Fall of Residency                   │
├──────────────────────────────────────┤                     ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Lala Jaidayal (लाला जयदयाल)       │                     │ • Date: 15 October 1857.                         │
│    - Prominent advocate/clerk from   │                     │ • Residency besieged; Major Burton, sons Arthur  │
│      Kama (Bharatpur).               │                       and Frank, and Dr. Sadler executed.              │
│ 2. Mehrab Khan (मेहराब खां)          │                     │ • Burton's head severed and paraded through the  │
│    - Risaldar in Kota state cavalry  │                       streets of Kota.                                 │
│      from Karauli.                   │                     │ • Maharao Ram Singh II imprisoned in palace.     │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘                     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### The 9-Point Treaty of Capitulation
The revolutionaries held **Maharao Ram Singh II of Kota** captive inside his royal palace (*Garh*).
- Under the mediation of Goswami Kanhaiyalal of Mathuradheesh Temple, they compelled the Maharao to sign a humiliating **9-point treaty**.
- Clause 1 of the treaty explicitly forced the Maharao to state: *"I, Maharao Ram Singh, take full personal responsibility for the murder of Major Burton and his sons, and the sepoys acted upon my orders."*
- For nearly **six months (October 1857 to March 1858)**, the revolutionary civil administration of Jaidayal and Mehrab Khan collected taxes, operated the treasury, and governed Kota.

#### The Liberation of Kota (March 1858) & Re-alignment of Gun Salutes
- **Joint Relief Operation**: In March 1858, British forces under **General H.G. Roberts** attacked Kota, supported by a 2,000-man relief army dispatched by **Maharaja Madan Pal of Karauli**.
- Kota was recaptured after ferocious street-to-street fighting on **30 March 1858**.
- **Execution of Leaders**: **Mehrab Khan was hanged** from a tree near the Agency on 12 October 1859, and **Lala Jaidayal was hanged** at Kota on 17 September 1860.
- **The Gun Salute Alteration (*Topon ki Salami*)**:
  - The British held Maharao Ram Singh II guilty of cowardice/collusion; his official gun salute was **reduced from 17 guns to 13 guns**.
  - In gratitude for his loyal intervention, Maharaja Madan Pal of Karauli had his gun salute **increased from 13 guns to 17 guns** and was decorated with the title **G.C.S.I.** (Knight Grand Commander of the Star of India).

### 4.1 The Dholpur Revolt — External Sepoys & Patiala Rescue
- In October 1857, approximately 1,000 rebel troops from **Gwalior and Indore**, led by **Ramchandra** and **Hira Lal (Deva)**, invaded Dholpur.
- Joined by local state forces, they seized the palace, looted the treasury, and held **Maharaja Bhagwant Singh** captive for nearly two months.
- **Restoration**: Order was restored only in December 1857 when the ruler of **Patiala (Punjab)**, a Sikh ally of the British, sent a 2,000-strong army with artillery to liberate Dholpur.

### 4.2 The Tonk Revolt & Armed Participation of Women
- **Nawab Wazir-ud-Daulah** supported the British administration, but his army, led by his maternal uncle **Mir Alam Khan**, revolted and joined Tatya Tope.
- **Female Combatants**: The drama *Teesra Farishta* by Mohammad Mujeeb chronicles that women in Tonk took up arms, wore soldier uniforms, and fought British detachments directly on the battlefield.

---5d:Ta9b,### 5.1 Amar Chand Bathiya (अमरचंद बांठिया, 1793–1858 CE)
- **Identity**: Native of **Bikaner**; served as the hereditary royal treasurer (*Nagar Seth* / Cashier) of the Gwalior Scindia treasury.
- **The Supreme Financial Sacrifice**: Inspired by the freedom struggle, Bathiya unlocked the entire imperial Gwalior treasury and handed over all funds, gold, and resources to **Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi** and **Tatya Tope** to finance their army.
- **Martyrdom (22 June 1858)**: Captured by the British and publicly **hanged from a Neem tree** at the Sarafa market in Gwalior.
- **Historiographical Titles**:
  1. **The Mangal Pandey of Rajasthan (राजस्थान का मंगल पांडे)**: The first martyr from Rajasthan in the 1857 Revolution.
  2. **The Bhama Shah of 1857 (1857 की क्रांति का भामाशाह)**: Honoring his selfless financing of Rani Lakshmibai’s army.

---

### 5.2 Tatya Tope's Campaigns in Rajasthan (1857–1859 CE)
Ramchandra Pandurang Topi (**Tatya Tope**), the legendary general of Nana Saheb Peshwa, entered Rajasthan twice to mobilize the Rajput princes:
- **First Entry (June 1858)**: Entered Mewar via Bhilwara.
  - **Battle of Kuwada (कुवाड़ा का युद्ध, 9 August 1858)**: Fought near Kothari River (Bhilwara); defeated by British General Roberts.
  - Advanced to Kankroli, Rukmangarh, and captured Jhalawar (ousted Maharao Prithvi Singh).
- **Second Entry (December 1858)**: Entered Banswara via Mewar, temporarily captured Banswara (Maharawal Laxman Singh fled to the jungle).
- **The Betrayal & Martyrdom (1859 CE)**: Betrayed by his trusted friend, Jagirdar **Man Singh Naruka** of Narwar (who revealed his forest hideout in the Paron jungles to British Major Meade). Captured and publicly **hanged at Shivpuri (Madhya Pradesh)** on **18 April 1859**.

---

### 5.3 Suryamal Misran (सूर्यमल्ल मीसण, 1815–1868 CE) — The National Poet
- **Identity**: Court poet (*Raj Kavi*) of Maharao Ram Singh of **Bundi**.
- **Literary Resistance**: Authored **Veer Satsai (वीर सतसई)**, **Vansh Bhaskar (वंश भास्कर)**, *Balwant Vilas*, and *Chhandomayukh*.
- Dispatched fiery letters and Dingal couplets to Rajput princes urging them to overthrow the British yoke:
  > *"इला न देणी आपणी, हालरिये हुलराय।*  
  > *पूत सिखावै पालणै, मरण बड़ाई माय॥"*  
  *(Never yield your sacred motherland to the foreigner! The mother rocks the cradle, singing to her newborn: die on the battlefield, for therein lies eternal honor!)*

---5e:Te55,### 6.1 The Princely Houses: "Breakwaters in the Storm"
With the exception of minor Jagirdars (Auwa, Asop, Gular, Kothariya, Salumber), **every single crowned ruling prince of Rajasthan actively supported the British East India Company** with money, camels, horses, and armies to suppress the 1857 uprising:

```
┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Princely State               │ Reigning Monarch (1857)      │ Specific Active Support Rendered to the British        │
├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ **Mewar (Udaipur)**          │ Maharana Swaroop Singh       │ Sheltered 40 Neemuch British refugees at Jag Mandir    │
│ **Marwar (Jodhpur)**         │ Maharaja Takht Singh         │ Sent royal army under Onad Singh to crush Auwa patriots│
│ **Jaipur**                   │ Sawai Ram Singh II           │ Dispatched state army; Rewarded with Kotputli pargana  │
│ **Bikaner**                  │ Maharaja Sardar Singh        │ Personally marched outside state to crush rebels!      │
│ **Kota**                     │ Maharao Ram Singh II         │ Maintained secret loyalty despite 6-month rebel captivity│
│ **Karauli**                  │ Maharaja Madan Pal           │ Sent 2,000 troops to liberate Kota; Salute raised to 17│
│ **Bharatpur**                │ Maharaja Jaswant Singh (Minor) Dispatched state cavalry to patrol Agra-Delhi road    │
│ **Alwar**                    │ Maharao Raja Vinay Singh     │ Sent army & artillery to relieve British at Agra      │
│ **Sirohi**                   │ Maharao Shiv Singh           │ Sheltered British officers evacuated from Mount Abu   │
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### The Sole Exception: Maharaja Sardar Singh of Bikaner
- **Maharaja Sardar Singh (सरदार सिंह, Bikaner)** was the **only ruler in all of India** who personally rode out at the head of his military army **beyond the territorial borders of his princely state (marching into Badlu, Punjab/Haryana)** to hunt down and suppress Indian mutineers on behalf of the British crown.
- **British Reward**: An immensely grateful British Government rewarded Sardar Singh with **41 villages of the fertile Tibbi Pargana (टिब्बी परगना)**, annexed to Bikaner state.

#### Lord Canning's Famous Pronouncement
Governor-General **Lord Canning** summarized the indispensable support of the Rajput monarchs in his official post-war despatch:
> *"If the Rajput princes had not acted as **Breakwaters in the storm (तूफान में तरंग-रोधक)**, our British Empire in India would have been swept away in a single sweep of the wave."*

---60:T16f7,1. **Trap 1: The First vs Last State to Sign 1818 Treaties**:
   - *Trap*: Stating Sirohi was first or Bharatpur was first under Hastings.
   - *Fact*: Under Lord Hastings (1817–1823), **Karauli (9 Nov 1817)** was the first state to sign; **Sirohi (11 Sept 1823)** was the 17th and last state to sign.

2. **Trap 2: Princely States Paying Zero Tribute (*Khiraj*)**:
   - *Trap*: Assuming all 17 states paid Khiraj.
   - *Fact*: **Jaisalmer, Bikaner, and Alwar** paid **zero Khiraj** because they had no historical liability for Maratha Chauth.

3. **Trap 3: The Secret Clause of Kota’s Treaty**:
   - *Trap*: Believing the clause favored Maharao Ummed Singh.
   - *Fact*: The secret supplementary clause preserved hereditary administration for **Faujdar Zalim Singh Jhala** and his lineage, sidelining the royal dynasty.

4. **Trap 4: Reason for Sirohi's 5-Year Delay**:
   - *Trap*: Thinking Sirohi militarily resisted the British.
   - *Fact*: Delayed because **Maharaja Man Singh of Jodhpur** falsely claimed Sirohi was a subordinate fiefdom of Marwar.

5. **Trap 5: The Non-Participating Cantonments of 1857**:
   - *Trap*: Stating all 6 cantonments revolted.
   - *Fact*: **Beawar (Mer Battalion)** and **Kherwara (Mewar Bhil Corps)** did **NOT** revolt!

6. **Trap 6: The Epicenter / First Center of 1857 in Rajasthan**:
   - *Trap*: Selecting Meerut or Neemuch.
   - *Fact*: The first outbreak occurred at **Naseerabad on 28 May 1857** (18 days after Meerut).

7. **Trap 7: The Fate of the 40 Neemuch British Refugees**:
   - *Trap*: Claiming they were killed at Doongla.
   - *Fact*: Sheltered by peasant **Rungaram** at Doongla, then safely escorted by Major Showers to Udaipur, where Maharana Swaroop Singh lodged them at **Jag Mandir Palace**.

8. **Trap 8: The Slogan "Chalo Dilli, Maro Firangi"**:
   - *Trap*: Attributing the slogan to Naseerabad sepoys.
   - *Fact*: Coined and raised by the soldiers of the **Jodhpur Legion at Erinpura** (21 August 1857).

9. **Trap 9: Date & Opponents at Battle of Bithoda**:
   - *Trap*: Thinking George Lawrence fought at Bithoda.
   - *Fact*: **Bithoda (8 September 1857)** was fought against **Onad Singh** (Jodhpur army) and **Captain Heathcote**. Lawrence fought ten days later at **Chelawas (18 September 1857)**.

10. **Trap 10: "The Battle of Black and White" (*Goron-Kalon ka Yuddha*)**:
    - *Trap*: Confusing Bithoda with Chelawas.
    - *Fact*: It is the **Battle of Chelawas (18 September 1857)** where Mock Mason was killed and George Lawrence was routed.

11. **Trap 11: Iconography of Sugali Mata**:
    - *Trap*: Describing Sugali Mata with 8 or 10 arms.
    - *Fact*: Sugali Mata has **10 heads and 54 arms**; Kuldevi of the Champawat clan of Auwa.

12. **Trap 12: Major Taylor Commission Verdict**:
    - *Trap*: Assuming Thakur Kushal Singh was sentenced to death.
    - *Fact*: The commission **acquitted Kushal Singh** of murder charges in 1860, recognizing Mock Mason’s death as a casualty of open war.

13. **Trap 13: Nature of the Kota Revolt**:
    - *Trap*: Believing regular cantonment troops mutinied in Kota.
    - *Fact*: Kota had **no British military cantonment**. The revolt was led by state soldiers and civilians (**Lala Jaidayal and Mehrab Khan**), establishing 6 months of civil administration.

14. **Trap 14: Gun Salute Adjustment Post-1857**:
    - *Trap*: Thinking Kota’s salute was increased.
    - *Fact*: **Kota’s salute was decreased from 17 to 13 guns**; **Karauli’s salute was increased from 13 to 17 guns** (for sending 2,000 troops under Madan Pal to liberate Kota).

15. **Trap 15: The Only Ruler Who Campaigned Outside His State**:
    - *Trap*: Naming Takht Singh or Swaroop Singh.
    - *Fact*: **Maharaja Sardar Singh of Bikaner**, who marched with his forces into **Badlu (Punjab/Haryana)**, rewarded with 41 villages of Tibbi pargana.

16. **Trap 16: The First Martyr of Rajasthan in 1857**:
    - *Trap*: Naming Thakur Kushal Singh or Mehrab Khan.
    - *Fact*: **Amar Chand Bathiya** of Bikaner, hanged at Gwalior on 22 June 1858; known as the *"Mangal Pandey of Rajasthan"*.

17. **Trap 17: "The Bhama Shah of 1857"**:
    - *Trap*: Conferred upon Bhama Shah of Mewar.
    - *Fact*: Bestowed upon **Amar Chand Bathiya** for giving the imperial Gwalior treasury to Rani Lakshmibai and Tatya Tope.

18. **Trap 18: Betrayer of Tatya Tope**:
    - *Trap*: Claiming a British spy betrayed him.
    - *Fact*: Betrayed by his close friend, **Man Singh Naruka** (Jagirdar of Narwar), in the Paron forests.

19. **Trap 19: Execution Site of Tatya Tope**:
    - *Trap*: Hanged at Ajmer or Gwalior.
    - *Fact*: Hanged at **Shivpuri (Madhya Pradesh)** on 18 April 1859.

20. **Trap 20: The Dholpur Liberation Force**:
    - *Trap*: Liberated by British European troops from Agra.
    - *Fact*: Liberated by a 2,000-man army sent by the **Maharaja of Patiala (Punjab)**.

21. **Trap 21: Women Combatants in 1857 Rajasthan**:
    - *Trap*: Believing women fought only in Jhansi.
    - *Fact*: Women actively took up arms and fought in the **princely state of Tonk**.

22. **Trap 22: First Agent to the Governor-General (AGG)**:
    - *Trap*: Believing George Lawrence was the first AGG.
    - *Fact*: **Major Abraham Lockett** was the first AGG (1832 CE); George Lawrence was AGG during 1857.

23. **Trap 23: Summer Capital of the Rajputana Agency**:
    - *Trap*: Shifted to Mount Abu in 1832.
    - *Fact*: Shifted to **Mount Abu in 1845 CE** (remained at Ajmer from 1832 to 1845).

24. **Trap 24: Author of Veer Satsai**:
    - *Trap*: Bankidas Asiya.
    - *Fact*: **Suryamal Misran** (Court poet of Bundi). Bankidas wrote *Aayo Angrez Mulk re Upar*.

25. **Trap 25: "Breakwaters in the Storm"**:
    - *Trap*: Uttered by Lord Dalhousie.
    - *Fact*: Uttered by Governor-General **Lord Canning** to describe the collaborative loyalty of the Rajput princes.

---61:T2549,### 9.1 Section A: 2-Mark High-Density Formulations (15–20 Words)

#### Q1: Which was the first and last princely state in Rajasthan to sign the 1818 treaties?
**Answer**: Under Lord Hastings' policy, **Karauli** signed first on 9 November 1817; **Sirohi** signed last on 11 September 1823.

#### Q2: Name the two military cantonments in Rajasthan that did not participate in the 1857 Revolt.
**Answer**: **Beawar** (manned by the Merwara Battalion) and **Kherwara** (manned by the Mewar Bhil Corps) did not revolt.

#### Q3: What is the significance of the Battle of Chelawas (18 September 1857)?
**Answer**: Known as the *"Battle of Black and White"*, revolutionaries routed AGG Lawrence's army and decapitated Jodhpur Political Agent **Mock Mason**, hanging his head on Auwa Fort.

#### Q4: Why is Amar Chand Bathiya revered as the "Mangal Pandey of Rajasthan"?
**Answer**: A Bikaner native and Gwalior state treasurer, he financed Rani Lakshmibai’s army with royal funds; hanged by the British on 22 June 1858 as Rajasthan’s first martyr.

#### Q5: State the primary reason for the alteration of gun salutes of Kota and Karauli after 1857.
**Answer**: Kota's salute was reduced from 17 to 13 for royal negligence during Burton's execution; Karauli's was raised from 13 to 17 for sending 2,000 troops to liberate Kota.

#### Q6: What was the historic slogan of the Jodhpur Legion soldiers at Erinpura?
**Answer**: *"Chalo Dilli, Maro Firangi"* (चलो दिल्ली, मारो फिरंगी), coined on 21 August 1857 under Subedar Moti Khan, Tilakram, and Sheetaldas.

#### Q7: Who was Sugali Mata?
**Answer**: The 10-headed, 54-armed tutelary deity of Thakur Kushal Singh Champawat of Auwa, venerated as the patron goddess of 1857 freedom fighters in Rajasthan.

---

### 9.2 Section B: 5-Mark Analytical Blueprints (50 Words)

#### Q8: Analyze the strategic provisions and consequences of the Subordinate Alliance Treaties of 1818 in Rajasthan.
**Answer**:
Negotiated primarily by Charles Metcalfe under Lord Hastings:
- **Core Covenants**: Princely states surrendered foreign affairs and defense to the British Company, paid annual tribute (*Khiraj*), and received internal territorial guarantees.
- **Consequences**:
  - Severed external defense autonomy; institutionalized British Political Agents (*PAs*) who usurped sovereign power.
  - Sapped princely treasuries via heavy tribute, prompting rulers to impose excessive *Lāg-Bāg* (taxes) on peasants and feudals, creating the seeds of the 1857 uprising and peasant movements.

#### Q9: Detail the unique popular character of the 1857 uprising in Kota.
**Answer**:
The Kota uprising (15 October 1857) represented the pinnacle of popular civil resistance in Rajasthan:
- **Absence of Cantonment**: Not a sepoy mutiny, but an organized rebellion by state forces and citizens led by **Lala Jaidayal** and **Mehrab Khan**.
- **Residency Assault**: Executed Political Agent Major Charles Burton and his sons; imprisoned Maharao Ram Singh II in his palace.
- **Civil Administration**: Ran an independent people's government for nearly six months, collecting taxes and administering justice until liberated by General Roberts and Karauli troops in March 1858.

#### Q10: Evaluate the role of Thakur Kushal Singh of Auwa in the 1857 resistance.
**Answer**:
Thakur Kushal Singh Champawat served as the focal point of military resistance against British imperialism in Marwar:
- **Military Victories**: United Erinpura mutineers with local feudal levies, achieving back-to-back victories at **Bithoda** (8 Sept 1857, killing Onad Singh) and **Chelawas** (18 Sept 1857, slaying PA Mock Mason).
- **Spiritual & Feudal Symbol**: Fought beneath the banner of **Sugali Mata**, inspiring the peasantry across Marwar.
- **Honor Preserved**: Evacuated Auwa before Holmes' siege; later acquitted by the Major Taylor Commission (1860) of murder charges.

---

**Conclusion**: While regional Jagirdars (Auwa, Asop) and common folk revolted passionately, the sovereign princes identified their dynastic survival with British paramountcy. Their armies, treasuries, and logistics insulated British garrisons, preventing the uprising from consolidating a unified provincial front.

#### Q12: Trace the chronological progression, major centers, and underlying causes of failure of the 1857 Revolution in Rajasthan.
**Answer**:
The 1857 Revolution in Rajasthan developed across several vibrant military theaters before succumbing to imperial firepower:

1. **Chronological Trajectory & Key Centers**:
   - **Naseerabad (28 May)**: Initial spark by 15th/30th BNI sepoys; Spottiswoode killed; marched to Delhi.
   - **Neemuch (3 June)**: Led by Mohammad Ali Beg; 40 British rescued at Doongla, sheltered at Jag Mandir.
   - **Erinpura & Auwa (Aug–Sept)**: Jodhpur Legion marched with *"Chalo Dilli, Maro Firangi"*; Kushal Singh annihilated royal/British forces at Bithoda (8 Sept) and Chelawas (18 Sept).
   - **Kota (15 Oct)**: Popular democratic uprising under Jaidayal and Mehrab Khan; Major Burton beheaded; 6 months of citizen governance.

2. **Underlying Causes of Failure**:
   - **Princely Treachery**: Monolithic support of Rajput rulers (Udaipur, Jodhpur, Jaipur, Bikaner) to the British, denying local rebels state patronage.
   - **Absence of Unified Command**: Insurgents at Naseerabad and Erinpura left Rajasthan for Delhi rather than converging on the British central arsenal at Ajmer.
   - **Logistical & Artillery Deficit**: Rebels lacked heavy siege ordnance to withstand British counter-attacks under General Roberts and Brigadier Holmes.
   - **Betrayal of Leadership**: Key coordinators like Tatya Tope were betrayed by local Jagirdars (Man Singh Naruka), terminating guerrilla momentum by early 1859.

[Chapter 06 Complete ➔ Next: Chapter 07: Peasant & Agrarian Movements (Bijolia, Bengu, Bundi, Alwar, Shekhawati)]62:Td6c,### 1.1 The Feudal Agrarian Architecture: Khalsa vs Jagir
During the 19th and early 20th centuries, Rajasthan’s agrarian economy was split into two distinct tenurial systems:
1. **Khalsa Land (खालसा भूमि)**: Direct state crown land (~20–25% of total territory), where peasants paid revenue directly to the state administration and enjoyed relatively secure occupancy rights.
2. **Jagir Land (जागीर भूमि)**: Feudal estates (~75–80% of total territory), governed by hereditary Rajput Thakurs (*Jagirdars / Samants*). In Jagir areas, peasants possessed zero tenancy protection, held lands entirely at the landlord's arbitrary will (*Gair-Khatedar*), and were subjected to extortionate feudal extraction.

---63:T2c50,### 2.1 Feudal Profile & The Three Historic Phases
- **Geographical & Historical Setting**: Located in modern **Bhilwara district** (erstwhile Mewar state), **Bijolia (बिजोलिया)** was an ancient cultural center (*Vijyavalli*).
- **The First-Grade Jagir**: Bijolia was the premier **First-Grade Jagir (Solah Singar / 16 Jagirs)** of Mewar, originally granted by **Maharana Sangram Singh I (Sanga)** to **Ashok Parmar** (of Jagner, Bharatpur) in reward for his valor at the Battle of Khanwa (1527 CE).
- **Peasant Demographics**: Over 60% of the agrarian population belonged to the industrious **Dhakar (धाकड़)** caste.
- **The 84 Cesses (*Chaurasi Lāg-Bāg*)**: Peasants were subjected to 84 distinct forms of feudal taxation alongside crushing land revenue (*Bhog*).

---

### 2.2 Phase 1 (1897–1915): Spontaneous Protest & Initial Oppression
- **The 1897 Spark at Girdharpura**: In 1897, peasants assembled at **Girdharpura village** for the *Mausar* (post-funeral community feast) of Gangaram Dhakar’s father. Under the guidance of local library clerk **Sadhu Sitaram Das**, the peasants resolved to dispatch two elder representatives, **Nanji Patel** and **Thakari Patel**, to Udaipur to lodge a direct grievance with Maharana Fateh Singh against Rao Krishna Singh’s extortions.
- **The Hamid Hussain Inquiry**: The Maharana appointed Assistant Revenue Officer **Hamid Hussain** to investigate. Hussain confirmed excessive cesses in his official report; however, the Maharana took no punitive action. Emboldened, Rao Krishna Singh expelled Nanji and Thakari Patel from Bijolia.
- **Chanwari Tax (चंवरी कर, 1903 CE)**:
  - Imposed by **Rao Krishna Singh**: Every peasant was mandated to pay an extortionate fee of **5 rupees** (a fortune in 1903) upon the marriage of his daughter, and obtain royal permission.
  - Peasant Strike: In protest, peasants refused to marry their daughters for two consecutive years, marching 200 unmarried daughters to the palace gates. Faced with mass agricultural strike, Krishna Singh was forced to withdraw Chanwari tax and reduce land revenue.
- **Talwar Bandhai Tax (तलवार बंधाई कर, 1906 CE)**:
  - Upon Krishna Singh's death, successor **Rao Prithvi Singh** imposed the heavy succession tax (**Talwar Bandhai** / feudal investiture fee) entirely onto the peasantry.
  - Led by **Sadhu Sitaram Das**, **Fateh Karan Charan**, and **Brahmadeo**, the peasants initiated a complete no-tax boycott, refusing to plough the fields in 1913. Prithvi Singh unleashed brutal police terror, imprisoning leaders.

---

### 2.3 Phase 2 (1916–1923): Vijay Singh Pathik & Nationalization

#### The Entry of Vijay Singh Pathik (1916 CE)
- **Identity & Background**: Born as **Bhoop Singh Gujjar** at Guthawali (Bulandshahr, UP). Sent to Rajasthan by revolutionary leaders Ras Bihari Bose and Sachindra Sanyal to organize armed mutiny at Todgarh alongside Thakur Gopal Singh of Kharwa. Jailed at Todgarh Fort, he escaped, altered his identity to **Vijay Singh Pathik**, wore Rajasthani attire, and commenced mass education work.
- **Induction into Bijolia**: Impressed by Pathik's erudition at Chittorgarh’s *Vidya Pracharini Sabha*, Sadhu Sitaram Das invited him to lead Bijolia in 1916.

#### Nationalization & Gandhi's Blessing
- **Pratap Newspaper**: Published from Kanpur by revolutionary **Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi**, *Pratap* gave front-page coverage to Bijolia, turning an isolated Mewari estate into an anti-imperial symbol.
- **National Leaders**:
  - **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**: Raised the issue of Bijolia in the British Parliament and wrote scathing editorials in his Marathi newspaper *Maratha*.
  - **Mahatma Gandhi**: Expressed deep solidarity; dispatched his personal secretary **Mahadev Desai** to Bijolia in 1919 to inspect conditions. Gandhi conferred upon Pathik the revered title **"Rashtriya Pathik" (राष्ट्रीय पथिक)**.

#### The Historic 1922 Agreement
In February 1922, alarmed by the parallel rise of the Non-Cooperation Movement, the British Government intervened directly.
- A high-level commission led by **Agent to the Governor-General (AGG) Robert Holland**, Political Agent Wilkinson, and Mewar Diwan Prabhash Chandra Chatterjee arrived in Bijolia.
- **Agreement (11 February 1922)**: Signed an accord with the peasant panchayat, permanently abolishing **35 unjust Lāg-Bāgs**.
- **Betrayal**: The Thikana’s administrator reneged on the accord after the cooling of the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1923, arresting Pathik and Verma.

---

### 2.4 Phase 3 (1923–1941): Land Surrender & Final Triumph
- **The Land Resignation Crisis (1927 CE)**: Following internal disagreements with Pathik over tactical escalation, **Manikya Lal Verma**, **Ramnarayan Chaudhary**, and **Haribhau Upadhyaya** took operational command, assisted by national Congress leader **Seth Jamnalal Bajaj**.
  - In 1927, to force the Jagirdar’s hand, peasants collectively surrendered their fertile hereditary tenancy lands (*Mal-Guzari*).
  - The Thikana auctioned these confiscated lands to wealthy outside loyalist farmers.
- **The Final Settlement (1941 CE)**:
  - In 1941, the Prime Minister of Mewar, **Sir T. Raghavachari**, realized the political danger of persistent peasant unrest amid World War II.
  - Dispatched Revenue Minister **Dr. Mohan Singh Mehta** to Bijolia to finalize negotiations with Manikya Lal Verma.
  - **The Settlement**: All 84 Lāg-Bāgs were irrevocably abolished, begar was banned, and all auctioned lands were restored to their original Dhakar peasant cultivators.
- **Historic Invariant**: Spanning **44 continuous years (1897–1941)**, Bijolia stands as the **longest, completely non-violent, and successful peasant movement in world history**.

---64:T106d,### 3.1 Genesis & The Menal Assembly (1921 CE)
- **Feudal Setting**: Bengu (located in modern Chittorgarh district) was a First-Grade Jagir of Mewar, governed by reactionary Jagirdar **Rawat Anoop Singh**.
- **Peasant Composition**: Overwhelmingly populated by Dhakar caste peasants suffering under 25 types of cesses and begar.
- **The Menal Outbreak (1921 CE)**: Inspired by Bijolia, peasants assembled at the sacred shrine of **Bhairav Kund (Menal)** in May 1921.
- **Leadership**: Vijay Singh Pathik directed **Ramnarayan Chaudhary** to assume field leadership on behalf of the Rajasthan Seva Sangh.

### 3.2 The "Bolshevik Agreement" & The Trench Commission
- **The Compromise with Rawat Anoop Singh (1922 CE)**: Facing sustained agricultural strikes, Rawat Anoop Singh concluded a bilateral compromise treaty with Ramnarayan Chaudhary, agreeing to abolish major cesses.
- **Mewar State Repudiation**: Maharana Fateh Singh and the British Residency refused to ratify the agreement, deriding it as a dangerous socialist **"Bolshevik Agreement" (बोल्शेविक फैसला)**. Anoop Singh was placed under house arrest in Udaipur, and **Lala Amritlal** was installed as Musahib/Administrator.
- **The Govindpura Massacre (13 July 1923)**:
  - British Settlement Commissioner **Mr. Trench** surrounded an unarmed gathering of peasants holding a panchayat at **Govindpura village (गोविंदपुरा)**.
  - Trench ordered open firing on the gathering; cavalry charges burned down the settlement.
  - **The Martyrs**: Two fearless peasant leaders, **Rupa Ji Dhakar (रूपा जी धाकड़)** and **Kripa Ji Dhakar (कृपा जी धाकड़)**, were martyred on the spot.

---65:T661,### 4.1 Socio-Economic Catalysts
- **Geographical Setting**: Centered in the harsh, rocky **Barad (बरड़)** region of Bundi state, inhabited largely by **Gujjar** and peasant communities.
- **Causes**: Heavy land revenue assessment, 25 unjust taxes, and compulsory forced labor (*Begar*) imposed by the state.

### 4.2 The Dabi Massacre (2 April 1923) & The Song "Arzi"
- **The Gathering at Dabi**: On 2 April 1923, thousands of Gujjar and peasant men and women convened a peaceful panchayat at **Dabi village (डाबी)** to protest state begar.
- **Police Firing**: Bundi State Police Superintendent **Ikram Hussain (इकराम हुसैन)** surrounded the gathering and opened indiscriminate rifle fire.
- **The Martyrdom of Nanak Ji Bhil**:
  - While bullets sprayed across the gathering, a brave peasant bard, **Nanak Ji Bhil (नानक जी भील)**, proudly waved the national flag and continued singing the patriotic Flag Song (*Jhanda Geet*), falling dead with the flag clutched firmly to his chest.
  - Alongside him, **Devi Lal Gurjar (देवीलाल गुर्जर)** was also martyred.
- **Manikya Lal Verma’s Elegy "Arzi"**:
  - Deeply moved by Nanak Ji Bhil’s supreme sacrifice, **Manikya Lal Verma** composed the immortal patriotic elegy:
    > **"Arzi" (अर्जी — The Petition)**
  - This song became the spiritual anthem of the peasant struggle across southern Rajasthan.

---66:Tef8,### 5.1 Root Causes: Wild Boars & Revenue Enhancement
- **The Wild Boar Menace (*Suar Samasya*)**: Maharaja Jai Singh of Alwar strictly prohibited the killing of wild boars (*Suars*), maintaining them as protected game for royal hunting expeditions. Herds of boars destroyedstanding crops across Bansur and Thana Ghazi tehsils, reducing farmers to starvation.
- **The 1924 Revenue Hike**: In 1924, Maharaja Jai Singh announced a new land settlement that increased land revenue rates by **40%**, triggering massive non-cooperation among Rajput and Brahmin cultivators.

---

### 5.2 The Nimuchana Massacre (14 May 1925) — "Dyerism Double Distilled"
- **The Assembly**: On **14 May 1925**, over 800 Rajput farmers assembled at **Nimuchana village (नीमूचना, Bansur tehsil)** to protest against the tax hikes.
- **State Assault**: Alwar state troops commanded by **Chhaju Singh (छज्जू सिंह)** surrounded the village with machine guns and artillery.
- **The Carnage**: Chhaju Singh ordered open fire on the defenseless crowd and set fire to the village. Over 144 residential houses were gutted, dozens of men, women, and children were slaughtered, and cattle were incinerated alive.

---67:T129a,### 6.1 The Feudal Framework: Panchpana Estates
In the semi-arid northern tract of Shekhawati (under nominal suzerainty of Jaipur state), power was concentrated in five principal Rajput Jagirs known collectively as **Panchpana (पंचपाना)**:
1. **Nawalgarh (नवलगढ़)**
2. **Mandawa (मंडावा)**
3. **Dundlod (डूंडलोद)**
4. **Bissau (बिसाऊ)**
5. **Khetri / Udaipurwati (खेतड़ी / उदयपुरवाटी)**

The peasant movement in Shekhawati was primarily driven by the sturdy **Jat peasantry**, resisting arbitrary cesses (*Dhaani*), land evictions, and feudal humiliation.

#### The Katrathal Women's Conference (25 April 1934 / कटराथल महिला सम्मेलन)
One of the most glorious chapters in Indian women's peasant history:
- **Catalyst**: The brutal physical assault and humiliation of peasant women at **Sotia ka Bas village** by the feudal Thakur of Sihot, **Man Singh**.
- **The Historic Gathering**: Defying strict feudal bans, over **10,000 peasant women** congregated at **Katrathal (कटराथल, Sikar)** on **25 April 1934**.
- **Leadership**:
  - **President**: **Kishori Devi (किशोरी देवी)**, the courageous wife of peasant leader Sardar Harlal Singh.
  - **Keynote Orator**: **Durga Devi Sharma (दुर्गा देवी शर्मा)**, wife of Tadkeshwar Sharma, who delivered an electrifying speech condemning feudal tyranny.
  - Other Leaders: Uttama Devi, Rama Devi, Phoolan Devi.

#### The Kudan Incident (1935 CE) & British Parliament
- At **Kudan village (कूदन, Sikar)** in 1935, Jat peasants led by an elderly matriarch, **Dhatapi Devi**, refused to pay inflated land taxes.
- British officer **Captain Webb** opened fire on the gathering; several peasants were martyred, and over 100 were arrested.
- **International Resonance**: The atrocities at Kudan were formally raised by British MPs in the **House of Commons in London**, forcing the Rao Raja of Sikar to concede tax reductions.

---68:T44a,### 7.1 The Meo Peasant Movement of Mewat (Alwar-Bharatpur, 1932–1933)
- **Catalyst**: High land taxes, forced labor, and wild boar preservation affecting the **Meo Muslim peasantry** of Mewat.
- **Leaders**: **Dr. Mohammad Ali** and **Chaudhary Yasin Khan** (of Gurgaon), operating under the banner of **Anjuman Khadim-ul-Islam**.
- Led to communal flare-ups; British troops placed Alwar under temporary administrative receivership.

### 7.2 The Dabra Massacre (13 March 1947 / डाबड़ा कांड)
- **Location**: **Dabra village (डाबड़ा, Didwana)**, Marwar state.
- **The Incident**: A joint convention of the **Marwar Lok Parishad** and the **Marwar Kisan Sabha** was held at the residence of peasant activist **Motiram Chaudhary**.
- **The Feudal Ambush**: Armed mercenaries hired by local Jagirdars attacked the unarmed convention with swords, guns, and spears.
- **Martyrdom**: Brave activists **Pannaram**, **Rugharam**, **Chunaram**, and **Nandaram** were slaughtered on the spot. Prominent freedom fighter **Chhaganraj Chopasniwala** was critically wounded.
