### 1.1 Thewa Art, Pratapgarh (थेवा कला) — Gold-on-Glass Filigree
- **Geographic Seat**: Consecrated exclusively in **Pratapgarh district**.
- **Foundational Era & Patronage**: Emerged around **1775 CE** during the reign of **Maharawat Samant Singh of Pratapgarh**, who bestowed the royal title of **"Rajsoni" (राजसोनी)** upon the master artisan family.
- **Pioneer Patriarch**: **Nathu Ji Soni (नाथूजी सोनी)**.
- **Craft Mechanics**:
  - The process involves carving microscopic, lace-like filigree patterns from **24-carat pure gold foil (*Wark*)** and fusing it onto the surface of specially imported **colored Belgian glass** (vibrant emerald green, royal sapphire blue, ruby red, and amber).
  - The glass is set within a silver frame (*Kanthi*) and backed with colored metal foil to reflect maximum luminescence.
  - Motifs include royal hunting pageants (*Shikar*), Maharana Pratap on Chetak, Radha-Krishna, peacocks, and floral arabesques.
- **The Secret Guild Invariant**: The technical secret of fusing gold to molten glass without cracking is an **undisclosed family secret** guarded across eight generations. The knowledge is passed down strictly from father to son; by customary law, it is **never taught to daughters** to prevent the technique from leaking to other families upon marriage!
- **Celebrated Masters**:
  - **Mahesh Raj Soni (महेश राज सोनी)**: Awarded the prestigious **Padma Shri in 2015**.
  - Ramprasad Soni, Veni Ram Soni, and Girish Kumar Soni.
- **State & Global Honor**: Protected under the **Geographical Indications (GI) Registry**; Queen Victoria possessed a celebrated Thewa brooch gifted by the Maharawat.

---

### 1.2 Blue Pottery, Jaipur (ब्लू पॉटरी) — The Glazed Ceramic Wonder
- **The Clay-Free Formulation**: Unlike conventional ceramic pottery, **Blue Pottery uses NO clay/mud whatsoever**! It is handcrafted from an indigenous dough formulated from five specific ingredients:
  1. Ground **Quartz powder** (*क्वाट्ज़ चूर्ण*)
  2. **Cullet** (pulverized recycled glass powder)
  3. **Multani Mitti** (Fuller’s earth)
  4. Natural **Gum** (*Gond*)
  5. Water containing natural sodium salts (*Sajji*)
- **Historical Migration**:
  - Originated in Turko-Persian ateliers; introduced to India via Lahore during the reign of **Raja Man Singh I of Amber**.
  - Experienced its modern renaissance under **Sawai Ram Singh II (1835–1880 CE)**, who sent two potters, **Kaluram** and **Chudaman**, to Delhi to master glazed ceramic techniques under Bhola Potter.
- **The Modern Legend: Kripal Singh Shekhawat (कृपाल सिंह शेखावत)**:
  - Born in Mau village (Sikar); studied at Santiniketan under Nandalal Bose.
  - Single-handedly rescued Blue Pottery from extinction in the 1960s. He expanded the traditional two-tone palette (cobalt blue and copper green) by inventing **25 new mineral shades**, including turquoise, golden yellow, purple, and crimson.
  - His studio style is celebrated worldwide as **"Kripal Kumbh" (कृपाल कुंभ)**; honored with the **Padma Shri in 1974** and titled *Shilpi Guru*.
- **GI Tag Status**: Inscribed as a protected **Geographical Indication (GI)**.

```

│ Style Name                 │ Geographic Center           │ Diagnostic Invariants       │
├────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤

### 1.3 Usta Art & Camelskin Craft, Bikaner (उस्ता कला / मुनव्वती कला)
- **Genesis & Royal Patronage**: Introduced from Multan and Lahore during the reign of **Maharaja Rai Singh**; flourished under **Maharaja Anup Singh**.
- **Material Technique**:
  - Gilded embossed lacquer and pure gold-leaf relief work (*Munawwati*) executed upon cured, dried **camel hide (*Oont ki Khaal*)**, wooden palace ceilings (such as the Anup Mahal in Junagarh Fort), and marble.
  - Craftsmen fashion ornamental water containers (**Kuppi / कुप्पी**), perfume flasks (*Itardan*), lamp shades, and photo frames from camel leather.
- **The Master of the Century: Hisam-ud-din Usta (हिसामुद्दीन उस्ता)**:
  - Decorated with the **Padma Shri in 1986** for unmatched virtuosity in camel-hide gilding.
  - Established the *Camel Hide Training Centre* at Bikaner to train future generations.
- **GI Tag Status**: Formally registered as a **Geographical Indication (GI Tag in 2023)**.

### 1.4 Metal Enameling & Damascus Inlay: Minakari & Koftgiri

```

#### 1. Minakari, Jaipur (मीनाकारी)
- **Origin**: Brought from Lahore to Jaipur in the late 16th century by **Raja Man Singh I**, who settled Sikh craftsmen from Punjab.
- **Craft Mechanics**: The art of engraving intricate recesses onto the surface of gold or silver jewelry and fusing powdered mineral enamel into the grooves via kiln heating. Red (*Kundan*), green, and white are the hallmark colors.
- **Supreme Maestro**: **Kudrat Singh (कुदरत सिंह)**, awarded the Padma Shri in 1988; GI Tagged.

#### 2. Koftgiri & Tah-Nishan (कोफ्तगिरी एवं तह-निशां)
- **Koftgiri**: An ancient Damascus weapon-decorating craft centered in **Udaipur and Jaipur**. Steel weapon blades, sword hilts (*Mutthi*), daggers, and shields are cross-hatched with fine chisels, after which pure gold or silver wire is embedded and burnished smooth with agate stone; awarded **GI Tag in 2023**.
- **Tah-Nishan**: Deep-groove silver wire inlay on steel or bronze.

#### 3. Badla, Jodhpur (बादला)
- Traditional water containers fashioned from **zinc metal (*Jasta*)**, lined with inner tin and encased in outer felt or cloth. Operating on evaporative cooling principles, Badlas keep drinking water chilled during 48°C desert summers. Unique to Jodhpur.

### Detailed Invariants of Woodcraft & Puppetry:

1. **Bassi Woodcraft (Chittorgarh)**:
   - **Kavad (कावड़)**: A portable, multi-tiered wooden shrine equipped with numerous hinged, illustrated folding doors. As the itinerant Bhat/Bhopa storyteller recites sacred epics, he progressively opens each door, revealing colorful miniature paintings of the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
   - **Viman / Vaikunthi (विमान / बेवाण)**: Ornate carved wooden palanquins used for carrying temple deities in festive processions (*Jaljhulani Ekadashi*).
   - Carved wooden **Torans** for wedding portals and **Gangaur-Isar wooden effigies**.
2. **Kathputli (कठपुतली — String Puppetry)**:
   - Handcrafted from the lightweight timber of the **Adusa tree (*Aadhoo*)**; dressed in colorful flared Rajasthani skirts with attached string controls.
   - Preserved and popularized internationally by **Padma Shri Devi Lal Samar (देवीलाल सामर)**, who established the premier **Bharatiya Lok Kala Mandal, Udaipur** in 1952. Formally inscribed with a **GI Tag**.

### 3.1 Hand Block Printing Traditions

#### 1. Sanganeri Hand Block Print (सांगानेरी प्रिंट — Jaipur)
- **Foundational Base**: Practiced by the **Chippa (Nama) community** along the Sanjariya river in Sanganer; patronized by Sawai Jai Singh II.
- **Diagnostic Characteristics**:
  - Printed exclusively on **pure white, off-white, or pale cream cotton bases**.
  - Characterized by delicate, refined floral sprigs (**Bootis** and *Bel*), including lotuses, roses, lilies, and flying nightingales.
  - Uses natural vegetable and mineral dyes (indigo, alum, pomegranate rind, iron rust); awarded **GI Tag**.

#### 2. Bagru Hand Block Print (बगरू प्रिंट — Jaipur)
- **The Dabu Mud-Resist Method**:
  - Famous for **Dabu (दाबू)** printing: areas of fabric intended to resist dye are stamped with a thick paste of clay, lime, and gum (*Dabu mitti*) before immersion in dye vats.
  - Background is earthy, rustic, and dark (contrasting sharply with Sanganer’s white base).
  - Hallmark colors: Natural **Red (Hinglu/Begar)** and deep **Black (Syahi/Kashish)** extracted from fermented iron shavings and jaggery; awarded **GI Tag**.

#### 3. Akola Dabu Print (आकोला — Chittorgarh)
- Centered at **Chhipon ka Akola** on the banks of the Bedach river.
- Specializes in heavy bedcovers, floor coverings (**Jajam Print**), and traditional women's cloths (**Fadath Print**).
- Uses specialized localized resist pastes:
  - *Mitti ka Dabu* (Clay resist)
  - *Gond ka Dabu* (Gum resist)
  - *Mom ka Dabu* (Wax resist)

#### 4. Barmer Prints: Ajrakh vs Malir
- **Ajrakh Print (अजरक प्रिंट — Barmer)**:
  - **Double-Sided Printing**: Fabric is stamped on **both sides** in perfect optical registration.
  - Dominant palette: Deep **Indigo Blue** and rich **Crimson Red**.
  - Motifs: Geometric star lattices and Islamic tile arabesques; worn traditionally by Sindhi Muslims and Maldhari pastoralists; awarded **GI Tag**.
- **Malir Print (मलीर प्रिंट — Barmer)**:
  - Printed on one side only; dominant palette: **Dark Brown, Muddy Mustard, and Black**.

---

### 3.2 Specialty Weaves & Embroidery

#### 1. Kota Doria / Masuria Saree (कोटा डोरिया / मसूरिया साड़ी)
- **Epicenter**: **Kaithoon (कैथून, Kota)**.
- **Historical Migration**: Introduced from Mysore in the late 17th century by Maharao Shatrushal and prime minister Zalim Singh Jhala, who brought master weaver **Mahmud Masuria** to Kota.
- **Structural Blueprint**:
  - Woven on pit looms in a distinct gossamer-fine square check grid termed **Khat (खट)** (precisely 300 to 360 squares per square inch).
  - High-count cotton warp blended with raw mulberry silk and real gold/silver **Zari** borders; awarded **GI Tag**.

#### 2. Tie & Dye (Bandhej / बंधेज) & Gotawork
- **Bandhej**: Concentrated in **Jaipur, Jodhpur, and Sikar**. Fabric is pinched into thousands of tiny knots using fingernails (*Bandi*) and dipped into progressive color vats (*Rangrez / Neelgar*). Styles include *Ekdali*, *Trikunti*, *Chowbandi*, and *Shikari*.
- **Gotawork (गोटा-किनारी)**: Centered at **Khandela (Sikar)**; gold and silver ribbon weaving. Varieties include **Lappa, Lappi, Kiran, Bankadi, and Bijia**.

---ae:T2c86,### 6.1 2-Markers (15–20 Words)

#### Q1: What is Thewa Art, and where did it originate?
**Answer**:
A delicate handicraft originating in Pratapgarh (c. 1775 CE, Nathu Ji Soni) involving the intricate fusing of 24-carat pure gold filigree onto colored Belgian glass.

---

#### Q2: Name the ingredients used in manufacturing Jaipur Blue Pottery.
**Answer**:
Prepared without clay using: quartz powder, pulverized glass cullet, Fuller's earth (*Multani Mitti*), natural gum, and sodium salt water (*Sajji*).

---

#### Q3: What is "Kavad" in Rajasthani woodcraft?
**Answer**:
A portable wooden temple shrine made in Bassi (Chittorgarh) by Suthar artisans, featuring multi-tiered painted folding doors opened sequentially during storytelling.

---

#### Q4: Why is Sojat Mehndi famous, and when did it receive the GI Tag?
**Answer**:
Cultivated in Sojat (Pali); globally renowned for high natural lawsone dye pigment and skin-cooling aroma; granted an official Geographical Indication (GI) Tag in 2021.

---

#### Q5: State the distinct characteristic of Ajrakh block printing.
**Answer**:
A traditional Barmer block-print executed with geometric motifs in deep indigo blue and crimson red, uniquely stamped on **both sides** in perfect registration.

---

### 6.2 5-Markers (50 Words)

#### Q6: Explain the technique, themes, and maestro of Molela Terracotta art.
**Answer**:
Centered in Molela village (Nathdwara) on the Banas river, this craft involves hand-modeling unglazed red clay mixed with donkey dung:
1. **Technique**: Hollow relief clay plaques sculpted by hand without potter's wheels, sun-dried, and baked in indigenous kilns without chemical glazes.
2. **Themes**: Traditional religious deities for tribal and pastoral communities: Lord Devnarayanji mounted on horseback, Goraji, and Bhairav.
3. **Master Artisan**: **Mohanlal Kumhar** was awarded the Padma Shri in 2012 for elevating this rural craft to international museums.

---

#### Q7: Differentiate between Sanganeri and Bagru hand block print traditions.
**Answer**:
Both are world-renowned block-printing centers in Jaipur district, differing sharply in aesthetics, base fabric, and dyeing techniques:
1. **Sanganeri Print**: Characterized by fine, delicate floral sprays (*Bootis*) and creepers printed on an **off-white or pure white** cotton base using natural vegetable dyes; patronized by Sawai Jai Singh.
2. **Bagru Print**: Characterized by the **Dabu mud-resist method**, printed on an earthy, dark background using bold geometric motifs and a distinct natural palette of **Hinglu red and Syahi black** derived from fermented iron.

---

#### Q8: Write a concise note on the contribution of Kripal Singh Shekhawat to Blue Pottery.
**Answer**:
Trained at Santiniketan, **Kripal Singh Shekhawat (1922–2008)** revived Jaipur's dying Blue Pottery tradition in the mid-20th century:
1. **Color Expansion**: Transcended the traditional two-tone blue-green constraint by inventing **25 new mineral and vegetable shades** (brown, yellow, violet, crimson).
2. **Artistic School**: Established the renowned **"Kripal Kumbh"** studio, training hundreds of artisans in classical Indian decorative painting.
3. **Recognition**: Awarded the Padma Shri in 1974 and the title *Shilpi Guru*, securing global market recognition for the craft.

---

│                           │   Mehndi (cosmetic exports), and Nathdwara Pichhwais.      │
├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 4. Preservation of Oral   │ • Recent 2023 additions (Udaipur Koftgari, Bikaner Usta,   │
│    Heritage Systems       │   Kashidakari, Jodhpur Bandhej) incentivize younger        │
│                           │   generations to master time-tested generational skills.   │
└───────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
**Conclusion**: By converting vernacular heritage into legally protected economic assets, GI Tags bridge Rajasthan’s feudal artisanal glory with modern commercial sovereignty.

### 1.1 The Great Boundary Fault of Rajasthan (GBF / महान सीमा भ्रंश)
- **Tectonic Nature**: A massive reverse fault line marking the suture zone between the ancient **Aravalli-Delhi Metamorphic Complex** (to the northwest) and the flat, undeformed **Vindhyan Sedimentary Basin** (to the southeast).
- **Extent & Trace**: Extends approximately **800 kilometers** across southeastern Rajasthan, traversing through **Chittorgarh $\rightarrow$ Kota $\rightarrow$ Bundi $\rightarrow$ Sawai Madhopur $\rightarrow$ Karauli $\rightarrow$ Dholpur**.
- **Geomorphological Expression**: Expressed on the surface as steep, vertical sandstone escarpments (*Vindhyan Scarps*) overlooking the Chambal and Banas drainage basins.

---

### 1.2 Historiography of Geographic Regionalization
1. **Dr. V.C. Misra (1967)**: In his seminal treatise *Geography of Rajasthan* (National Book Trust), Dr. Misra pioneered the first academic regionalization, dividing Rajasthan into **7 Geographic Regions**:
   - (1) Western Arid Region, (2) Semi-Arid Region, (3) Canal Irrigated Region (Ganganagar), (4) Aravalli Region, (5) Eastern Agricultural Region, (6) South-Eastern Agricultural Region, and (7) Chambal Ravine Region.
2. **Dr. A.K. Sen (1968)**: Classified the state based on agro-climatic boundaries and rainfall isohyets.
3. **Prof. Ram Lochan Singh (1971)**: Divided Rajasthan into **2 Macro Regions** (Western Rajasthan and Eastern Rajasthan), subdivided into **4 Meso Regions** and **12 Micro Regions**.
4. **The Standard Fourfold Canonical Division (Dr. H.M. Saxena & Dr. L.R. Bhalla)**:
   Universally adopted by the Rajasthan Board (RBSE) and RPSC for examination benchmarking:

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               THE FOUR CANONICAL MORPHOTECTONIC DIVISIONS OF RAJASTHAN                 │
├───────────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────┤
│ Physical Division │ % Area of Raj│ % Population │ Geological Origin│ Diagnostic Soil   │
├───────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────┼───────────────────┤
│ **1. Western Sandy│ **61.11%**   │ **40.0%**    │ Tethys Sea       │ Desert Sand       │
│    Plain** (Thar) │              │              │ (Quaternary era) │ (Aridisols)       │
├───────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────┼───────────────────┤
│ **2. Aravalli     │ **9.0%**     │ **10.0%**    │ Gondwanaland     │ Red-Loamy / Rocky │
│    Mountains**    │              │              │ (Pre-Cambrian)   │ (Inceptisols)     │
├───────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────┼───────────────────┤

### 2.1 Demarcating Climatic Isohyets (समवर्षा रेखाएँ)
- **50 cm Isohyet Line**: Runs along the western foothills of the Aravalli range; separates the entire Western Sandy Plain from Eastern Rajasthan.
- **25 cm Isohyet Line**: Bisects the Western Sandy Plain into two distinct zones:
  - Western flank: **Pure Arid Marusthali** (< 25 cm annual precipitation).
  - Eastern flank: **Semi-Arid Transitional Plain (Rajasthan Bagar)** (25 cm to 50 cm annual precipitation).

---

### 2.2 Macro-Zone A: The Pure Arid Marusthali (< 25 cm)

#### 1. Desert Surface Typology
- **Erg (इर्ग)**: Pure sandy desert composed of shifting, undulating sand dunes (*Dhrian*); prevalent in Jaisalmer and western Bikaner.
- **Hamada (हम्मादा)**: Bleak, rocky, boulder-strewn desert pavement barren of sand; runs in a broad arc from **Pokhran (Jaisalmer) to Phalodi and Ramgarh**.
- **Reg (रेग)**: Mixed stony-gravel desert combining sandy patches with rocky debris.

#### 2. Sand Dune Typology (बालुका स्तूप — CAZRI Classification)
According to the Central Arid Zone Research Institute (CAZRI, Jodhpur), the sand dunes (*Tibba* / बालुका स्तूप) of Rajasthan exhibit distinct morphodynamic behaviors:

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   TYPOLOGY & DYNAMICS OF RAJASTHANI SAND DUNES                         │
├────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┤
│ Dune Classification        │ Morphological Geometry      │ Regional Distribution & Risk│
├────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
│ **1. Barkhan / Barchan**   │ • Crescent-shaped dunes;    │ • **Highest desertification │
│    (बरखान)                 │   horns point downwind.     │   hazard** (unstable/moving)│
│                            │ • Gentle convex windward,   │ • **Bhaleri (Churu)**,      │
│                            │   steep concave leeward.    │   Suratgarh, Osian, Deshnoke│

│    (अनुदैर्ध्य / सीफ)      │   prevailing SW-NE winds.   │   Jodhpur. Corridors between│
│                            │ • Formed by high wind shears│   dunes termed **Gasi / Karva│
├────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
│ **3. Transverse Dunes**    │ • Perpendicular (90° angle) │ • Bikaner, Hanumangarh,     │
│    (अनुप्रस्थ)             │   to prevailing wind vector.│   Ganganagar, Churu.        │
├────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
│ **4. Parabolic Dunes**     │ • U-shaped dunes anchored   │ • **Most widespread dune    │
│    (पैराबोलिक)             │   by vegetation; reverse    │   type in Rajasthan**       │
│                            │   horns point upwind.       │   (present in all districts)│
├────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
│ **5. Star Dunes**          │ • Multi-armed pyramid stars │ • **Mohangarh & Pokhran**   │
│    (तारा बालुका स्तूप)     │   formed by multidirection  │   (Jaisalmer), Suratgarh    │

│    **Nebkha (नेबखा)**      │   around desert shrubs like │   *Kair*, *Phog*, and       │
│                            │   *Phog* and *Lana*.        │   *Khejri* bushes.          │
└────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘
```

#### 3. The Dune-Free Tract (बालुका स्तूप मुक्त प्रदेश)
- Encompasses **41.5%** of the arid desert zone, stretching across **Pokhran, Ramgarh (Jaisalmer), and Phalodi**.
- Underlain by marine sedimentary limestone, sandstone, and shale of the Jurassic and Eocene epochs, providing incontrovertible proof that this region was submerged beneath the **Tethys Sea**.
- **Akal Wood Fossil Park (आकल वुड फॉसिल पार्क)**: Located 21 km southeast of Jaisalmer; preserves 25 petrified fossilized tree trunks dating back **180 million years (Jurassic Period)**, proving the ancient desert was once a lush, warm equatorial rain forest.
- **Lathi Series (लाठी सीरीज)**:
  - A 60-kilometer-long subterranean geological aquifer stretching from **Pokhran to Mohangarh** along the paleo-channel of the mythical **Saraswati river**.
  - Yields sweet, perennial potable water trapped in Cretaceous sandstone strata.
  - **Chandan Tube Well (चांदन नलकूप)**: Located here; dubbed the **"Thar ka Ghada" (घड़ा of Thar)** due to its inexhaustible flow.
  - Ground cover dominated by protein-rich **Sewan grass (*Lasiurus scindicus*)**, the prime nesting sanctuary of Rajasthan’s State Bird, the critically endangered **Great Indian Bustard (Godawan)**.

---

### 2.3 Macro-Zone B: The Semi-Arid Transitional Plain (Rajasthan Bagar)
Bounded by the 25 cm isohyet to the west and the 50 cm isohyet (Aravalli foothills) to the east, this transitional eco-zone is subdivided into four morphotectonic units:

1. **Luni Basin (Godwar Tract / लूनी बेसिन)**:
   - Drained by the ephemeral Luni river and its left-bank tributaries across **Pali, Jalore, Sanchor, and Balotra**.
   - Characterized by granitic inselbergs and volcanic domes:
     - **Chhappan ki Pahadiyan (56 Hills / छप्पन की पहाड़ियाँ)**: Fifty-six round granitic hills located around **Siwana (Balotra)**; home to the sacred Jain pilgrimage of **Nakoda Parvat** (Mewa Nagar) and the hill station of **Haldeshwar Mahadev** (titled *"Mount Abu of Marwar"*).
     - **Jalore Granite & Rhyolite**: Rose-pink granitic dome hills (*Inselbergs*) around Jalore city.
2. **Nagauri Upland (नागौरी उच्च भूमि)**:
   - Elevation 300–500 meters; underlain by subterranean sodium, gypsum, and limestone beds.
   - **Kobar Patti / Banka Patti (Hump / Fluorosis Belt / कूबड़ पट्टी)**:
     - An infamous subterranean groundwater zone stretching between **Nagaur and Didwana-Kuchaman to Ajmer**.
     - Extremely high fluoride concentrations in drinking water cause widespread dental fluorosis and skeletal deformities (hunched backs, *Kobar*), bending the spines of the local population.
3. **Shekhawati Internal Drainage Tract (कांतली बेसिन / शेखावाटी)**:
   - Covers Sikar, Jhunjhunu, Neem Ka Thana, and Churu. Characterized by shifting dunes and streams that terminate in sand before reaching any sea (e.g., the Kantli river).
   - **Johad (जोहड़)**: Traditional vernacular raw rainwater storage wells dug down to the limestone hardpan; revolutionized by waterman Rajendra Singh.
   - **Beed (बीड़)**: Fenced community grasslands utilized for rotational village livestock grazing.
4. **Ghaggar Plain (घग्घर का मैदान)**:
   - Covers **Ganganagar and Hanumangarh**; formed by rich alluvial silt deposited by the ancient Saraswati and Drishadvati rivers (now represented by the ephemeral Ghaggar).
   - **Nali (नाली)**: The flat, broad, fertile river bed of the Ghaggar in Hanumangarh; famous for intensive wheat, mustard, and long-staple cotton cultivation.
   - **Hakra (हकरा)**: The spillover course of the Ghaggar when monsoon floods cross into Fort Abbas, Pakistan.

---b1:T3d28,The Aravalli Range is the geomorphological spine of Rajasthan, functioning as a continental water divide, mineral treasure trove, climatic barrier, and tribal homeland.

> (**गुरु** = गुरु शिखर, **से** = सेर, **दिल** = देलवाड़ा, **जरा** = जरगा, **अचूक** = अचलगढ़).

---

### 3.3 High Plateaus & Geological Formations of the Southern Aravallis
1. **Oriya Plateau (उड़िया का पठार)**:
   - Elevated at **1,360 meters** above sea level; situated immediately beneath Guru Shikhar in Mount Abu (Sirohi).
   - The **highest plateau in Rajasthan**.
2. **Abu Block Plateau**: Second highest plateau (1,200 m); a granitic batholith with steep fault scarps.
3. **Bhorat Plateau (भोराट का पठार)**:
   - Elevated at **1,225 meters**; stretches between **Kumbhalgarh (Rajsamand)** and **Gogunda (Udaipur)**.
   - Functions as the continental water divide between the Arabian Sea (Sabarmati/Vakil) and the Bay of Bengal (Banas).
4. **Mesa Plateau (मेसा का पठार)**:
   - Elevated at **616 meters** in Chittorgarh at the confluence of the Gambhiri and Bedach rivers; supports the colossal **Chittorgarh Fort**.
5. **Uparmal Plateau (ऊपरमाल का पठार)**:
   - Elevated rocky tableland stretching from **Bijolia (Bhilwara)** to **Bhainsrorgarh (Chittorgarh)**.
6. **Lashadiya Plateau (लसाड़िया का पठार)**:
   - Severely dissected, jagged, wave-eroded rocky plateau situated immediately east of Jaisamand Lake in newly organized **Salumbar district** (formerly Udaipur).
7. **Desh-Haro (देशहरो)**:
   - The high valley nestled between the **Jarga and Raga mountain peaks** (Udaipur); remains perpetually lush and verdant throughout the year (*Desh-Haro* = Ever-Green Country).
8. **Bhakar (भाकर)**:
   - Steep, extremely sharp, jagged ridges characteristic of the **western Sirohi** district.
9. **Girwa (गिरवा)**:
   - The amphitheater-like, saucer-shaped ring of hills surrounding the city of **Udaipur** (*Girwa* = Neck of hills).

---

### 3.4 Key Mountain Passes (*Naal / Ghat*)
- **Connecting Marwar to Mewar / Ajmer**:
  - **Bar Pass (बर दर्रा)**: Located in Beawar district; traversed by National Highway connecting Ajmer to Jodhpur.
  - **Desuri ki Naal (देसूरी की नाल)**: Connects Pali (Desuri) with Rajsamand (Charbhuja).
  - **Jhilwa / Paglya Naal (झीलवा / पगल्या नाल)**: Historical military pass connecting Marwar to Mewar through the Aravalis.
  - **Someshwar Naal**: Rugged gorge in Rajsamand.
  - **Hathi Guda Naal (हाथी गूड़ा की नाल)**: Scenic mountain pass leading to Kumbhalgarh Fort.

### 4.1 Chambal Basin: Utkhat Bhumi & Dang Region
- **Gully Erosion (अवनलिका अपरदन)**: Heavy monsoon discharges flowing over friable alluvial clay have gouged out deep vertical trenches and ravines (*Beehad* / बीहड़) reaching depths of 15 to 30 meters.
- **Utkhat Bhumi (Badland Topography / उत्खात भूमि)**: The most extensive badland labyrinth in India, covering 4,500 sq km across **Dholpur, Karauli, and Sawai Madhopur**.
- **The Dang Tract (डांग क्षेत्र)**: Elevated, barren, scrub-covered rocky ridges between the ravines; **Karauli** is officially known as the **"Queen of Dang" (डांग की रानी)**.

---

### 4.2 Banas-Banganga Basin
- **Piedmont Plain**: A gently undulating erosion plain (*Peneplain*) underlain by Archaean gneiss and granite, elevation 280–500 meters.
- **Two Sub-Basins**:
  1. **Mewar Plain (Western)**: Elevated higher (Bhilwara, Chittorgarh, Rajsamand); drained by the Berach, Kothari, and Khari rivers.
  2. **Malpura-Karauli Plain (Eastern)**: Flat alluvial plain covering Tonk, Sawai Madhopur, and Dausa; deep tertiary silt deposits.

---

### 4.3 Mahi Basin: Chappan Plain & Kanthal
- **Chappan ka Maidan (छप्पन का मैदान)**:
  - The fertile alluvial basin located between **Banswara and Pratapgarh**.
  - Derives its name from the **56 drainage streams (*Chhappan Nale*) and 56 agricultural villages (*Chhappan Gaon*)** drained by the Mahi river and its tributaries.
- **Kanthal (कांठल)**:
  - The narrow coastal bank strip along the Mahi river in **Pratapgarh district** (*Kanthal* = Shore/Edge); hence the local rulers were titled *Kanthal-Pati*.

### 5.1 Specialized Micro-Units of Hadoti
1. **Mukundara Hills (मुकुंदरा की पहाड़ियाँ)**:
   - S-shaped crescentic ridgelines extending from **Kota to Jhalawar**; slopes drain into the Ahu and Kali Sindh rivers.
   - Highest peak: **Chandwadi (चाँदवाड़ी — 517 m)** in Jhalawar.
2. **Shahbad Upland (शाहबाद उच्च भूमि — Baran)**:
   - Eastern highland elevation up to 450 meters; highest peak: **Kastoorba (456 m)**.
   - **Ramgarh Crater (रामगढ़ क्रेटर)**: A circular, horseshoe-shaped geological depression formed by a **meteorite impact** millions of years ago; declared the 106th National Geological Monument and India's 3rd recognized meteorite impact crater (after Lonar in Maharashtra and Dhala in MP).
3. **Dag-Gangdhar Upland (डग-गंगधार उच्च भूमि)**:
   - Low, rolling basaltic plateau region situated in southwestern **Jhalawar district**.

   - Remnants of **Gondwanaland**: **Aravalli Range** and **Hadoti Plateau**.
   - Remnants of **Tethys Sea**: **Western Sandy Plain** and **Eastern Alluvial Plain**.
2. **The Isohyet Boundary Numbers**:
   - **50 cm Isohyet**: Separates the Western Sandy Plain from the rest of Rajasthan.
   - **25 cm Isohyet**: Bisects the Thar Desert into Pure Arid Marusthali and Semi-Arid Bagar.
3. **The Most Widespread Sand Dune**: **Parabolic Dunes** are the most widespread in Rajasthan (present across all desert districts), NOT Barkhans!
4. **The Most Dangerous Dune for Desertification**: **Barkhan (Barchan)** dunes; highly mobile, crescent-shaped, fast-moving.
5. **Dune-Covered vs Dune-Free Tract Percentages**:
   - Dune-Covered Tract: **58.5%**.
   - Dune-Free Tract (*Hamada*): **41.5%** (Pokhran, Ramgarh, Phalodi).
6. **Akal Wood Fossil Park Epoch**: **Jurassic Period (180 million years old)**, NOT Cretaceous or Tertiary.
7. **Lathi Series Water & Grass**: Groundwater aquifer between Pokhran and Mohangarh; supports sweet-water **Chandan Tube Well** and protein-rich **Sewan grass (*Lasiurus scindicus*)**.
8. **Chhappan ka Maidan vs Chhappan ki Pahadiyan (Top Trap!)**:
   - **Chhappan ka Maidan**: Alluvial plain of 56 streams between **Banswara and Pratapgarh** (Mahi Basin).
   - **Chhappan ki Pahadiyan**: Fifty-six granitic round hills located in **Siwana (Balotra)**.
9. **Kobar Patti (Banka Patti) Geography**: A fluoride groundwater belt stretching between **Nagaur/Didwana and Ajmer**, causing fluorosis.
10. **Aravalli Length: Total vs Rajasthan**:
    - Total length: **692 km** (Palanpur, Gujarat to Raisina Hill, Delhi).
    - Length within Rajasthan: **550 km** (approx. **79.6% ~ 80%** of total length).
11. **Highest Peak in North Aravalli**: **Raghunathgarh (1,055 m)** in Sikar, NOT Kho or Bairat.
12. **Highest Peak in Central Aravalli**: **Goramji (934 m)** in Beawar, followed closely by **Moramji / Todgarh (933 m)** and Taragarh (870 m).
13. **Guru Shikhar's Elevation Distinction**: **1,722 meters** (1,727 meters if the Dattatreya temple on the summit is included). Tod called it *"Santoka Shikhar"*.
14. **Highest Plateau in Rajasthan**: **Oriya Plateau (1,360 m)** in Mount Abu, NOT Bhorat.
15. **Bhorat Plateau Boundaries**: Stretches between **Kumbhalgarh (Rajsamand)** and **Gogunda (Udaipur)**, average elevation 1,225 m.
16. **Lashadiya Plateau Updated District**: Now located in **Salumbar district** (formerly Udaipur), situated east of Jaisamand Lake.
17. **Desh-Haro Location**: The perennially green valley between **Jarga and Raga hills** in Udaipur.
18. **Bhakar Topography**: Extremely steep, sharp-edged jagged hills situated in **western Sirohi**.
19. **Girwa Topography**: Saucer-shaped, amphitheater-like ring of hills encircling **Udaipur city**.
20. **Utkhat Bhumi (Badland) Epicenter**: Caused by Chambal’s gully erosion in **Dholpur, Karauli, and Sawai Madhopur**.
21. **"Queen of Dang" (डांग की रानी)**: **Karauli district** is officially called Dang ki Rani.
22. **Kanthal Region**: The narrow shore plain along the Mahi river in **Pratapgarh district**.
23. **Ramgarh Meteorite Crater**: Located in **Baran district** (Shahbad Upland); recognized as India's 3rd meteorite impact crater.
24. **Mukundara Hills Peak**: Highest peak is **Chandwadi (517 m)** in Jhalawar.
25. **Great Boundary Fault (GBF) Alignment**: Fault line separating Aravallis and Vindhyans; runs from **Chittorgarh to Dholpur**.

---b6:T2c6a,### 8.1 2-Markers (15–20 Words)

#### Q1: What is the "Lathi Series" in the Thar Desert?
**Answer**:
A 60-km subterranean paleo-aquifer stretching from Pokhran to Mohangarh (Jaisalmer) underlain by sweet groundwater, famous for Chandan Tube Well and Sewan grasslands.

---

#### Q2: Distinguish between Barkhan and Seif sand dunes.
**Answer**:
Barkhans are mobile crescent-shaped dunes formed perpendicular to wind with downwind horns; Seifs are elongated longitudinal ridges formed parallel to wind directions.

---

#### Q3: What is the Bhorat Plateau? State its geographical boundary.
**Answer**:
A high Aravalli plateau (1,225 m) serving as a continental water divide, situated between **Kumbhalgarh (Rajsamand)** in the north and **Gogunda (Udaipur)** in the south.

---

#### Q4: What is the "Kobar Patti" of Rajasthan?
**Answer**:
A subterranean geological belt between Nagaur and Ajmer containing hazardous fluoride concentrations, causing widespread skeletal and dental fluorosis (*Banka Patti*).

---

#### Q5: State the geological significance of the Great Boundary Fault (GBF).
**Answer**:
An 800-km regional reverse fault running from Chittorgarh to Dholpur, marking the structural boundary between the folded Pre-Cambrian Aravallis and the Vindhyan sedimentary plateau.

---

### 8.2 5-Markers (50 Words)

#### Q6: Explain the morphotectonic characteristics of the South-Eastern Hadoti Plateau.
**Answer**:
Covering 6.89% of Rajasthan across Kota, Baran, Bundi, and Jhalawar, the Hadoti Plateau forms the northwestern edge of the Deccan Traps:
1. **Lithology**: Underlain by Cretaceous basaltic lava sheets and sandstone scarps of the Vindhyan Supergroup, weathering into fertile black **Vertisols (Regur)**.
2. **Relief Features**:
   - *Vindhyan Scarpland*: Massive sandstone escarpments facing the Chambal river.
   - *Mukundara Hills*: S-shaped crescentic ridges (highest peak: Chandwadi 517 m).
   - *Shahbad Upland*: Houses the horseshoe-shaped **Ramgarh Meteorite Crater**.

---

#### Q7: Differentiate between Chhappan ka Maidan and Chhappan ki Pahadiyan.
**Answer**:
Despite phonetic similarity, they represent completely different geographic divisions, rock systems, and locations:
1. **Chhappan ka Maidan (Mahi Basin)**: A fertile alluvial plain located in southern Rajasthan between **Banswara and Pratapgarh**, formed by the drainage network of **56 streams and 56 villages** of the Mahi river.
2. **Chhappan ki Pahadiyan (Luni Basin)**: A cluster of fifty-six round, dome-shaped granitic hills (*Inselbergs*) located around **Siwana (Balotra district)** in the arid Thar, housing Nakoda Parvat and Haldeshwar Mahadev.

---

#### Q8: Write a concise note on the physical divisions and significance of the Eastern Plains.
**Answer**:
Formed by Pleistocene alluvium and occupying 23% of Rajasthan’s area, the Eastern Plains support 39% of the state's population (highest density):
1. **Sub-Basins**:
   - *Chambal Basin*: Characterized by intense gully erosion forming deep ravines (**Utkhat Bhumi / Badlands**) across Dholpur and Karauli.
   - *Banas-Banganga Plain*: Vast fertile *Piedmont* plain divided into Mewar and Malpura-Karauli plains.
   - *Mahi Basin*: Southern alluvial tract encompassing the *Chappan Plain* and *Kanthal*.
2. **Economic Role**: Represents the agricultural heartland of the state, yielding intensive wheat, mustard, and gram harvests under Alfisols.

### 1.1 The Aravalli Alignment Paradox
The single most critical factor producing the aridity of western Rajasthan is the **structural strike of the Aravalli Range**:
1. The Aravallis run in a **South-West to North-East** direction.
2. The **Arabian Sea branch** of the Southwest Monsoon enters Rajasthan from Gujarat and travels along the exact same South-West to North-East axis.
3. Because the mountains lie **parallel** to the path of the monsoon winds rather than perpendicular (transverse) to them, the moisture-laden clouds pass unobstructed into Punjab and Himachal Pradesh without undergoing orographic ascent or adiabatic condensation.
4. Conversely, the **Bay of Bengal branch** sheds most of its moisture over the Gangetic plains. By the time it crosses eastern Rajasthan and strikes the eastern slopes of the Aravallis, it has shed over 90% of its moisture, leaving the western side in an intense **rain-shadow zone**.

---

### 1.2 Seasonal Cycles & Vernacular Weather Phenomena

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               THE THREE CLIMATIC SEASONS & VERNACULAR PHENOMENA                        │
├───────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Season (Vernacular│ Calendar Duration           │ Climatic Characteristics & Phenomena │
├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ **1. Summer**     │ Mid-March to June           │ • Extreme heat (45°C to 49°C).       │
│    (*Unhalo /     │                             │ • **Loo**: Scorching, desiccating    │
│     उन्हाळो*)     │                             │   westerly dust winds.               │
│                   │                             │ • **Baboolya**: Local dust devils.   │
├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ **2. Monsoon**    │ Late June to September      │ • Receives **90% of annual rain**.   │
│    (*Chau-masa /  │                             │ • **Purvaiya**: Moist easterly winds │
│     चौमासा*)      │                             │   from the Bay of Bengal.            │
├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ **3. Winter**     │ October to February         │ • Cold wave (*Sheet-Lehar*); frost.  │
│    (*Siyalo /     │                             │ • **Mahawat**: Winter rainfall from  │
│     सियाळो*)      │                             │   Mediterranean cyclones; **"Golden  │
│                   │                             │   Drops"** for Rabi crops.           │
└───────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Detailed Anatomy of Vernacular Phenomena:
1. **Loo (लू)**: Extremely hot, dry, dust-laden winds blowing from the Thar Desert during May and June with velocities of 30 to 40 km/h, pushing afternoon temperatures above 45°C and causing acute dehydration and heatstroke.
2. **Baboolya / Bhabhoolya (बबूल्या)**: Intense, localized convective thermal dust whirlwinds (dust devils). In peak summer, extreme ground heating creates a localized low-pressure pocket; rushing peripheral winds create a spiraling vertical dust vortex that lifts sand hundreds of feet into the sky.
3. **Purvaiya / Purwai (पुरवैया)**: The moist easterly monsoon winds arriving from the Bay of Bengal through the Gangetic plain, bringing life-giving monsoon downpours to eastern and southern Rajasthan.
4. **Mahawat (मावठ) — The "Golden Drops" (स्वर्ण बूँदें)**:
   - **Meteorological Origin**: Occurs during winter (December to February) caused by **Western Disturbances (पश्चिमी विक्षोभ)** — temperate extratropical cyclonic depressions originating over the **Mediterranean Sea** and carried into northwestern India by the **Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream**.
   - **Precipitation**: Brings light showers (2 cm to 5 cm) across northern and western Rajasthan (Ganganagar, Bikaner, Churu, Hanumangarh, Jaipur).
   - **Agronomic Miracle**: Termed **"Golden Drops"** (*Swarn Boondein*) by farmers because it provides critical irrigation during the grain-filling stage of **Rabi crops** (Wheat, Mustard, Barley, and Gram), dramatically boosting agricultural yields.

### 3.3 Dr. G.T. Trewartha’s Classification (ट्रेवार्था का जलवायु वर्गीकरण)
Trewartha simplified Köppen’s boundaries to reflect practical vegetation-rainfall thresholds:
1. **BWh**: Tropical Desert Arid (Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Phalodi).
2. **BSh**: Semi-Arid Steppe (Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur, Shekhawati, Pali, Jalore).
3. **Caw**: Sub-Humid Monsoon with Dry Winter (Jaipur, Alwar, Bharatpur, Sawai Madhopur, Bhilwara).
4. **Aw**: Tropical Humid (Banswara, Dungarpur, Jhalawar, Mount Abu).

---bc:Te91,1. **Aravalli Alignment & Aridity**: The Thar Desert is arid because the Aravallis run **parallel to the Southwest Monsoon's Arabian Sea branch**, providing **zero orographic lift**.
2. **Rainfall Contribution by Monsoon Branches**:
   - **Bay of Bengal Branch**: Provides **approx. 90%** of Rajasthan's total precipitation.
   - **Arabian Sea Branch**: Provides only **approx. 10%** (largely restricted to southern slopes around Mount Abu).
3. **Meteorological Source of Mahawat**: Mahawat is caused by **Western Disturbances originating in the Mediterranean Sea**, brought by the Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream, NOT by retreating monsoons!
4. **Beneficiary Crop of Mahawat**: Mahawat specifically benefits **Rabi crops** (Wheat, Gram, Mustard), NOT Kharif crops (Bajra, Jowar).
5. **Köppen's Largest Climatic Zone in Rajasthan**: **BShw (Semi-Arid Steppe)** covers the largest land area, NOT BWhw or Cwg!
6. **Thornthwaite's Largest Climatic Zone in Rajasthan**: **DA'w (Tropical Semi-Arid)** covers the largest territory in Thornthwaite’s scheme.
7. **Largest vs Smallest Agro-Climatic Zone**:
   - **Largest**: **Zone I-C** (Hyper-Arid Partially Irrigated — Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Churu).
   - **Smallest**: **Zone IV-B** (Humid Southern Plain — Dungarpur, Banswara, Pratapgarh, Salumbar).
8. **Wettest Place vs Wettest District**:
   - Wettest **Place**: **Mount Abu** (150 cm).
   - Wettest **District**: **Jhalawar** (100 cm).
9. **Driest Place vs Driest District**:
   - Driest **Place**: **Sam** (Jaisalmer, < 5 cm).
   - Driest **District**: **Jaisalmer** (10 cm).
10. **The Dust Storm Champion**: **Sri Ganganagar** experiences the maximum number of dust-storm (*Aandhi*) days in a year (**27 days**); Jhalawar experiences the lowest (only 3 days).
11. **Highest Diurnal Temperature Range**: **Jaisalmer** (due to quartz sand absorbing heat rapidly by day and radiating it into cloudless desert skies at night).
12. **Highest Annual Temperature Range**: **Churu** (records both the highest summer highs of 50°C and sub-zero winter lows of -2°C).
13. **Purvaiya Direction**: Moist easterly winds blowing from the **East (Bay of Bengal)** toward the West.
14. **Baboolya Meteorological Nature**: A localized **convective thermal dust devil** caused by sudden summer low-pressure pockets.
15. **Köppen Code for Mount Abu & Jhalawar**: Classified as **Aw** (Tropical Humid / Savanna), NOT Cwg!
16. **Köppen Code for Shekhawati & Nagaur**: Classified as **BShw** (Steppe), characterized by Khejri and scrub.
17. **Cwg District Coverage**: Encompasses the **Eastern Plains** (Jaipur, Alwar, Dausa, Tonk, Sawai Madhopur, Bharatpur), representing sub-humid monsoon with dry winters.
18. **The 100 cm Isohyet Location**: Passes exclusively through **Jhalawar and Mount Abu**.
19. **The 25 cm Isohyet Division**: Divides **BWhw from BShw** in Köppen's classification, and separates Pure Arid Desert from Semi-Arid Bagar.
20. **Agro-Climatic Zone of Kota & Baran**: **Zone V (Humid South-Eastern Plain)**, characterized by black Vertisols and soybean crops.
21. **Agro-Climatic Zone of Ganganagar & Hanumangarh**: **Zone I-B (Irrigated North-Western Plain)**, irrigated by the Indira Gandhi Canal and Gang Canal.
22. **Agro-Climatic Zone of Jaipur & Dausa**: **Zone III-A (Semi-Arid Eastern Plain)**.
23. **Month of Maximum Humidity**: **August** (coinciding with the peak of the Southwest Monsoon).
24. **Month of Minimum Humidity**: **April and May** (prior to the onset of monsoon).
25. **"October Heat" (क्वार की धूप)**: The uncomfortable sultry weather experienced in late September and October caused by rising temperatures and high residual humidity following the retreat of the monsoon.

---bd:T37ea,### 7.1 2-Markers (15–20 Words)

#### Q1: What is "Mahawat"? State its economic significance.
**Answer**:
Winter precipitation in Rajasthan caused by Mediterranean **Western Disturbances**; known as **"Golden Drops"** (*Swarn Boondein*) for providing life-saving irrigation to Rabi crops (wheat and mustard).

---

#### Q2: Why does Western Rajasthan receive scanty rainfall?
**Answer**:
The Aravalli range runs parallel to the Southwest Monsoon's Arabian Sea branch, offering zero orographic barrier, while easterly Bay of Bengal winds exhaust moisture before crossing the range.

---

#### Q3: Which is the largest Agro-Climatic Zone of Rajasthan, and which districts does it cover?
**Answer**:
**Zone I-C (Hyper-Arid Partially Irrigated Zone)**; covers **Bikaner, Jaisalmer, and Churu**, spanning over 7.7 million hectares.

---

#### Q4: Define "Baboolya" in Rajasthani weather.
**Answer**:
A localized, intense convective whirlwind (dust devil) formed during summer afternoons when intense solar insolation creates sudden local low-pressure pockets that draw spiraling peripheral winds.

---

#### Q5: Differentiate between Köppen's BWhw and BShw zones in Rajasthan.
**Answer**:
**BWhw** represents the hyper-arid desert (<20 cm rain, xerophytic vegetation; Jaisalmer, Bikaner); **BShw** represents the semi-arid steppe (20–40 cm rain, grasslands; Jodhpur, Nagaur, Sikar).

---

### 7.2 5-Markers (50 Words)

#### Q6: Explain Dr. Vladimir Köppen’s climatic classification of Rajasthan with a diagrammatic overview.
**Answer**:
Köppen utilized vegetation boundaries as the primary indicator of temperature and precipitation, classifying Rajasthan into four distinct zones:
1. **BWhw (Tropical Desert Climate)**: Extreme aridity (<20 cm rain); xerophytic scrub (*Marudbhid*); covers Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Phalodi, and Anupgarh.
2. **BShw (Semi-Arid Steppe)**: Largest zone by area; 20–40 cm rain; steppe grasses and Khejri; covers Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur, Pali, and Shekhawati.
3. **Cwg (Sub-Humid Monsoon)**: 40–80 cm rain with dry winters; mixed deciduous Dhok forests; covers Jaipur, Alwar, Dausa, Tonk, and Sawai Madhopur.
4. **Aw (Tropical Savanna)**: >80 cm rain; teak forests; covers Dungarpur, Banswara, Jhalawar, and Mount Abu.

---

#### Q7: Delineate the characteristics and agricultural significance of Agro-Climatic Zone V.
**Answer**:
Known as the **Humid South-Eastern Plain**, Zone V covers the Hadoti tract (**Kota, Baran, Bundi, and Jhalawar**):
1. **Soil & Climate**: Deep, heavy black clayey **Vertisols (Regur)** with high water-retention capacity; receives 75 to 100 cm rainfall.
2. **Crop Matrix**: Serves as Rajasthan's primary **Soybean Bowl**; dominates statewide production of commercial spices (**Coriander** in Ramganj Mandi, **Garlic** in Baran, and **Mandarin Oranges** in Jhalawar).
3. **Irrigation Network**: Highly irrigated through the Chambal Canal network and perennial tributaries.

---

#### Q8: What are Western Disturbances? Analyze their impact on the winter agro-economy of Rajasthan.
**Answer**:
Extratropical cyclonic storms originating over the Mediterranean Sea, steered into northwestern India by the Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream during December–February:
1. **Rainfall Pattern**: Brings 2 to 5 cm of light, non-destructive showers across northern and western districts (Ganganagar, Bikaner, Hanumangarh, Jaipur).
2. **Impact on Rabi Crops**: Termed **Mahawat ("Golden Drops")**, it accelerates tillering and grain-filling in wheat, mustard, and barley, reducing groundwater pumping costs and significantly improving grain quality.
3. **Cold Wave Hazard**: Followed immediately by severe northerly cold waves (*Sheet-Lehar*) and ground frost, occasionally injuring vegetable nurseries and cumin crops.

---

### 7.3 10-Markers (100 Words)

#### Q9: "The climate of Rajasthan is a complex mosaic of extreme aridity, spatial rainfall disparity, and seasonal vulnerabilities." Critically analyze with reference to its meteorological determinants and drought susceptibility.
**Answer**:
Rajasthan exhibits the most volatile thermal and precipitation regimes in India, shaped by its unique location on the subtropical arid belt:

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   METEOROLOGICAL MOSAIC OF RAJASTHAN'S CLIMATE                         │
├───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Climatic Dimension        │ Meteorological Causes & Spatial Manifestations             │
├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Extreme Spatial        │ • Rainfall decreases sharply from Southeast to Northwest:  │
│    Disparity              │   - Mount Abu receives **150 cm**; Jhalawar receives **100 │
│                           │   - Sam (Jaisalmer) receives **less than 5 cm**.           │
│                           │ • Western Thar receives only 10% of state precipitation.   │
├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. Aravalli Barrier &     │ • South-West to North-East strike of the Aravallis runs    │
│    Monsoonal Behavior     │   parallel to the Arabian Sea branch, denying orographic   │
│                           │   lift; Bay of Bengal branch exhausts moisture in plains.  │
├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. Severe Thermal         │ • Low cloud cover and high quartz albedo create intense    │
│    Oscillations           │   diurnal ranges (20°C in Jaisalmer).                      │
│                           │ • Churu swings from **50°C** in summer to **-2°C** winter. │

```
**Conclusion**: Mitigating Rajasthan’s climatic vulnerability demands expanding watershed resilience, micro-irrigation (drip/sprinkler), and drought-resistant agro-forestry suited to its distinct agro-climatic zones.

### A. Alignment of the Continental Water Divide (*Jal Vibhajak Rekha*)
The Aravalli Mountain Range functions as the **Continental Water Divide of Northern-Western India**. Running diagonally across Rajasthan from southwest to northeast, it bifurcates the state into two disparate hydrological regimes:
1. **The Western & South-Western Slope**: Directs precipitation runoff towards the **Arabian Sea** (via the Rann of Kutch and Gulf of Khambhat) or locks it into endorheic desert basins.
2. **The Eastern & South-Eastern Slope**: Directs runoff towards the **Bay of Bengal** via the Yamuna-Ganga river system.

#### Exact Trace of the Continental Divide Line across Rajasthan:
- Enters northeastern Rajasthan along the **Delhi Ridge – Khetri – Alwar** uplands.
- Passes through **Sambhar Lake** (south of the lake) and crosses **Ajmer** (Peeplu / Nag Pahar ridge).
- Traverses **Beawar** and runs atop the **Bhorat Plateau** (at an elevation of 1,225 m between Kumbhalgarh in Rajsamand and Gogunda in Udaipur).
- Descends south-southeast between the catchments of the **Sabarmati** and **Mahi** in southern Udaipur/Salumbar.
- Passes east of **Pratapgarh (Chhoti Sadri)** and leaves Rajasthan into Madhya Pradesh.

> **Crucial Geomorphological Invariant**: Any drop of rain falling to the **west** of the Bhorat Plateau crest flows via the Sei, Wakal, or Jawai rivers into the Arabian Sea. Any drop falling to the **east** of the crest flows via the Ayad/Bedach or Banas rivers into the Bay of Bengal!

---

### B. Tripartite Quantitative Hydrographic Classification

| Drainage Category | Share of State Drainage Area | Terminal Outflow Sink | Primary Rivers Included | Defining Hydrological Character |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Inland Drainage System** (*अंतःप्रवाही तंत्र*) | **~60.2%** | Disappears in desert sands or terminal saline playas (*Ranns* / *Playa Lakes*) | **Ghaggar, Kantli, Sabi, Ruparel, Mendha, Rupangarh, Kakney** | Ephemeral, short-lived flash streams lacking sufficient hydraulic gradient or volume to reach the sea. |
| **2. Bay of Bengal System** (*बंगाल की खाड़ी तंत्र*) | **~22.4%** | Yamuna River ➔ Ganga River ➔ Bay of Bengal | **Chambal, Banas, Banganga, Gambhir, Parbati, Kali Sindh, Berach, Kothari, Khari** | Well-developed dendritic drainage; accounts for the largest surface water volume, perennial flows, and gorge incisions. |
| **3. Arabian Sea System** (*अरब सागर तंत्र*) | **~17.4%** | Rann of Kutch & Gulf of Khambhat ➔ Arabian Sea | **Luni, Mahi, Sabarmati, West Banas, Som, Jakham, Jawai, Sukri** | Seasonal southwest rivers; characterized by extreme gradient variation (mountain cascades in Mahi to saline braided pans in Luni). |

### A. Luni River (*लव Flowvati / Sagarmati / Maruasya / आधी मीठी-आधी खारी*)

#### 1. Statutory Genesis & Nomenclature
- **Rigvedic / Ancient Name**: Mentioned as *Lavnavati* (saline river) in ancient Sanskrit scriptures.
- **Kalidasa's Epithet**: Renowned Sanskrit poet Kalidasa termed it **Antah-Salila** (*अन्तःसलिला* — subterranean water flowing with hidden purity).
- **Originating Names**: Originates at **Nag Pahar (Ajmer)** as the **Sagarmati**. Simultaneously, a holy stream named **Saraswati** originates from Pushkar Lake. The two streams converge at **Govindgarh** (Ajmer), from where the combined river is formally christened **Luni**.

#### 2. Hydrographic Profile & Route (50-District Lens)
- **Total Length**: **495 km** (approximately **330 to 350 km** within Rajasthan).
- **Districts Traversed (8 Districts)**:
  $$\text{Ajmer} \longrightarrow \text{Nagaur} \longrightarrow \text{Beawar} \longrightarrow \text{Jodhpur Rural} \longrightarrow \text{Pali} \longrightarrow \text{Balotra} \longrightarrow \text{Barmer} \longrightarrow \text{Sanchore}$$
- **Outflow / Terminal Sink**: Crosses the Rajasthan border at Sanchore and discharges into the marshes of the **Rann of Kutch (Gujarat)**.
- **The Balotra Salinity Phenomenon (*आधी मीठी - आधी खारी*)**:
  - Up to **Balotra (now a district, formerly in Barmer)**, the river water remains potable and sweet (*Meetha*).
  - Downstream of Balotra, the river water becomes violently saline (*Khara*).
  - **Scientific Explanation**:
    1. High evaporation rates in the hyper-arid plain leave crusts of soluble salts.
    2. Subterranean soils in the lower basin contain high concentrations of sodium chloride ($NaCl$) and gypsum deposited by the receding prehistoric Tethys Sea.
    3. Runoff passing through the deeply weathered Malani Rhyolite and granitic bedrocks leaches sodium ions into the unconfined shallow aquifer via capillary action.

```text
[Nag Pahar (Ajmer)] ──(Sagarmati)──┐
                                   ├──> [Govindgarh] ──(Luni River)──> [Balotra] ──(Saline)──> [Rann of Kutch]
[Pushkar Lake]      ──(Saraswati)──┘                        ▲             │
                                                            │             ▼
                                            Sweet Water Tract (0–200 km)  Brackish / Saline (>200 km)
```

#### 3. Complete Tributary Network of Luni

```text
                                     LUNI RIVER SYSTEM
                                             │
      Right-Bank Tributary (North)           │        Left-Bank Tributaries (Aravalli Origin)
      ────────────────────────────           │        ───────────────────────────────────────
      • JOJARI (जोजड़ी)                      │        • GUHIYA (गुहिया)
        - Origin: Pondlu village (Nagaur)    │        • BANDI (बांडी - Hemawas Dam)
        - Only right-bank tributary          │        • SUKRI (सुकड़ी - Bankli Dam)
        - Only non-Aravalli tributary        │        • MITHARI (मीठड़ी)
        - Flows North to South-West          │        • JAWAI (जवाई - Sumerpur Dam)
                                             │        • KHARI (खारी)
                                             │        • SAGI (सागी - Jaswantpura Hills)
```

1. **Jojari (*जोजड़ी*) — The Supreme Invariant Trap**:
   - **Origin**: Pondlu village, Nagaur district.
   - **Length**: ~83 km; joins Luni near Doli village (Jodhpur Rural / Balotra border).
   - **Exam Singularities**:
     - It is the **ONLY tributary of the Luni that joins from the right bank**.
     - It is the **ONLY tributary that does NOT originate from the Aravalli Range** (originates in the flat semi-arid plain of Nagaur).
     - It flows in a north-to-southwest trajectory, contrary to all other Aravalli tributaries that flow west/northwest.
2. **Bandi (*बांडी*)**:
   - **Origin**: Hemawas village hills, Pali district.
   - **Reservoir**: **Hemawas Dam** (Pali).
   - **Environmental Status**: Often dubbed the **"Chemical River" of Rajasthan**; notorious as the most polluted river in western Rajasthan due to untreated toxic effluents discharged from Pali's textile dyeing and printing industrial clusters.
3. **Guhiya (*गुहिया*)**:
   - Origin: Khariya Sodha hills, Pali; joins Bandi before Bandi joins Luni.
4. **Sukri (*सुकड़ी*)**:
   - **Origin**: Desuri pass / hills, Pali district.
   - **Course**: Flows through Pali and Jalore, joining Luni near Samdari (Balotra).
   - **Reservoir**: **Bankli Dam** (*बांकली बांध*) constructed at Bankli village in Jalore.
5. **Jawai (*जवाई*) — The Monarch Tributary**:
   - **Origin**: Goriyan village hills, Bali tehsil, Pali district.
   - **Course**: Flows through Pali, Jalore, and Balotra before meeting Luni near Sayla.
   - **Reservoir**: **Jawai Dam (*जवाई बांध*)** at Sumerpur (Pali):
     - Known as the **"Amrit Sarovar of Marwar" (*मारवाड़ का अमृत सरोवर*)**.
     - Commissioned in 1946 by Maharaja Umaid Singh of Jodhpur, completed in 1957 (Engineers: Edgar & Ferguson).
     - Largest reservoir by volume in Western Rajasthan; serves as the lifeline drinking source for Jodhpur and Pali cities.
     - **Sei Diversion Project**: When water levels deplete, water is imported via the **Sei Tunnel** (Rajasthan's first inter-basin water transfer tunnel, 6.7 km long) from the Sei River (Sabarmati catchment) into the Jawai Dam.
     - Surroundings declared the **Jawai Bandh Leopard Conservation Reserve**.
6. **Khari (*खारी*)**:
   - Origin: Shergaon hills, Sirohi district; joins Jawai near Sayla before Jawai joins Luni.
7. **Sagi (*सागी*)**:
   - Origin: Jaswantpura hills, Jalore district; joins Luni near Gandhav (Sanchore).

---

### B. Mahi River (*माही — वागड़ की गंगा / कांठल की गंगा / दक्षिण राजस्थान की स्वर्ण रेखा*)

#### 1. Mythological & Geographic Significance
- Known as the **"Kamdhenu of South Rajasthan"** and **"Ganga of the Tribals" (*आदिवासियों की गंगा*)**.
- **Unique World Feature**: It is the **only river in the world that crosses the Tropic of Cancer (23°30' N latitude) TWICE**. It cuts it first on its northward entry from MP into Banswara, loops around Pratapgarh-Dungarpur, and cuts it a second time on its southward exit from Dungarpur into Gujarat.
- Flows in the distinctive shape of an **Inverted 'U' (अंग्रेजी के उल्टे 'U' का आकार)** or a horseshoe.

```text
                         [Tropic of Cancer: 23°30' N] ── cuts 2nd time (Exit to Gujarat)
                                      ▲
                                      │
            Dungarpur ◄──────── Banswara-Dungarpur Border ◄──────── Pratapgarh
                │                                                        ▲
                │ (Turns Southward)                                      │ (Flows Northward)
                ▼                                                        │
          [Gujarat Entry]                                          [Entry: Khandu Village]
                │                                                        ▲
                ▼                                                        │
        [Gulf of Khambhat]                            [Origin: Amjhoru, Dhar (MP)]
                                                                         │
                                              [Tropic of Cancer: 23°30' N] ── cuts 1st time
```

#### 2. Hydrographic Profile & Course
- **Origin**: Amjhoru village, near Mehad Lake, Dhar district (Vindhyan Hills, Madhya Pradesh).
- **Entry Point into Rajasthan**: **Khandu village** (*खांदू गांव*), Banswara district.
- **Course**: Traverses Banswara, forms the natural geographical boundary between Banswara and Dungarpur, touches the border of Pratapgarh, loops south through Dungarpur, and enters Mahisagar district of Gujarat.
- **Terminal Sink**: Discharges into the **Gulf of Khambhat** (Arabian Sea).
- **Length**: Total length = **576 km**; Length inside Rajasthan = **171 km**.
- **Geomorphic Environs**:
  - **Chhappan ka Maidan**: The fertile alluvial floodplain formed by the 56 streams/drainage channels of the Mahi basin between Banswara and Pratapgarh.
  - **Kanthal Plain**: The coastal-like alluvial strip along the banks of Mahi in Pratapgarh (hence Mahi is called *Kanthal ki Ganga*).

#### 3. Major Hydraulic Projects on Mahi
1. **Mahi Bajaj Sagar Dam (*माही बजाज सागर बांध*)**:
   - Located at **Borkheda village**, 16 km north of Banswara.
   - Named after freedom fighter Jamnalal Bajaj.
   - Longest dam in Rajasthan (**3,109 metres** length).
   - Joint venture between Rajasthan (45% share) and Gujarat (55% share). However, **100% of power generated (140 MW) is allocated exclusively to Rajasthan**!
2. **Kagdi Pick-Up Dam**: Built immediately downstream in Banswara to regulate irrigation feeder canals (Bhikhabhai Sagwara Canal and Anandpuri Lift Canal).
3. **Kadana Dam (*कड़ाना बांध*)**: Built entirely in Mahisagar district of **Gujarat**, financed under the inter-state agreement to irrigate Gujarat tracts.

#### 4. The Tributary System of Mahi
1. **Som (*सोम*)**:
   - **Origin**: Bichhameda hills (*बीछामेड़ा की पहाड़ियां*), Babalwara, Kherwara tehsil, Udaipur district.
   - **Projects**: **Som-Kagdar Irrigation Project** (Udaipur) and **Som-Kamla-Amba Irrigation Project** (Dungarpur).
2. **Jakham (*जाखम*)**:
   - **Origin**: Bhawarmata hills (*भंवरमाता की पहाड़ी*), Chhoti Sadri tehsil, Pratapgarh district.
   - **Flow**: Passes through the dense teak forests of Sita Mata Wildlife Sanctuary.
   - **Jakham Dam (*जाखम बांध*)**: Located in Pratapgarh; with a height of **81 metres**, it is the **tallest dam in Rajasthan**.
3. **Anas (*अनास*)**:
   - Origin: Amber village, near Jhabua, MP; enters Rajasthan at Mellakhera village (Banswara); joins Mahi near Dungarpur border.
4. **Erav / Iru (*इराॅव / ईरू*)**:
   - Origin: Pratapgarh hills; **crucial trap**: It is the **only tributary that joins Mahi before it enters the Mahi Bajaj Sagar Dam reservoir**!
5. **Chap, Moran, and Haran**: Minor tribal streams of Banswara and Dungarpur.

#### 5. The Baneshwar Dham Triveni Sangam (*त्रिवेणी संगम*)
- **Location**: Nawata-para village (*नवाटापारा*), Aspur tehsil, Dungarpur district.
- **Convergence**: Three sacred rivers unite here: **Som + Mahi + Jakham**.
- **Religious Eminence**: Known as the **"Kumbh of the Tribals" (*आदिवासियों का कुंभ*)** or *Puskhar of Vagad*.
- Celebrated annually on **Magh Purnima**. Seat established by Sant Mavji; home to the world's only worshipped **Broken Shivalinga (*खंडित शिवलिंग*)**.

---

### C. Sabarmati River (*साबरमती*)
- **Origin**: Padarana hills (*पदारणा की पहाड़ियां*), near Jhadol tehsil, south-west of Udaipur.
- **Hydrological Paradox**: Though originating in Rajasthan, it is almost entirely celebrated as the **lifeline of Gujarat**.
  - Total length: **416 km**.
  - Length inside Rajasthan: Barely **44 to 45 km**!
  - Flows past Gandhinagar (Gujarat capital) and Ahmedabad, terminating in the Gulf of Khambhat.
- **Major Tributaries in Rajasthan**:
  - **Wakal (*वाकल*)**: Originates from Goram Ghat / Kotra hills, Udaipur.
  - **Sei (*सेई*)**: Originates from Padarana hills; source of the Sei diversion tunnel to Jawai Dam.
  - **Hathmati, Meshwo, Majam, and Vetrak**: Drain the southern spurs of Dungarpur and Udaipur into Gujarat.

---

### D. West Banas River (*पश्चिमी बनास*)
- **Origin**: Naya Sanwara village (*नया संवारा*), Pindwara tehsil, Sirohi district.
- **Course**: Drains the western slopes of Mount Abu and Sirohi, enters Banaskantha district of Gujarat, passes the commercial town of **Deesa**, and terminates in the **Little Rann of Kutch (कच्छ का छोटा रन)**.
- **Length**: Total length = **266 km** (~50 km in Rajasthan).
- **Major Tributary**: **Sukli / Sipu River** (*सुकली / सीपू* — not to be confused with Luni's Sukri).

### A. Chambal River (*चम्बल — चर्मण्वती / कामधेनु / नित्यवाही*)

#### 1. Identity & Hydrographic Superlatives
- **Perenniality**: The **only perennial (12-month continuous flow) river of Rajasthan** along with Mahi.
- **Epithets**: Mentioned as *Charmanvati* in the Mahabharata; revered as the *Kamdhenu of Rajasthan*.
- **Maximum Water Volume**: Carries the largest volume of surface runoff in the entire state.
- **Interstate Boundary**: Forms a natural interstate boundary of **241 km** between Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh (bordering Sawai Madhopur, Karauli, and Dholpur).

#### 2. Hydrographic Route & Physical Dimensions
- **Origin**: Janapav hills (*जानापाव पहाड़ी*), Vindhyan Range, near Mhow (Dr. Ambedkar Nagar), Indore district, Madhya Pradesh (elevation: 610 m).
- **Entry into Rajasthan**: Enters through a rocky gorge near **Chaurasigarh Fort (*चौरासीगढ़ दुर्ग*)**, Rawatbhata tehsil, Chittorgarh district.
- **Districts Traversed (6 Districts)**:
  $$\text{Chittorgarh (Rawatbhata)} \longrightarrow \text{Kota} \longrightarrow \text{Bundi} \longrightarrow \text{Sawai Madhopur} \longrightarrow \text{Karauli} \longrightarrow \text{Dholpur}$$
- **Terminal Confluence**: Discharges into the **Yamuna River** at **Muradganj** (near Chakarnagar / Panchnada), Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh.
- **Total Length**: 
  - Traditional metric: **965 km** (Length purely inside Rajasthan = **135 to 153 km**; Along MP-Rajasthan border = **241 km**; In MP = ~320 km; In UP = ~217 km).
  - Modern Survey of India measurement: **1,051 km**.

#### 3. Distinctive Geomorphological Features
1. **Chulia Waterfall (*चूलिया जलप्रपात*)**:
   - Located at **Bhainsrorgarh** (Chittorgarh), immediately downstream of the confluence where the Brahmani (Bamani) River meets Chambal.
   - Height: **18 metres** (highest waterfall in Rajasthan).
2. **Utkhat Bhumi (*उत्खात भूमि* — Badland Topography & Beehad Ravines)**:
   - Caused by accelerated vertical gully erosion (*अवनालिका अपरदन*) through soft alluvial mantles.
   - Creates labyrinthine, deep, vegetated ravines (*Beehad / खादर*) spanning Sawai Madhopur, Karauli, and Dholpur.
   - **Dang Region (*डांग क्षेत्र*)**: The rugged, dissected ravine plateau; **Karauli** is hailed as the **"Dang ki Rani" (*डांग की रानी*)**, while Dholpur is the "Dang ka Raja".
   - Special development programmes launched here: *Dang Area Development Programme* and *Kandhara Area Development Scheme*.
3. **Deep Gorges (*कंदराएं*)**:
   - The river carves magnificent narrow rocky canyons between Rawatbhata and Kota city (Garadia Mahadev canyon is often acclaimed as "The Grand Canyon of India").

#### 4. The Chambal Valley Multipurpose Hydel & Irrigation Project (1953–1972)
A 50:50 joint enterprise between **Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh**, executed in three systematic stages:

| Dam Name | Stage & Year | Exact Location | Reservoir & Structural Capacity | Hydroelectric Power Installed | Defining Role / Distinction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Gandhi Sagar Dam** (*गांधी सागर*) | Stage I (1960) | Bhanpura / Mandsaur district, **Madhya Pradesh** | Length: 514 m; Height: 62 m; Storage: 7,322 MCM | **115 MW** (5 units of 23 MW) | Largest storage reservoir of the Chambal cascade; located entirely in MP. |
| **2. Kota Barrage** (*कोटा बैराज*) | Stage I (1960) | Kota city, **Rajasthan** | Length: 552 m; 19 spillway gates | **0 MW (Purely Irrigation)** | **No power generation**; diverts water into Right Main Canal (goes to MP) & Left Main Canal (irrigates Kota, Bundi). |
| **3. Rana Pratap Sagar Dam** (*राणा प्रताप सागर*) | Stage II (1970) | Rawatbhata, **Chittorgarh district, Rajasthan** | Length: 1,143 m; Height: 54 m; Storage: 2,898 MCM | **172 MW** (4 units of 43 MW) | **Largest dam by storage volume in Rajasthan**; supplies cooling water to the Rajasthan Atomic Power Station (RAPS). |
| **4. Jawahar Sagar Dam** (*जवाहर सागर*) | Stage III (1972) | Borkheda, Kota–Bundi border, **Rajasthan** | Length: 440 m; Height: 45 m; Pick-up dam | **99 MW** (3 units of 33 MW) | Functions as a peak-load power station and pick-up dam 26 km upstream of Kota city. |

> **Chambal Power Sharing Arithmetic**: Total power capacity = $115 + 172 + 99 = 386\text{ MW}$. Rajasthan's sovereign 50% entitlement = **193 MW**.

#### 5. Tributaries of the Chambal River

```text
                                    CHAMBAL TRIBUTARIES
                                             │
      Left-Bank Tributaries                  │                  Right-Bank Tributaries
      ─────────────────────                  │                  ──────────────────────
      • BRAHMANI / BAMANI (Haripura Hills)   │                  • KALI SINDH (Bagli, MP)
      • MEJ (Mandalgarh Hills, Bhilwara)     │                  • AHU (Susner, MP)
      • BANAS (Khamnor Hills, Rajsamand)     │                  • PARWAN (Malwa, MP)
                                             │                  • PARBATI (Sehore, MP)
                                             │                  • NIWAJ, KUNO, CHAWALI
```

1. **Kali Sindh (*काली सिंध*)**:
   - **Origin**: Bagli village, Dewas district, Madhya Pradesh.
   - **Entry into Rajasthan**: Binda village, Jhalawar district.
   - **Confluence with Chambal**: Nonaire village, Kota district.
   - **Historic Confluence (*Gagron Jal Durg*)**: At Gagron (Jhalawar), Kali Sindh merges with the **Ahu River**. Right on this rocky promontory stands the foundationless **UNESCO World Heritage Gagron Fort**.
2. **Ahu (*आहू*)**:
   - Origin: Susner, MP; enters Rajasthan near Chachurni (Jhalawar); merges with Kali Sindh at Gagron.
3. **Parwan (*परवन*)**:
   - Origin: Malwa Plateau, MP; enters Rajasthan near Manohar Thana (Jhalawar); traverses Baran (flows through the **Shergarh Wildlife Sanctuary**); joins Kali Sindh near Ramgarh (Baran).
4. **Parbati (*पार्वती*)**:
   - Origin: Sehore hills, Vindhyan Range, MP; enters Rajasthan at Chhatarpura village (Baran); traverses Baran and Kota; meets Chambal at **Paliya village** on the Sawai Madhopur–MP border.
5. **Brahmani / Bamani (*ब्राह्मणी*)**:
   - Origin: Haripura village hills, Begun, Chittorgarh; merges with Chambal at **Bhainsrorgarh Fort** (forming the Chulia Falls).
6. **Mej (*मेज*)**:
   - Origin: Mandalgarh hills, Bhilwara; drains through Bundi; meets Chambal near Lakheri. Major tributaries: Kural, Mangali.
7. **Kuno (*कूनो*)**:
   - Origin: Shivpuri plateau, MP; enters Baran; rejoins MP and flows through Kuno National Park before terminating in Chambal.

---

### B. Banas River (*बनास — वन की आशा / वर्णाशा / वशिष्ठी*)

#### 1. Identity & Status
- **Title**: *Van Ki Asha* (Hope of the Forest) or *Varnasha*.
- **The Sovereign Invariant**: The **longest river flowing entirely and exclusively within Rajasthan**.
  - Total length: **480 km** (old metric) or **512 km** (modern satellite survey).
  - Its entire catchment area of ~47,060 sq km lies 100% inside the borders of Rajasthan.

#### 2. Hydrographic Route (50-District Lens)
- **Origin**: **Khamnor hills (*खमनोर की पहाड़ियां*)**, near Kumbhalgarh, Rajsamand district.
- **Districts Traversed (7 Districts)**:
  $$\text{Rajsamand} \longrightarrow \text{Chittorgarh} \longrightarrow \text{Bhilwara} \longrightarrow \text{Shahpura} \longrightarrow \text{Kekri} \longrightarrow \text{Tonk} \longrightarrow \text{Sawai Madhopur}$$
- **Terminal Confluence**: Discharges into the Chambal at **Rameswaram Ghat** (*रामेश्वरम धाम*), Padra village, Khandar tehsil, Sawai Madhopur district.

#### 3. The Three Great Triveni Sangams of the Banas Basin

```text
                                TRIVENI SANGAMS OF BANAS
                                           │
         ┌─────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                 ▼                                 ▼
1. BIGOD SANGAM (Bhilwara)        2. RAJMAHAL SANGAM (Tonk/Kekri)   3. RAMESWARAM GHAT (Sawai Madhopur)
   • Banas                           • Banas                           • Banas
   • Bedach (Ayad)                   • Khari                           • Chambal
   • Menal                           • Dai                             • Seep
```

1. **Bigod Sangam (*बीगोद संगम*)**: Located at Bigod (Bhilwara district); convergence of **Banas + Bedach + Menal**.
2. **Rajmahal Sangam (*राजमहल संगम*)**: Located at Rajmahal (on the border of Tonk and Kekri districts); convergence of **Banas + Khari + Dai**.
3. **Rameswaram Sangam (*रामेश्वरम संगम*)**: Located at Khandar (Sawai Madhopur); convergence of **Banas + Chambal + Seep**.

#### 4. Major Hydraulic Projects on Banas
1. **Bisalpur Dam (*बीसलपुर बांध*)**:
   - Located at Bisalpur village, Deoli tehsil, Tonk district.
   - Built in 1999 across a narrow gorge in the Banas River.
   - Gravity concrete dam (Length: 574 m; Height: 39.5 m; Crest capacity: 315.50 RL).
   - **Sovereign Role**: The **largest drinking water project in Rajasthan**; lifeline supplying potable drinking water to Jaipur city, Ajmer, Beawar, Dudu, Kekri, and Tonk.
2. **Isarda Dam (*ईसरदा बांध*)**:
   - Located at Isarda village, Sawai Madhopur district.
   - Constructed downstream of Bisalpur to impound surplus waters for drinking supply to Dausa, Sawai Madhopur, and Jaipur Rural.
3. **Matrikundiya Dam**: Located at Rashmi (Chittorgarh) on Banas; irrigates Mewar plains.
4. **Nand Samand Dam (*नंद समंद बांध*)**: Located in Rajsamand; hailed as the **"Lifeline of Rajsamand"**.

#### 5. Master Tributaries of the Banas
1. **Berach / Bedach (*बेड़च — पूर्व नाम: आयड़*)**:
   - **Origin**: **Gogunda hills (*गोगुंदा की पहाड़ियां*)**, Udaipur district.
   - **The Name-Change Paradox**:
     - Originates as the **Ayad River (*आयड़ नदी*)**.
     - Flows through Udaipur city, nourishing the ancient Chalcolithic site of **Ahar (आयड़ सभ्यता)**.
     - Dumps its water into **Udaisagar Lake** (constructed 1559–1565 by Maharana Udai Singh II).
     - **When it exits Udaisagar Lake, it is rechristened as the Bedach River (*बेड़च नदी*)**!
   - Meets Banas at Bigod (Bhilwara). Total length: 157 km.
   - Major tributary: **Gambhiri River** (origin: Jawad, MP; joins Bedach near Chittorgarh city; the historic Chittorgarh Fort is perched on the Mesa Plateau between the Bedach and Gambhiri rivers).
2. **Kothari (*कोठारी*)**:
   - **Origin**: **Diver hills (*दिवेर की पहाड़ियां*)**, Rajsamand district.
   - **Length**: ~145 km; traverses Rajsamand, Bhilwara, and Shahpura; meets Banas near Nandrai.
   - **Meja Dam (*मेजा बांध*)**: Built across Kothari in Bhilwara; historical drinking water source for the textile city ("Green Mount" park developed here).
   - **Archaeological Treasure**: The Mesolithic site of **Bagor** (oldest animal husbandry evidence in India) is situated directly on the bank of the Kothari River.
3. **Khari (*खारी*)**:
   - **Origin**: Bijral village hills (*बिजराल गांव की पहाड़ियां*), Rajsamand district.
   - **Course**: Traverses Rajsamand, Bhilwara, Shahpura, Kekri, and Tonk; meets Banas at Rajmahal. ( नारायण सागर बांध in Ajmer/Beawar is situated on a diversion of Khari).
4. **Dai (*डाई*)**: Originates from Nasirabad hills (Ajmer/Beawar border); joins Banas at Rajmahal.
5. **Morel (*मोरेल*)**: Originates from Dharla hills (Bassi, Jaipur Rural); traverses Dausa and Gangapur City; joins Banas in Sawai Madhopur. **Morel Dam** is located at Kaluwas (Dausa/Sawai Madhopur border). Major tributary: **Kalisil** (origin: Rajor, Karauli; near Kaila Devi Temple).
6. **Mashi (*माशी*)**: Originates from Kishangarh hills (Ajmer); joins Banas in Tonk.

---

### C. Banganga River (*बाणगंगा — अर्जुन की गंगा / ताला नदी / रुण्डित नदी*)
- **Mythological Origin**: Legend records that Arjuna shot an arrow (*Baan*) into the earth to quench the thirst of dying Bhishma Pitamaha, releasing this subterranean spring.
- **Physical Origin**: **Bairat hills (*बैराठ की पहाड़ियां*)**, Kotputli-Behror district (formerly Jaipur).
- **Districts Traversed**:
  $$\text{Kotputli-Behror} \longrightarrow \text{Jaipur Rural} \longrightarrow \text{Dausa} \longrightarrow \text{Bharatpur}$$
- **Hydrological Classification: The Severed / Beheaded River (*रुण्डित नदी / Rundhit Sarita*)**:
  - In hydrological science, a river that loses sufficient discharge to reach its master stream and terminates in an inland alluvial fan or swamp before its historic confluence is termed a **Severed / Beheaded River (*Rundhit Sarita*)**.
  - Banganga historically joined the **Yamuna River** at Fatehabad (Agra, UP) after a 240 km course.
  - Due to massive deforestation in the Bairat range, excessive siltation, and over-extraction via upstream check-dams, the river currently loses surface velocity in Bharatpur and terminates in the **Keoladeo Ghana National Park marshes**.
- **Hydraulic Landmark**: **Jamwa Ramgarh Dam (*जमवा रामगढ़ बांध*)** built in Jaipur Rural in 1897; served as the primary drinking water lifeline of Jaipur for nearly a century before drying up.

---

### D. Gambhir River (*गम्भीर — उटंगन नदी*)
- **Note of Caution**: Do NOT confuse the **Gambhir River (*गम्भीर*)** of eastern Rajasthan with the **Gambhiri River (*गम्भीरी*)** of Chittorgarh!
- **Origin**: Hindaun / Nadoti hills, Karauli district.
- **Course**: Karauli $\longrightarrow$ Sawai Madhopur $\longrightarrow$ Bharatpur $\longrightarrow$ enters Fatehabad (UP) and joins Yamuna.
- **Panchana Dam (*पांचना बांध*)**:
  - Located at Gudla village, Karauli district.
  - The **largest clay/earthen dam (*मिट्टी का सबसे बड़ा बांध*) in Rajasthan**, constructed with US financial aid.
  - Built at the hydrological confluence of **5 local rivulets**:
    1. **Ata (*अटा*)**
    2. **Machi (*माची*)**
    3. **Bhadrawati (*भद्रावती*)**
    4. **Barkheda (*बरखेड़ा*)**
    5. **Bhainsawat (*भैंसावट*)**
  - Supplies water downstream to the **Ajan Dam (*अजान बांध*)** in Bharatpur, which in turn feeds the wetland ecosystem of Keoladeo National Park.

---c1:T1e17,Rajasthan has the **largest inland drainage system in India**. Over **60% of the state's territory** belongs to endorheic basins, where ephemeral streams fail to break through the encircling sand barriers or mountain shadows to reach the oceans.

```text
                              INLAND DRAINAGE SYSTEM OF RAJASTHAN
                                             │
      ┌──────────────────┬───────────────────┼───────────────────┬──────────────────┐
      ▼                  ▼                   ▼                   ▼                  ▼
    GHAGGAR            KANTLI              SABI               RUPAREL             SAMBHAR
  (Shivalik HP)   (Khandela, Sikar)   (Sewar, Kotputli)   (Udainath, Alwar)      STREAMS
      │                  │                   │                   │                  │
• 465 km total     • 100 km length     • Flows to Haryana  • Enters Bharatpur  • Mendha (North)
• Enters Tibbi     • Torawati Basin    • Terminates at     • Sikri Dam         • Rupangarh (South)
• Bed: Nali        • Ganeshwar Site      Najafgarh Drain   • Moti Jheel Dam    • Khari, Khandela
• Flood: Hakra     • Sunari Site       • Jodhpura PGW Site • Sujan Ganga Canal • Feed 8.7% salt
```
