### A. Ghaggar River (*घग्घर — सरस्वती / मृत नदी / नट नदी / सोतर / हकरा*)

#### 1. Identity & Paleo-Hydrology
- **Rigvedic Lineage**: Identified by geologists (Dr. K.S. Valdiya) and ISRO satellite imagery as the desiccated relict channel of the sacred **Saraswati River** and the **Drishadvati**.
- **Popular Epithets**: *Mrit Nadi* (Dead River), *Sotar*, *Nata Nadi*.
- **International Status**: The **only international river of Rajasthan**; during episodic extreme monsoonal surges, its floodwaters cross the international border into Pakistan.

#### 2. Hydrographic Route & Morphology
- **Origin**: Shivalik Hills, near Kalka / Dagshai, Solan district, Himachal Pradesh (elevation: 1,927 m).
- **Course in Northern Plains**: Traverses Punjab and Haryana; enters Rajasthan at **Talwara village**, Tibbi tehsil, Hanumangarh district.
- **Districts Traversed (3 Districts)**:
  $$\text{Hanumangarh} \longrightarrow \text{Sriganganagar} \longrightarrow \text{Anupgarh}$$
- **Terminal Sink**:
  - Under normal rainfall: Dries up in the sandy tracts near Bhatner Fort (Hanumangarh) or Suratgarh.
  - Under severe monsoonal floods: Reaches **Fort Abbas** (Bahawalpur, Punjab, Pakistan).
- **Vernacular Basin Terms**:
  - **Nali (*नाली*)**: The flat, fertile, silt-rich channel bed of Ghaggar inside Hanumangarh and Sriganganagar; famous for high-yield Basmati rice and wheat cultivation.
  - **Hakra (*हकरा*)**: The name by which the Ghaggar channel is known downstream of the international border in **Pakistan**.
- **Archaeological Stratigraphy**: The world-renowned Indus Valley Civilisation sites of **Kalibangan**, **Pilibangan**, and **Rangmahal** are situated directly on the ancient dried terrace of the Ghaggar River.
- **Talwara Lake (*तलवाड़ा झील*)**: Formed in a low natural depression along the Ghaggar course in Hanumangarh; recognized as the **lowest situated lake in Rajasthan**.

---

### B. Kantli River (*कांटली — तोरावाटी की जीवन रेखा*)
- **Origin**: **Khandela hills (*खंडेला की पहाड़ियां*)**, Sikar district.
- **Course**: Sikar $\longrightarrow$ Neem Ka Thana $\longrightarrow$ Jhunjhunu.
- **Terminal Sink**: Dries up in the undulating sand dunes near **Mandrella village**, on the border of Jhunjhunu and Churu districts.
- **Basin Name**: The catchment area of Kantli across Sikar, Neem Ka Thana, and Jhunjhunu was ruled by Tanwar Rajputs and is culturally designated as **Torawati (*तोरावाटी*)**.
- **Length & Status**: ~**100 km**; recognized as the **longest purely inland river originating and terminating entirely within Rajasthan**.
- **Archaeological Eminence**:
  - **Ganeshwar (*गणेश्वर सभ्यता*)**: Located at Neem Ka Thana on Kantli's bank; excavated by R.C. Agrawala; recognized as the **Mother of Copper Age Civilizations in India (*ताम्रयुगीन सभ्यताओं की जननी*)**.
  - **Sunari (*सुनारी सभ्यता*)**: Located in Jhunjhunu on Kantli's bank; ancient iron-smelting furnaces found here.

---

### C. Sabi River (*साबी*)
- **Origin**: **Sewar hills (*सेवर की पहाड़ियां*)**, Kotputli-Behror district (formerly Jaipur).
- **Course**: Kotputli-Behror $\longrightarrow$ Khairthal-Tijara $\longrightarrow$ crosses into Haryana (Gurugram district) $\longrightarrow$ terminates in the **Najafgarh drain (*नजफगढ़ झील / नाला*)** near Pataudi.
- **Archaeological Site**: **Jodhpura (*जोधपुरा सभ्यता*)** located on the bank of Sabi in Kotputli-Behror; excavated by R.C. Agrawala; famous for Iron Age smelting culture and Painted Grey Ware (PGW).

---

### D. Ruparel River (*रूपारेल — वराह नदी / लसवारी*)
- **Origin**: **Udainath hills (*उदयनाथ की पहाड़ियां*)**, Thanagazi tehsil, Alwar district.
- **Nomenclature**: Also referred to in local epigraphy as the **Varaha Nadi (*वराह नदी*)** and **Laswari (*लसवारी*)**.
- **Course**: Alwar $\longrightarrow$ enters Deeg and Bharatpur districts.
- **Hydraulic Management & Historic Disputes**:
  - Caused historic water-sharing conflicts between the princely states of Alwar and Bharatpur.
  - Maharaja Suraj Mal constructed the **Sikri Dam (*सीकरी बांध*)** to divert its waters into the **Moti Jheel Dam (*मोती झील*)** in Bharatpur.
  - **Moti Jheel** is acclaimed as the **"Lifeline of Bharatpur" (*भरतपुर की जीवन रेखा*)**. From Moti Jheel, the **Sujan Ganga Canal** carries water into the deep protective moat surrounding the impregnable mud-walled Lohagarh Fort.

---

### E. Mendha & Rupangarh Rivers (Sambhar Catchment)
- **Mendha River (*मेन्था / मेन्ढा*)**:
  - Origin: Manoharpur hills, Jaipur Rural.
  - Course: Flows westward through Jaipur Rural and Didwana-Kuchaman; enters **Sambhar Lake from the north**.
  - **Diagnostic Trap**: Brings the **highest concentration of soluble salts into Sambhar Lake** among all inflowing streams!
- **Rupangarh River (*रूपनगढ़*)**:
  - Origin: Salemabad hills, Kishangarh, Ajmer.
  - Course: Flows north; enters **Sambhar Lake from the south**.
  - Historical seat: The chief all-India pontifical seat of the **Nimbarka Sect (*निम्बार्क संप्रदाय की पीठ*)** is situated at Salemabad on the banks of Rupangarh.
- **Khari & Khandela**: Minor seasonal streams entering Sambhar Lake from the northwest and northeast.

---

### F. Kakney / Masurdi River (*काकनेय / काकनी / मसूरदी*)
- **Origin**: **Kotari village (*कोठारी गांव*)**, approximately 27 km south of Jaisalmer city.
- **Course**: Flows north for barely **17 km**; empties into and forms the ephemeral **Bhuj Lake (*बुझ झील*)**.
- **Length & Distinction**: At **17 km**, it is the **shortest named river in Rajasthan**. In seasons of rare intense rain, it overspills Bhuj Lake and terminates at Meetha Khadi.

---c2:T4900,Rajasthan's lakes represent a dual heritage: ancient tectonic/paleo-climatic brine depressions in the desert (*Saline Lakes*), and medieval monumental royal embankments (*Freshwater Lakes*) engineered for drought security, agricultural survival, and neoclassical leisure.

```text
                                  LAKES OF RAJASTHAN (झीलें)
                                              │
         ┌────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                                         ▼
   SALINE LAKES (खारे पानी की झीलें)                                         FRESHWATER LAKES (मीठे पानी की झीलें)
  [Remnants of Tethys Sea + Capillary Action]                              [Royal Embankments & Volcanic Calderas]
  • SAMBHAR (8.7% India's salt, Ramsar 1990)                               • JAISAMAND / DHEBAR (Salumbar, 7 Islands)
  • PACHPADRA (Balotra, 98% pure NaCl)                                     • RAJSAMAND (Raj Prashasti on 25 Slabs)
  • DIDWANA (Industrial salt, Sodium Sulphate)                             • PICHHOLA (Jag Mandir, Jag Niwas)
  • Lunkaransar, Phalodi, Pokhran, Rewasa                                  • FATEH SAGAR (Solar Observatory, USO)
                                                                           • NAKKI (Mt. Abu, Highest, Caldera)
                                                                           • ANA SAGAR (Baradari by Shah Jahan)
                                                                           • PUSHKAR (52 Ghats, Brahma Temple)
```

---

### A. Saline Lakes (*खारे पानी की झीलें*)

#### 1. Geomorphological Origin of Desert Salinity
- **Tethys Sea Remnant Hypothesis**: The shallow depression left behind by the receding Mesozoic-Cenozoic Tethys Sea accumulated thick evaporite beds.
- **Capillary Action (*केशिकाकर्षण*)**: High ambient summer temperatures ($>45^\circ\text{C}$) induce tremendous evaporation. Subterranean moisture holding dissolved sodium, magnesium, and calcium salts is drawn upwards through microscopic soil pores via capillary action, depositing salt crusts on the playa floor.
- **Wind-Borne Marine Halite**: Strong south-westerly summer monsoon winds transport microscopic airborne salt particles from the Rann of Kutch and Arabian Sea coastline into inland basins.

---

#### 2. Detailed Anatomy of Major Saline Lakes

| Saline Lake | District (50-District Lens) | Salt Extraction Method & Units | Chemical Composition & Salt Grade | Historic / Ecological Distinction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Sambhar Lake** (*सांभर झील*) | Tri-junction: **Jaipur Rural, Didwana-Kuchaman, Ajmer** | • *Kyār* (Large evaporation pans)<br>• *Reshta* (Wind-formed crystals)<br>• **Sambhar Salts Ltd.** (Subsidiary of Hindustan Salts Ltd.) | Edible salt; produces **8.7% of India's total salt** (largest inland saline resource) | • Largest natural inland saline lake in India (32 km long, 3–12 km wide).<br>• Declared **Ramsar Wetland Site in 1990**.<br>• Winter breeding ground for Flamingos (*राजहंस*).<br>• Bijolia Inscription attributes its 551 CE foundation to Vasudeva Chauhan. |
| **Pachpadra Lake** (*पचपदरा झील*) | **Balotra district** (formerly Barmer) | • Traditional **Kharwal caste** (*खारवाल जाति*)<br>• Uses branches of **Moroli bush** (*मोरली झाड़ी*) to crystallize salt | Contains **98% Sodium Chloride ($NaCl$)**; **Highest purity edible salt in India** | • Salt produces a clean, sharp taste preferred for culinary preservation.<br>• Now adjacent to the mega HPCL Rajasthan Refinery Complex. |
| **Didwana Lake** (*डीडवाना झील*) | **Didwana-Kuchaman district** (formerly Nagaur) | • Extracted via traditional brine pits called **Dêval (*देवल*)**<br>• **Rajasthan State Chemical Works** (est. 1964) | High in **Sodium Sulphate ($Na_2SO_4$)** and Sodium Sulphide; **Non-edible salt** | • Salt is strictly industrial; utilized for leather tanning, dye manufacturing, and glass processing. |

| **Tal Chhapar** (*ताल छापर*) | **Churu district** | Seasonal evaporite playa | Highly saline depression | Surrounded by the Tal Chhapar Blackbuck Sanctuary (*Mothiya* grass). |

---

### B. Freshwater Lakes (*मीठे पानी की झीलें*)

#### 1. Jaisamand Lake (*जयसमंद झील — ढेबर झील*)
- **Builder & Epoch**: Built between **1685 and 1691 CE** by **Maharana Jai Singh** of Mewar by damming the **Gomati River** (along with the Jhamri, Ruparel, and Bhagar rivulets).
- **Location**: **Salumbar district** (historically in Udaipur).
- **Status**: The **largest artificial (man-made) freshwater lake in Rajasthan** and the second largest in India (after Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar).
- **Dimensions**: Length: 15 km; Width: 1.5 to 8 km; Circumference: ~88 km.
- **The Seven Islands (*सात टापू*)**:
  - The lake houses **seven natural inhabited islands** populated by Bhil and Mina tribes.
  - **Largest Island**: **Baba ka Bhagra** (*बाबा का भागड़ा / बाबा का मगरा*).
  - **Smallest Island**: **Pyari (*प्यारी*)**.
  - A luxury resort island is named *Baba ka Island*.
- **Canal Infrastructure**: In 1950, two irrigation feeder canals were carved out from the southern embankment:
  1. **Shyampura Canal (*श्यामपुरा नहर*)**
  2. **Bhatbhat Canal (*भाटभट नहर*)**
- **Architectural Splendor**: The massive eastern embankment (*Pal*) is embellished with **six exquisite white marble Chhatris (cenotaphs)**, each fronted by a carved elephant statue with an upturned trunk, and an ancient Shiva temple (*Narmadeshwar Mahadev*).
- **Jaisamand Wildlife Sanctuary**: Surrounds the lake; celebrated for leopards, chital, and aquatic birds, historically known as the "Water Sanctuary" (*जलचरों की बस्ती*).

---

#### 2. Rajsamand Lake (*राजसमंद झील — कांकरोली*)
- **Builder & Epoch**: Built between **1662 and 1676 CE** by **Maharana Raj Singh I** by constructing an embankment across the **Gomati River** at Kankroli, Rajsamand.
- **Purpose**: Conceived as a grand **Famine Relief Project (*अकाल राहत कार्य*)** to provide livelihood and food security to thousands of starving subjects during devastating droughts.
- **The Nine-Step Embankment (*नौचौकी की पाल*)**:
  - The massive northern embankment is termed *Nauchowki ki Pal* due to its flights of marble steps descending to the water in descending tiers of nine.
- **Raj Prashasti (*राज प्रशस्ति*) — The Epigraphic Monument of the World**:
  - Embedded into the niches of the Nauchowki embankment are **25 monumental slabs of polished black marble**.
  - Engraved on them is the **Raj Prashasti**, authored by Telugu Dravidian Brahmin **Ranchhod Bhatt Telang**.
  - Consists of **24 cantos (*सर्ग*) and 1,106 Sanskrit verses**.
  - Recognized as the **largest stone inscription in the world**. It documents the complete history of Mewar from Bappa Rawal down to Maharana Raj Singh, including details of the 1615 Mughal-Mewar Treaty and the engineering expenditure of the dam.
- **Dwarikadhish Temple**: The sacred Vaishnava Vallabh-sect seat of **Dwarikadhish Ji** at Kankroli overlooks the lake. The shrine of **Ghevar Mata** (the virtuous lady who placed the foundation stone without being widowed) is situated on the embankment.

---

#### 3. Pichhola Lake (*पिछोला झील — उदयपुर*)
- **Builder & Epoch**: Constructed in the late **14th century (c. 1388 CE)** during the reign of **Maharana Lakha** by a wealthy nomadic grain merchant (Banjara) named **Pichhu Banjara / Chhitarmal Banjara** to allow his pack bullocks to cross the muddy Kotra and Sisarma streams.
- **Subsequent Expansion**: Strengthened and enlarged by Maharana Udai Singh II in 1559 CE after founding Udaipur city.
- **Inflowing Streams**: **Sisarma (*सीसारमा*)** and **Bujhada (*बुझड़ा*)** nullahs.
- **Palatial Islands & Monuments**:
  1. **Jag Mandir (*जग मंदिर*)**:
     - Commenced in 1620 by Maharana Karan Singh, completed in 1651 by Maharana Jagat Singh I.
     - Provided sovereign asylum to Mughal prince **Khurram (later Emperor Shah Jahan)** during his 1623–24 rebellion against Emperor Jahangir. The marble dome architecture and pietra dura work directly inspired the design of the **Taj Mahal**.
     - Provided refuge to British families fleeing Neemuch during the 1857 Mutiny under Maharana Swaroop Singh.
  2. **Jag Niwas (*जग निवास — Lake Palace*)**:
     - Built in 1746 CE by **Maharana Jagat Singh II** as a summer pleasure palace; now a luxury heritage hotel managed by the Taj Group.
  3. **Mohan Mandir & Arsi Vilas**: Small islands built by Maharana Jagat Singh and Maharana Ari Singh (Arsi Vilas houses an ammunition depot and bird nesting sanctuary).
  4. **Natni ka Chabutra (*नटनी का चबूतरा*)**: A memorial platform raised on the western bank opposite the City Palace to commemorate the tragic legendary rope-dancer *Galgi*.

---

#### 4. Fateh Sagar Lake (*फतेह सागर झील — उदयपुर*)
- **Builder & Epoch**:
  - Originally excavated in **1678 CE by Maharana Jai Singh**.
  - Destroyed by severe flood breaches, it was completely reconstructed in **1889 CE by Maharana Fateh Singh**.
  - The foundation stone of the reconstructed embankment was laid by the **Duke of Connaught** (son of Queen Victoria); hence the lake's primary bund is officially christened the **Connaught Dam (*कनॉट बांध*)**.
- **Hydraulic Interlinking (*Swaroop Sagar Canal*)**:
  - Linked to Lake Pichhola via the narrow **Swaroop Sagar Canal (*रंगसागर / स्वरूप सागर*)**. When Pichhola overflows, surplus waters automatically spill through sluice gates into Fateh Sagar.
  - Linked to the downstream **Badi Lake** and **Chhota Madar / Bada Madar** reservoirs.
- **Islands & Scientific Institutions**:
  1. **Nehru Park (*नेहरू गार्डन*)**: An island developed into an oval public botanical park with boat connectivity.
  2. **Udaipur Solar Observatory (USO)**:
     - Established on an isolated island in Fateh Sagar in 1975 by renowned astrophysicist **Dr. Arvind Bhatnagar**.
     - Modeled on the Big Bear Solar Observatory in California; surrounded by water which reduces thermal ground turbulence, providing the finest solar imaging clarity in Asia.
     - Houses the advanced **MAST (Multi-Application Solar Telescope)**.

---

#### 5. Nakki Lake (*नक्की झील — माउंट आबू, सिरोही*)
- **Elevation & Character**: Perched at an altitude of approximately **1,200 metres (3,937 ft)** above sea level at Mount Abu; recognized as the **highest and deepest lake in Rajasthan**.
- **The Dual Origin Debate**:
  - **Mythological Legend**: Believed to have been scooped out by Hindu gods using their fingernails (*Nakh / नाखून*) to escape the demon Bashkali.
  - **Geomorphological Fact**: Recognized by geologists as a volcanic **Caldera / Crater Lake (*ज्वालामुखी क्रेटर झील*)** or a tectonic fault depression formed during the Tertiary uplifting of the Abu granitic horst block.
- **The Freezing Superlative**: It is the **only lake in Rajasthan that freezes solid** during sub-zero December–January winter spells.
- **Tribal Sacredness**: Sacred pilgrimage water for the **Garasia tribe**, who immerse the mortal ashes of their ancestors in Nakki Lake during their ancestral festivals.
- **Diagnostic Sculpted Granitic Rocks**:
  - **Toad Rock**: Resembles a giant toad poised to leap into the water.
  - **Nun Rock**: Resembles a veiled praying Christian nun.
  - **Camel Rock**: Resembles a kneeling camel.
  - **Nandi Rock**: Resembles Lord Shiva's bull.

---

#### 6. Ana Sagar Lake (*आना सागर झील — अजमेर*)
- **Builder & Epoch**: Built between **1135 and 1137 CE** by Chauhan king **Arnoraja (Ana Ji)**, the grandfather of Prithviraja Chauhan III.
- **Historic Purpose**: Conceived to cleanse the valley of the blood shed during a bloody massacre repelling an invading Ghaznavid Turkish army; dammed the waters of the seasonal **Luni / Chandra stream** between Taragarh and Nag Pahar.
- **Mughal Architectural Additions**:
  1. **Daulat Bagh (*दौलत बाग — वर्तमान सुभाष उद्यान*)**: Laid out along the embankment by Mughal Emperor **Jahangir** in 1615–1618 (Sir Thomas Roe, the first British ambassador from King James I, held frequent diplomatic audiences with Jahangir here).
  2. **Baradari (*बारहदरी*)**: In **1637 CE, Emperor Shah Jahan** erected **five exquisite pavilions of polished white Makrana marble** along the paved bund (*Pal*).

---

#### 7. Pushkar Lake (*पुष्कर झील — तीर्थराज / आदि तीर्थ / पंचम तीर्थ*)
- **Sovereign Status**: Reared as the **"King of Pilgrimages" (*तीर्थराज*)**, *Aditirtha*, or *Konkan Tirtha*; the most sacred Hindu wetland in Western India.
- **Form**: A natural crescent-shaped (*अर्धचंद्राकार*) semi-caldera aquifer fed by subterranean springs from the Aravalli hills.
- **The 52 Sacred Ghats**:
  - Encircled by **52 historical bathing ghats** (Varaha Ghat, Brahma Ghat, Gau Ghat, Badri Ghat).
  - **Gandhi Ghat (formerly Queen Mary Zenana Ghat)**: Built in 1911 for Queen Mary's visit; in 1948, a portion of **Mahatma Gandhi's mortal ashes** was immersed here.
- **The Jagatpita Brahma Temple**: Houses the world's most preeminent temple dedicated to Lord Brahma (enshrined by Adi Shankaracharya; present marble structure erected by Gokul Chand Parekh in 1809 CE).
- **Pushkar Fair**: Celebrated annually from **Kartik Shukla Ekadashi to Kartik Purnima**; famous for colorful camel trading, folk dances, and spiritual **Deepdan (*दीपदान*)** ceremonies.
- **Ostracization of Cleanliness**: Cleaned under Canadian aid in 1997–98 under the *Pushkar Sarovar Cleanliness Project*.

---

#### 8. Exhaustive Roster of Other Freshwater Lakes

| Lake Name | District (50-District Lens) | Builder & Historical Peculiarities | Sovereign Functional Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| **Kolayat Lake** (*कोलायत झील*) | **Bikaner** | Ancient natural oasis; historic hermitage (*Ashram*) of **Maharshi Kapil Muni** (founder of Samkhya philosophy). | Features **52 ghats** shaded by peepal trees; grand fair on **Kartik Purnima** with Deepdan. **Crucial Taboo: People of the Charan caste never bathe in or visit Kolayat Lake**! |

| **Navlakha Lake** (*नवलखा झील*) | **Bundi** | Excavated by Rao Raja Ummed Singh in Bundi city. | Features a semi-submerged statue of Lord Varuna in the center. |
| **Gaib Sagar** (*गैब सागर*) | **Dungarpur** | Constructed by **Maharawal Gopinath** in the heart of Dungarpur. | Adorned by the exquisite **Badal Mahal** and the sacred **Shrinathji Temple** complex; houses the statue of brave tribal girl **Kalibai**. |
| **Bada Bagh & Amar Sagar** | **Jaisalmer** | Bada Bagh built by Maharawal Jait Singh II; Amar Sagar built by Amar Singh in 1688. | Desert oasis reservoirs watering royal gardens and cenotaph necropolises. |
| **Chhappan / Bhopal Sagar** | **Chittorgarh** | Constructed for local agricultural retention. | Supported Rajasthan's first private sugar mill (*Mewar Sugar Mills*, 1932). |
| **Umaid Sagar** | **Bhilwara / Shahpura** | Built by Maharaja Umaid Singh. | Primary drinking water asset of the Shahpura-Bhilwara tract. |

---c4:T1577,1. **Jojari Tributary Trap**: Jojari is the **ONLY right-bank tributary of the Luni** and the **ONLY one that does not originate from the Aravallis** (it originates in the flat plains of Pondlu, Nagaur). All other Luni tributaries originate on the western slopes of the Aravalli Range and join from the left bank.
2. **Balotra Salinity Boundary**: Luni's water is NOT saline from its source; it remains sweet, fresh, and potable for over 200 km until it crosses **Balotra**, where subterranean saline soil, capillary halite action, and industrial effluents render it intensely brackish.
3. **Longest River: Overall vs In Rajasthan**:
   - Longest river *flowing through* Rajasthan: **Chambal** (965 km total).
   - Longest river *flowing entirely and exclusively within Rajasthan*: **Banas** (480–512 km).
4. **Perennial Rivers of Rajasthan**: Rajasthan has only **TWO perennial ( बारहमासी ) rivers**: the **Chambal** and the **Mahi**. All other rivers (including Banas, Luni, and Banganga) are seasonal/ephemeral (*बरसाती*).
5. **Tropic of Cancer Intersection**: **Mahi** is the ONLY river globally to intersect the Tropic of Cancer ($23^\circ 30'\text{ N}$) **twice** — once entering Rajasthan from MP (flowing north), and once exiting Rajasthan into Gujarat (flowing south).
6. **Mahi Bajaj Sagar Power Sharing Trap**: In the Mahi project, cost is shared 45% (Rajasthan) : 55% (Gujarat). However, **100% of the hydroelectric power generated (140 MW) belongs exclusively to Rajasthan**!
7. **Tallest Dam vs Longest Dam in Rajasthan**:
   - Tallest Dam: **Jakham Dam** (81 metres, Pratapgarh).
   - Longest Dam: **Mahi Bajaj Sagar Dam** (3,109 metres, Banswara).
   - Largest Dam by Water Storage: **Rana Pratap Sagar Dam** (Rawatbhata, Chittorgarh).
8. **Kota Barrage: Zero Hydropower**: Out of the 4 dams on the Chambal River, **Kota Barrage produces ZERO MW of hydroelectric power**; it is exclusively an irrigation diversion structure. The other three (Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar, Jawahar Sagar) generate power.
9. **Chambal Dam Locations (The MP Trap)**: **Gandhi Sagar Dam is NOT in Rajasthan**! It is located in Mandsaur district of Madhya Pradesh. The remaining three dams are located in Rajasthan.
10. **Chulia Waterfall Height & Location**: The Chulia waterfall is **18 metres high** and is located at **Bhainsrorgarh (Chittorgarh)**, NOT in Kota or Bundi!
11. **Dang ki Rani vs Dang ka Raja**:
    - *Dang ki Rani*: **Karauli**.
    - *Dang ka Raja*: **Dholpur**.
12. **The Two Distinct Gambhir Rivers**:
    - **Gambhir River (*गम्भीर*)**: Originates in Karauli, feeds Panchana Dam, terminates in Yamuna.
    - **Gambhiri River (*गम्भीरी*)**: Originates in MP, joins the Bedach River near Chittorgarh city.
13. **Panchana Dam Composition**: Panchana Dam is the **largest earthen / clay dam (*मिट्टी का बांध*) in Rajasthan**, formed by 5 rivulets: Ata, Machi, Bhadrawati, Barkheda, and Bhainsawat.
14. **Ayad to Bedach Name Transition**: The river is called **Ayad** from its origin at Gogunda until it pours into **Udaisagar Lake**. Downstream of Udaisagar, its official geographic name becomes the **Bedach**.
15. **Rundhit Sarita Classification**: **Banganga** is scientifically termed a *Rundhit Sarita* (severed river) because it no longer reaches its parent river (Yamuna), instead drying up in the alluvial wetlands of Bharatpur.
16. **Longest Inland River: Purely Rajasthan vs Total**:
    - Longest inland river originating and terminating within Rajasthan: **Kantli River** (~100 km).
    - Longest inland river overall passing through Rajasthan: **Ghaggar River** (~465 km).
17. **Talwara Lake vs Nakki Lake (Elevation Extremes)**:
    - Lowest elevation lake in Rajasthan: **Talwara Lake** (Hanumangarh, bed of Ghaggar).
    - Highest elevation lake in Rajasthan: **Nakki Lake** (Mount Abu, 1,200 m).
18. **Ghaggar Terminology: Nali vs Hakra**:
    - The bed inside Rajasthan is termed **Nali**.
    - The bed across the border in Pakistan is termed **Hakra**.
19. **Sambhar Lake Salt Percentage**: Sambhar produces **8.7% of India's total salt production** (NOT 80%! A classic multiple-choice numerical trap where candidates confuse 8.7% of national production with high local figures).
20. **Pachpadra vs Didwana Salt Grades**:
    - **Pachpadra**: 98% pure sodium chloride ($NaCl$), supreme edible culinary quality.
    - **Didwana**: High sodium sulphate ($Na_2SO_4$), **non-edible**, strictly industrial.
21. **Kolayat Lake Taboo**: Members of the **Charan community** abstain from visiting or bathing in Kolayat Lake because legend records that Karni Mata's adopted son, Lakhan, drowned in it on Kartik Purnima.
22. **Lake Pichhola Originator**: Lake Pichhola was NOT built by Maharana Udai Singh or Maharana Lakha; it was built by a nomadic grain merchant, **Chhitarmal / Pichhu Banjara**, in the late 14th century. Udai Singh only expanded its bund later.
23. **Connaught Dam Real Name**: The Duke of Connaught laid the foundation stone of **Fateh Sagar Lake's** rebuilt dam, hence its main bund is called the *Connaught Dam*.
24. **World's Largest Stone Inscription Location**: The **Raj Prashasti** is engraved on 25 black marble slabs at **Rajsamand Lake** (on the *Nauchowki ki Pal*), NOT at Jaisamand Lake!
25. **Jaisamand's Modern District**: Following the 2023 administrative reorganizations, **Jaisamand Lake is now located in Salumbar district**, NOT in Udaipur!

---c5:T17d6,### 2-Marker Benchmark Responses (15 Words)

#### Q1. What is a *Rundhit Sarita*? Give an example from Rajasthan.
**Model Answer**:  
A river that fails to reach its master stream due to decreased discharge, terminating in its own alluvial silt before confluence. Example: **Banganga River** in eastern Rajasthan.

#### Q2. Name the five rivulets that converge at Panchana Dam.
**Model Answer**:  
**Ata, Machi, Bhadrawati, Barkheda, and Bhainsawat**. Located in Karauli, it is Rajasthan's largest earthen dam.

#### Q3. Why does the Luni River turn saline downstream of Balotra?
**Model Answer**:  
Due to high evaporation, subterranean halite deposits from the ancient Tethys Sea, and capillary leaching of sodium chloride from weathered granitic soils.

#### Q4. What is the geological significance of the Raj Prashasti?
**Model Answer**:  
Engraved on 25 black marble slabs at Rajsamand Lake by Ranchhod Bhatt; with 1,106 Sanskrit verses, it is the **world's largest stone inscription**.

---

### 5-Marker Benchmark Responses (50 Words)

#### Q5. Delineate the geomorphological alignment of the Great Indian Continental Divide across Rajasthan.
**Model Answer**:  
The Aravalli Range acts as the Great Continental Divide, separating the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal drainages:
1. **Trace**: Runs from Delhi Ridge through Khetri, Alwar, Sambhar Lake, Ajmer (Nag Pahar), Beawar, and the Bhorat Plateau (1,225 m).
2. **Hydrological Bifurcation**: 
   - Western slopes feed the **Arabian Sea** (~17.4% area via Luni, Mahi, Sabarmati, West Banas).
   - Eastern slopes feed the **Bay of Bengal** (~22.4% area via Chambal, Banas, Gambhir).
   - Rain falling on the western edge of Bhorat flows into the Arabian Sea; rain falling on the eastern edge flows to the Bay of Bengal.

#### Q6. Analyze the hydro-electric and irrigation architecture of the Chambal Valley Project.
**Model Answer**:  
The Chambal Project is a 50:50 joint venture between Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh executed in three stages:
1. **Four Cascading Dams**:
   - **Gandhi Sagar** (MP, 1960): 115 MW; largest storage reservoir.
   - **Rana Pratap Sagar** (Chittorgarh, 1970): 172 MW; largest storage dam in Rajasthan; feeds RAPS nuclear plant.
   - **Jawahar Sagar** (Kota/Bundi, 1972): 99 MW; peak-load hydel station.
   - **Kota Barrage** (Kota, 1960): 0 MW; pure irrigation diversion feeding Right and Left Main Canals.
2. **Power & Water Equity**: Total hydel output of 386 MW is shared equally (Rajasthan gets 193 MW); irrigates over 5 lakh hectares in Hadoti.

### 10-Marker Analytical Essay (100 Words / 200 Words)

#### Q7. Provide a comprehensive comparative evaluation of the Inland Drainage System of Rajasthan. Analyze its geomorphological origins, spatial distribution, ecological challenges, and archaeological significance.

**Model Answer Architecture**:

```text
                                INLAND DRAINAGE EVALUATION MATRIX
                                                │
         ┌──────────────────┬───────────────────┼───────────────────┬──────────────────┐
         ▼                  ▼                   ▼                   ▼                  ▼
1. GEOMORPHIC ORIGINS   2. SPATIAL PROFILE      3. ARCHAEOLOGY      4. LIMNOLOGY       5. ECOLOGICAL ISSUES
   • Tethys Sea retreat    • 60.2% state area      • Kalibangan        • Sambhar Lake      • Flash floods
   • Saraswati desiccation • Ghaggar, Kantli,      • Ganeshwar           (8.7% salt)       • Siltation
   • Sand dune barriers      Sabi, Ruparel         • Jodhpura          • Didwana           • Waterlogging
```

1. **Geomorphological Origins & Extent**:
   - Comprises **~60.2% of Rajasthan's total geographical area**, making it the largest endorheic system in India.
   - Caused by the hyper-arid climate, low hydraulic gradients, extreme evaporation, and towering longitudinal/barkhan sand dunes that block river flow, preventing surface runoff from reaching the sea.
   - Represents the desiccated remnants of the Vedic Saraswati and Drishadvati river systems.

2. **Spatial Distribution & Major Rivers**:
   - **Ghaggar River**: Only international river; traverses Hanumangarh, Sriganganagar, and Anupgarh in its fertile *Nali* bed; floodwaters historically reach Fort Abbas (*Hakra*) in Pakistan.
   - **Kantli River**: 100 km long river of Torawati (Sikar, Neem Ka Thana, Jhunjhunu); longest purely inland river originating and terminating within Rajasthan.
   - **Sabi River**: Originates at Sewar (Kotputli); drains into Haryana's Najafgarh wetland.
   - **Ruparel River**: Originates at Udainath (Alwar); feeds Moti Jheel ("Lifeline of Bharatpur").
   - **Sambhar Catchment**: Inflowing streams Mendha, Rupangarh, Khari, and Khandela feed India's largest inland saline lake.

3. **Archaeological Stratigraphy**:
   - These dry channels hosted India's greatest prehistoric cultures:
     - **Kalibangan & Rangmahal** on the Ghaggar (Indus Valley Civilization).
     - **Ganeshwar** on the Kantli (Copper Age mother culture).
     - **Jodhpura** on the Sabi (Painted Grey Ware and Iron Age furnaces).

4. **Contemporary Ecological Challenges & Management**:
   - **Siltation & Course Choking**: Severe deforestation in Aravalli headwaters has accelerated sediment yield, choking river channels and causing localized flash floods during erratic monsoon bursts.
   - **Pollution of Terminal Playas**: Heavy industrial and municipal discharge into ephemeral streams (such as textile dyes in Bandi and chemical salts in Mendha) degrades critical Ramsar habitats like Sambhar Lake (evidenced by the 2019 Avian Botulism disaster).
   - **Sustainable Interventions**: Requires extensive catchment afforestation, desilting of traditional check-dams (*Johads*), and integrated watershed management under the State Water Policy.

### A. Breakdown of Irrigation Sources in Rajasthan
According to the latest land-use statistics of the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES, Rajasthan):
- **Net Sown Area (*शुद्ध बोया गया क्षेत्रफल*)**: ~180 lakh hectares.
- **Gross Cropped Area (*सकल कृषित क्षेत्रफल*)**: ~260–270 lakh hectares.
- **Gross Irrigated Area (*सकल सिंचित क्षेत्रफल*)**: ~105–112 lakh hectares (~42–44% of gross cropped area).

```text
                         SOURCES OF IRRIGATION IN RAJASTHAN
                                         │
         ┌───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                               ▼                               ▼
    TUBE-WELLS & WELLS                CANALS                           TANKS
    (नलकूप एवं कुएं)                  (नहरें)                         (तालाब)
        ~71.5% - 73%                  ~25% - 26%                       ~1% - 1.5%
         │                               │                               │
• Tube-wells: ~47.5% (Largest source) • Sriganganagar, Hanumangarh,   • Historically dominant
• Open Wells: ~24.0%                  Kota, Bundi, Bikaner, Jaisalmer • in Bhilwara, Chittorgarh,
• Dominant in Eastern Rajasthan       • Fed by IGNP, Gang Canal,        Udaipur; now severely
  (Jaipur, Alwar, Dausa, Bharatpur)     Chambal Canals, Narmada         depleted.
```

1. **Tube-wells (*नलकूप*) — 47.5% to 48% (The Largest Source)**:
   - Primary concentration: **Jaipur, Alwar, Dausa, Bharatpur, Sikar, Jhunjhunu**.
   - Causes severe groundwater exploitation; over 70% of groundwater assessment blocks in Rajasthan are classified as **"Over-Exploited" (*Dark Zones*)**.
2. **Open Wells (*कुएं*) — ~23.5% to 24%**:
   - Concentrated in the Aravalli piedmont and Central Plains (Jaipur, Ajmer, Udaipur).
   - Combined Wells and Tube-wells account for nearly **three-fourths (~72%)** of total net irrigation in the state.
3. **Canals (*नहरें*) — ~25% to 26%**:
   - Geographically concentrated in the **North-Western Plain** (Sriganganagar, Hanumangarh, Bikaner, Jaisalmer via IGNP & Gang Canal) and the **South-Eastern Hadoti** (Kota, Bundi, Baran via Chambal Canal system).
   - District with highest canal-irrigated area: **Sriganganagar** (followed by Hanumangarh).
4. **Tanks (*तालाब*) — ~1.0% to 1.5%**:
   - Traditional stronghold: **Bhilwara** (highest tank-irrigated area historically), Chittorgarh, Rajsamand, and Udaipur.
   - Significant decline in recent decades due to siltation of feeder channels (*Agor*) and encroachment of catchment areas.

### B. Statutory Milestone: Rajasthan State Water Policy (2010)
- Rajasthan became the **first state in India to formulate a comprehensive State Water Policy** aligned with integrated water resources management (IWRM) based on **river basin planning**.
- **Statutory Priorities for Water Allocation**:
  1. **Drinking Water (*पेयजल*)** — Supreme unalterable priority.
  2. **Domestic & Livestock Use (*घरेलू एवं पशुधन उपयोग*)**.
  3. **Agriculture & Irrigation (*कृषि एवं सिंचाई*)**.
  4. **Power Generation (*विद्युत उत्पादन*)**.
  5. **Industrial & Commercial Use (*औद्योगिक एवं वाणिज्यिक उपयोग*)**.
  6. **Ecology, Tourism & Other Non-consumptive Uses**.

---c7:T34bb,The Indira Gandhi Nahar Pariyojana (IGNP) is the **largest irrigation canal project in the world**, conceived to transform the barren, wind-swept sands of the Great Indian Thar Desert into a lush agricultural breadbasket.

### A. Historical Genesis & Timeline
- **The Visionary Engineer**: **Rai Bahadur Kanwar Sain** (*राय बहादुर कंवर सेन*), Chief Engineer of Bikaner State.
- **The 1948 Benchmark Report**: In October 1948, Kanwar Sain published the seminal treatise: *"Bikaner Rajya Mein Paani ki Aavashyakta"* (Water Requirement in Bikaner State), proposing that surplus Himalayan river runoff from the Indus Basin (Satluj and Beas) could be gravitated through canals into the Thar desert.
- **Interstate Accord**: 1955 inter-state agreement allocating **8.60 Million Acre Feet (MAF)** of surplus Satluj-Beas-Ravi waters to Rajasthan.
- **Foundation Stone**: Laid on **31 March 1958** by then Union Home Minister **Govind Ballabh Pant**.
- **First Water Inflow**: On **11 October 1961**, Vice President of India **Dr. S. Radhakrishnan** released water into the Naurangdesar distributary at Masitawali Head.
- **Renaming**: Originally christened the **Rajasthan Canal (*राजस्थान नहर*)**; officially renamed the **Indira Gandhi Nahar Pariyojana (IGNP)** on **2 November 1984** following the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.

---

### B. Project Layout, Dimensions & Stages

#### 1. Rajasthan Feeder Canal (*राजस्थान फीडर*)
- **Origin**: **Harike Barrage** (Firozpur district, Punjab), built at the confluence of the **Satluj and Beas** rivers.
- **Total Feeder Length**: **204 km**.
  - Length in Punjab & Haryana: **170 km**.
  - Length in Rajasthan: **34 km**.
- **Entry Point into Rajasthan**: **Kharakhera village (*खराखेड़ा*)**, Tibbi tehsil, Hanumangarh district.
- **Defining Rule**: **No direct irrigation is permitted from the Feeder canal**; it serves strictly as an impermeable, lined transit aqueduct carrying water to the desert threshold.
- **Termination**: Terminates at **Masitawali Head (*मसीतावाली हेड*)**, Hanumangarh.

#### 2. IGNP Main Canal (*मुख्य नहर*)
- **Starting Point**: Masitawali Head, Hanumangarh.
- **Total Length of Main Canal**: **445 km**.
- **Total Conduit Length (Feeder + Main Canal)**: $204\text{ km} + 445\text{ km} = \mathbf{649\text{ km}}$.
- **Staged Execution**:
  - **Stage I**: Masitawali Head (Hanumangarh) to Chattargarh / Pugal / Sattasar (Bikaner) — **189 km**. Culturable Command Area (CCA): ~5.53 lakh hectares.
  - **Stage II**: From Sattasar (Bikaner) to **Mohangarh** (Jaisalmer) — **256 km**. Culturable Command Area (CCA): ~10.64 lakh hectares.
- **The Tail Points (Crucial Ambiguity Resolution)**:
  - **Terminal point of Main Canal**: **Mohangarh (*मोहनगढ़*)**, Jaisalmer.
  - **Terminal point of Irrigation Command**: Extended via the **Sagarmal Gopa Branch** and **Baba Ramdev Sub-Branch** up to **Ghadra Road (*गडरा रोड*)**, Barmer district (now named the Baba Ramdev Sub-Branch).

---

### C. The Flow Architecture: Branches vs Lift Canals

The geomorphological slope of western Rajasthan drops towards the southwest. Therefore:
1. **West of the Canal (Right Bank)**: Land elevation is lower than the canal bed $\rightarrow$ water flows by **natural gravity** $\rightarrow$ called **Branches (*शाखाएं*)**.
2. **East of the Canal (Left Bank)**: Land elevation is higher than the canal bed (Aravalli piedmont uplands) $\rightarrow$ water cannot flow by gravity; it must be **mechanically lifted by 30 to 60 metres using electric turbine pumps** $\rightarrow$ called **Lift Canals (*लिफ्ट नहरें*)**.

```text
                               IGNP DISTRIBUTION SCHEME
                                          │
         ┌────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                                 ▼
   RIGHT-BANK BRANCHES (GRAVITY FLOW)                             LEFT-BANK LIFT CANALS (MECHANICAL PUMP)
   • 8 on Right Bank + 1 Exception on Left Bank                   • ALL 7 Lift Canals are on the Left Bank
   • Rawatsar Branch (ONLY Left-Bank Branch!)                     • Uplift: 30 to 60 metres
   • Suratgarh, Anupgarh, Pugal, Dantoar,                         • Designed for drinking & light irrigation
     Birsalpur, Charanwali, Birbal, Sagarmal Gopa                  in high-elevation dune tracts
```

---

#### 1. The 9 Master Branches of IGNP (*शाखाएं*)

| Branch Name | Bank Position | Districts Benefited (50-District Lens) | Diagnostic Characteristic / Landmark |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Rawatsar Branch** (*रावतसर शाखा*) | **Left Bank (अपवाद)** | **Hanumangarh** | **The ONLY branch on the Left Bank of IGNP**! Because the ground east of Masitawali is naturally depressed, gravity flow is possible without pumping. |
| **2. Suratgarh Branch** (*सूरतगढ़ शाखा*) | Right Bank | Sriganganagar / Anupgarh | Feeds central northern agricultural belt; adjacent to Suratgarh Super Thermal Plant. |
| **3. Anupgarh Branch** (*अनूपगढ़ शाखा*) | Right Bank | Anupgarh / Sriganganagar | Irrigates newly formed Anupgarh border district. |
| **4. Pugal Branch** (*पूगल शाखा*) | Right Bank | Bikaner | Traverses arid northern Bikaner. |
| **5. Dantoar Branch** (*दांतौर शाखा*) | Right Bank | Bikaner | Expands command into central Bikaner dunes. |
| **6. Birsalpur Branch** (*बरसलपुर शाखा*) | Right Bank | Bikaner | High-yield mustard and groundnut tract. |
| **7. Charanwali Branch** (*चारणवाली शाखा*) | Right Bank | Bikaner and Jaisalmer | Bisects the inter-district desert boundary. |
| **8. Shaheed Birbal Branch** (*शहीद बीरबल शाखा*) | Right Bank | Jaisalmer | Named after 1946 Bikaner Prajamandal martyr Birbal Singh Dhaliwal. |
| **9. Sagarmal Gopa Branch** (*सागरमल गोपा शाखा*) | Right Bank | Jaisalmer | Named after Jaisalmer freedom fighter burned alive in 1946; terminates at Mohangarh, extending to Ghadra Road. |

### D. Ecological, Environmental & Social Impact of IGNP

#### 1. Transformative Positive Impacts
- **Green Revolution in the Thar**: Cultivated area in Thar increased by over 16 lakh hectares. Transformed Bikaner, Sriganganagar, and Hanumangarh into India's leading producers of **Kinnow citrus, Long-staple American Cotton (*Narma*), Wheat, Mustard, and Groundnut**.
- **Sand Dune Stabilization**: Massive afforestation strips along canal banks (*Canal Bank Plantations*) using *Acacia tortilis* (Israeli Babool), *Shisham*, and *Neem* arrested the eastward creep of sand dunes.
- **Famine Eradication**: Decimated the historical recurring curse of *Trikal* (simultaneous famine of grain, water, and fodder).

#### 2. Environmental Pathologies: The "Sem Problem" (*सेम की समस्या*)
- **Genesis of Waterlogging (*Sem*)**:
  1. **Subterranean Hardpan**: Underlying vast tracts of Hanumangarh and Bikaner (especially **Badopal, Rawatsar, and Suratgarh**) is an impermeable geological hardpan of **Gypsum (*जिप्सम की परत*)** and calcrete at a depth of 5 to 15 metres.
  2. **Percolation Barrier**: Excess seepage from the canal and unscientific flood irrigation cannot infiltrate into deeper strata; it strikes the gypsum bed and rises toward the surface.
  3. **Capillary Salt Crusting**: The water table rises within 1–2 metres of the surface. Intense desert heat evaporates the surface moisture, leaving a blinding white crust of efflorescent alkali salts (**Reh / Kallar**), rendering agricultural soils completely sterile and marshy.
- **Remedial Interventions**:
  - **Bio-drainage (*बायो-ड्रेनेज*)**: Large-scale plantation of **Eucalyptus (*सफेदा*)** trees along the canal banks; eucalyptus acts as biological pump, transpiring huge volumes of subsoil water.
  - **Indo-Dutch Waterlogging Project**: Subsurface drainage tile system installed in Badopal and Rawatsar.
  - Installation of solar pumps to dewater saline ponds into evaporation pans.

---c8:Tf30,The Eastern Rajasthan Canal Project (ERCP) is the most ambitious inter-basin water transfer project planned in the post-independence history of Rajasthan, designed to address the severe drinking and irrigation water crisis across **21 south-eastern and eastern districts**.

```text
                                 ERCP BASIN HARVESTING BLUEPRINT
                                                │
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                                             ▼
  SURPLUS SOUTHERN BASINS                                                      DEFICIT EASTERN BASINS
  [Harvesting Monsoonal Spills]                                                [Target Recharge Zones]
  • Chambal & Tributaries                                                      • Banas Basin
  • Kunnu, Kul, Parbati                                                        • Morel Basin
  • Kalisindh (Navnera Barrage)                                                • Banganga Basin
  • Mej River                                                                  • Gambhir Basin
                                                                               • Parbati & Ruparail Basins
```

---

### A. Core Conceptual Architecture
- **Hydrological Imbalance**: South-Eastern Rajasthan (Hadoti) receives copious monsoon precipitation ($>800\text{ mm}$), and sub-basins of the Chambal generate massive surplus runoff that drains unused into the Yamuna. Conversely, the Eastern Plains (Banas, Banganga, Gambhir) suffer from depleted rivers, dried check-dams, and depleted aquifers.
- **The Solution**: Constructing a series of barrages, feeder conduits, pumping stations, and interconnecting tunnels to harvest surplus monsoonal flows (at **75% dependable yield**) and redirect them across the Aravalli foothills to recharge **21 eastern districts**.

### C. Major Infrastructure Nodes of ERCP
1. **Navnera Barrage (*नवनेरा बैराज*)**: Constructed across the **Kali Sindh River** at Navnera village, Digod tehsil, Kota district. Acts as the primary collection and pumping hub of the project.
2. **Mej Barrage**: Proposed across the Mej River in Bundi.
3. **Galwa Dam & Isarda Dam**: Isarda Dam (Sawai Madhopur) integrated as a primary drinking storage node.
4. **Ramgarh Barrage & Mahalpur Barrage**: On the Kul and Parbati rivers.

### D. The Historic Tripartite Accord: Modified PKC-ERCP National Project (2024)
- **Date of Signing**: **28 January 2024** at New Delhi.
- **Signatories**:
  1. Ministry of Jal Shakti, Government of India
  2. Government of Rajasthan
  3. Government of Madhya Pradesh
- **Key Breakthrough**: Integrated the **Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal (PKC) Link** of the National Water Development Agency (NWDA) with the **ERCP**, christening it the **Modified PKC-ERCP Link Project**.
- **National Project Status**: Approved as a **National Project (*राष्ट्रीय परियोजना*)**, securing **90% Central Government grant funding**, with the remaining 10% shared by the two states.
- **Deliverables**: Guarantees secure drinking water for over **40% of Rajasthan's population** up to the year 2051, provides assured irrigation to **2.8 lakh hectares of new land**, and revives 1,487 traditional local tanks and check-dams.

### A. Key Dimensions & Trajectory
- **Origin**: **Sardar Sarovar Dam** (Kevadia, Narmada district, Gujarat) on the Narmada River.
- **Entry Point into Rajasthan**: **Silu village (*सीलू गांव*)**, Sanchore district (formerly in Jalore), on **27 March 2008**.
- **Canal Length**:
  - Total length from Sardar Sarovar: **532 km**.
  - Length of Main Canal inside Rajasthan: **74 km**.
  - Distributaries & minor network in Rajasthan: **~332 km**.
- **Water Allocation**: Rajasthan was allocated **0.50 MAF (Million Acre Feet)** of Narmada water under the Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal (NWDT) award.
- **Beneficiary Districts**: **Sanchore, Jalore, and Barmer**.

---

### B. The Supreme National Distinction: Mandatory Micro-Irrigation
- **The Invariant Law**: Narmada Canal Project is the **FIRST and ONLY irrigation project in the Republic of India where Pressurized Micro-Irrigation (Drip and Sprinkler / बूंद-बूंद एवं फव्वारा सिंचाई प्रणाली) has been made 100% STATUTORILY MANDATORY**.
- **Operational Reality**: Traditional flood irrigation (*खुली सिंचाई / प्लावित सिंचाई*) is strictly prohibited by law.
  - Every agricultural holding in the command area is fitted with piped pressure manifolds and solar/electric pump sets.
  - **Water Use Efficiency**: Achieves a staggering water-use efficiency of over **70–80%** (compared to barely 30–35% in conventional flood irrigation).
  - Expanded the culturable command area by nearly **three times** using the exact same volume of water, transforming Sanchore into a booming horticultural zone for **Pomegranate (*अनार*), Isabgol (*ईसबगोल*), and Cumin (*जीरा*)**.

---

### C. Lift Canals on Narmada
To supply water to elevated dune ridges, three lift canals were constructed:
1. **Sanchore Lift Canal** (Sanchore district)
2. **Bhadresh Lift Canal** (Jalore/Barmer)
3. **Panariya Lift Canal** (Jalore)

---ca:Ta97,The Gang Canal is the **pioneer modern irrigation canal of Rajasthan and Northern India**, transforming the northern wastes of the princely Bikaner State into an agricultural oasis decades before independence.

```text
                                GANG CANAL (1927)
                                       │
      • The "Bhagirath of Modern India": Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner
      • Headworks: Hussainiwala Headworks (Firozpur, Punjab) on Satluj River
      • Inauguration: 26 October 1927 by Viceroy Lord Irwin
      • Construction: Lined with lime-mortar concrete (Chuna-Kankar)
      • Total Length: 129 km (112 km in Punjab + 17 km in Rajasthan)
      • Beneficiary: Sriganganagar (The "Food Basket of Rajasthan")
```

---

### A. Architectural Genesis & Construction
- **The Architect**: **Maharaja Ganga Singh** of Bikaner, celebrated in Indian history as the **"Bhagirath of the Modern Era" (*आधुनिक भारत का भगीरथ*)**.
- **The Catalyst**: The catastrophic **Chhappaniya Akal (*छप्पनिया अकाल*)** of 1899–1900 CE, which wiped out hundreds of thousands of people and cattle, impelled Maharaja Ganga Singh to secure perennial water from the Punjab rivers.
- **The Tripartite Accord (1920)**: Satluj Valley Agreement signed on 4 September 1920 between Bikaner State, the British Government (Punjab), and Bahawalpur State.
- **Foundation & Inauguration**:
  - Construction commenced: **5 December 1925**.
  - Grand Inauguration: **26 October 1927** by Viceroy of India **Lord Irwin** at Shivpur Head.
- **Headworks & Origin**: **Hussainiwala Headworks** (Firozpur, Punjab) on the **Satluj River**.
- **Dimensions**:
  - Total length of main canal: **129 km**.
  - Length in Punjab: **112 km**.
  - Length in Rajasthan: **17 km** (enters at **Khaarkhan village**, near Sadulshahar, Sriganganagar).
  - Total distribution network: Over **1,280 km**.
- **Civil Engineering Marvel**: At a time when modern Portland cement was rare and prohibitively expensive, the entire canal was **lined with hydraulic lime concrete and kankar masonry (*चूना-कंकड़ गारा*)**, preventing percolation losses across porous sandy tracts.

---

### B. The Gang Canal Link Channel (1984)
- Over six decades of continuous abrasive scour degraded the original lime lining, reducing carrying capacity from 2,144 cusecs to under 1,400 cusecs.
- In **1984**, the Rajasthan Government constructed the **Gang Canal Link Channel** (**80 km** length), connecting the Indira Gandhi Feeder near Lohgarh (Haryana) directly to Sadulshahar (Sriganganagar), enabling IGNP water to feed the Gang Canal network during maintenance shutdowns.

---cc:T1c75,In the hyper-arid Thar Desert, water was not merely an economic input; it was an article of religious faith and civilizational survival. Ancient Rajasthani society evolved a brilliant taxonomy of decentralized, micro-level rainwater harvesting structures that captured every drop of precipitation before it could be lost to evaporation.

```text
                           TRADITIONAL WATER HARVESTING SYSTEMS
                                            │
         ┌──────────────────┬───────────────┼───────────────┬──────────────────┐
         ▼                  ▼               ▼               ▼                  ▼
      KHADIN              TANKA           BAORI          JHALRA             KUI / BERI
  (Paliwal Brahmins) (Subterranean)    (Stepwells)   (Seepage Tank)     (Khadia Patti)
  • 15th c. Jaisalmer • Agor / Paytan   • Ornate stone • Subterranean    • Deep, narrow (1-1.5m)
  • Silt retention    • Courtyard       • Chand Baori    seepage from    • Chezwano artisan
  • Winter Rabi crop    cistern         • Raniji Baori   adjacent lake   • Rajasthan ki Rajat
    without irrigation• Bacteria-free                  • Toorji Jhalra     Boondein (Mishra)
```

---

### A. Khadin (*खड़ीन / धोरा*)
- **Historical Genesis**: Developed in the **15th century by the intellectual Paliwal Brahmins of Jaisalmer**.
- **Geomorphological Landscape**: Engineered in natural desert valleys flanked on two or three sides by gentle rocky or gravelly mounds (*Hamada / Magra*).
- **Civil Engineering Mechanics**:
  - An earthen embankment (*Bund / Mitti ka Dhora*), typically 2 to 4 metres high, is thrown across the lower drainage mouth of the slope.
  - Rainwater running off the rocky slopes fills the shallow depression to a depth of 0.5 to 1.5 metres.
  - **Khadia (*खड़िया*)**: An earthen or masonry sluice gate built in the bund to safely spill excess flood runoff into an adjacent lower Khadin (*Dohra*).
  - **Chadar (*चादर*)**: A stone spillway designed to discharge excess water without breaching the earthen embankment.
- **The Miracle of Rabi Cultivation**:
  - The collected water stands in the Khadin bed for 2 to 3 months during the monsoon, saturated with mineral-rich wash from the surrounding hills.
  - In October–November, when the standing water recedes or is discharged through the Khadia, the deep silt bed retains tremendous capillary moisture.
  - Farmers sow **Rabi winter crops (Wheat, Chickpea / Gram, Mustard)** directly into this rich mud. **The crop matures to full harvest WITHOUT A SINGLE DROP OF SUBSEQUENT IRRIGATION**!

---

### B. Tanka (*टांका / कुंडी*)
- **Form & Anatomy**: A subterranean, masonry, cylindrical or rectangular domestic cistern constructed in individual residential courtyards (*Ghar ka Tanka*) or community grazing pastures (*Gaon ka Tanka*).
- **Agor / Paytan (*आगोर / पायतन*)**: The surrounding circular catchment apron, gently sloped towards the tanka inlet. It is meticulously plastered with fine clay, slaked lime, cattle dung, and ash to maximize surface runoff velocity and prevent dust infiltration.
- **Hygiene & Preservation**: Rainwater enters through fine wire-mesh strainers into the dark, sealed tank. Because sunlight cannot penetrate the sealed cistern, algal blooms and bacterial cultures cannot propagate; the water remains sweet, potable, and cool for **12 to 18 months**, serving as the domestic drinking lifeline.

---

### C. Nadi (*नाडी*)
- **Origin**: Natural rural village pond or earthen depression; historical records credit **Rao Jodha (1458 CE)** with constructing Rajasthan's first recorded historical Nadi in Jodhpur.
- **Maintenance**: Desilted annually in May–June by collective community volunteer labor (*Ghaad nikalna / श्रमदान*). Serves as the community livestock watering reservoir.

---

### D. Baori (*बावड़ी / वापी*)
- **Architectural Anatomy**: A monumental, subterranean stepwell combining water harvesting with exquisite temple-like stone architecture, pillared pavilions (*Chhatris*), arched galleries, and monumental flights of stone stairs descending to the unconfined water table.
- **Major Baoris**: **Chand Baori** (Abhaneri, 3,500 steps), **Raniji ki Baori** (Bundi, "City of Stepwells"), **Neemrana Baori** (9 storeys deep).

---

### E. Jhalra (*झालरा*)
- **The Essential Hydrological Trap**: A Jhalra does **NOT harvest surface rain runoff directly**!
- **True Hydraulic Mechanism**: A Jhalra is an ornate, deep stone-lined tank constructed at a lower elevation adjacent to a higher master lake, talab, or tanka. It collects **subterranean seepage and percolation water (*अंतःस्रवण जल*)** filtered through the intervening bedrock.
- **Usage**: Used exclusively for community religious bathing and ritual ablutions (never for direct culinary drinking).
- **Examples**: **Toorji ka Jhalra** and **Mahamandir Jhalra** in Jodhpur.

---

### F. Kui / Beri (*कुई / बेरी*)
- **The Epitome of Desert Engineering**: Documented in the immortal environmental classic *"Rajasthan Ki Rajat Boondein"* by **Anupam Mishra**.
- **Physical Dimensions**: An impossibly narrow, vertical cylindrical shaft dug into the sand:
  - Diameter: Barely **1 to 1.5 metres (3 to 4 feet)** — just enough for a single human artisan to squat.
  - Depth: **10 to 15 metres (30 to 50 feet)**.
- **The Geological Imperative: The Khadia Patti (*खड़िया पट्टी*)**:
  - A Kui is dug **only where a subterranean layer of Gypsum or Calcrete (*Khadia Patti*) exists** beneath the sand.
  - Sand allows monsoon rain to percolate rapidly. When this descending moisture strikes the impenetrable gypsum band, it is trapped in the overlying sand as **subterranean moisture (*रेजाणी पानी*)**.
- **The Artisan**: The specialist well-digger is called a **Chezwano (*चेंजवारो / चेजो*)** or **Khadkhoo**. Working in oppressive heat and cramped darkness, he excavates the earth while lining the sandy walls with coiled ropes woven from *Khip* grass or interlocking masonry blocks.
- **Drop-by-Drop Seepage**: The trapped moisture in the surrounding sand slowly seeps drop-by-drop through the porous masonry into the base of the Kui, providing crystal-clear, sweet drinking water.

---

### G. The Tripartite Water Taxonomy of the Thar
According to traditional Rajasthani hydrology (popularized by Anupam Mishra):
1. **Pālār Paani (*पालर पानी*)**: Direct rainwater received from the clouds; surface runoff collected in Nadis, Tankas, and Baoris; purest form of water.
2. **Pātāl Paani (*पाताल पानी*)**: Deep groundwater extracted from deep open wells and tube-wells; usually brackish, mineral-heavy, and saline in the Thar.
3. **Rejāṇi Paani (*रेजाणी पानी*)**: Rainwater trapped in the shallow unsaturated sand zone resting above the subterranean *Khadia Patti* (gypsum layer); tapped exclusively by **Kuis and Beris**; incredibly sweet and pure.

---cd:T110f,1. **IGNP Origin: Harike Barrage, NOT Bhakra Dam**: The Indira Gandhi Canal does NOT originate from the Bhakra Dam; it originates from the **Harike Barrage** in Firozpur (Punjab) at the confluence of the Satluj and Beas rivers.
2. **Feeder Canal Irrigation Ban**: **ZERO irrigation is permitted from the 204-km Rajasthan Feeder Canal**. It functions strictly as an impermeable transit channel. Irrigation commences only downstream of **Masitawali Head**.
3. **The Rawatsar Branch Exception**: There are 9 branches of IGNP. **8 branches are on the Right Bank**, but **Rawatsar Branch is the ONLY branch on the Left Bank** because the topography east of Masitawali allows gravity flow.
4. **All Lift Canals on the Left Bank**: Every single one of the 7 IGNP lift canals originates on the **Left (Eastern) Bank** of the Main Canal because the terrain rises toward the east.
5. **IGNP Tail Points**:
   - The official terminal point of the IGNP Main Canal is **Mohangarh (Jaisalmer)**.
   - The absolute zero tail-end of the extended distribution system (Baba Ramdev Sub-branch) is **Ghadra Road (Barmer)**.
6. **Narmada Canal 100% Micro-Irrigation**: Narmada Canal Project is the **ONLY project in India where pressurized drip and sprinkler irrigation is 100% statutorily compulsory**. Conventional flood irrigation is illegal in its command area.
7. **Narmada Entry Point**: Enters Rajasthan at **Silu village in Sanchore district** (formerly Jalore) on 27 March 2008.
8. **Gang Canal Construction Material**: Built in 1927 using **hydraulic lime-mortar concrete and kankar masonry (*चूना-कंकड़*)**, NOT modern Portland cement!
9. **Oldest & Longest IGNP Lift Canal**: **Kanwarsain Lift Canal** (formerly Bikaner-Lunkaransar) is the oldest and longest lift canal, hailed as the "Lifeline of Bikaner".

11. **Mahi Power Allocation**: In Mahi Bajaj Sagar, project costs are shared 45% (Rajasthan) : 55% (Gujarat), but **100% of the 140 MW hydel power generated belongs exclusively to Rajasthan**!
12. **Bhakra Nangal Share**: Rajasthan's share in the Bhakra Nangal Project is **15.22%** in both water and electricity.
13. **Bisalpur Dam Capacity**: Crest capacity of Bisalpur Dam is **315.50 RL** (Reduced Level in metres).
14. **Jakham Dam Height**: Jakham Dam in Pratapgarh is **81 metres high**, making it the **tallest dam in Rajasthan**.
15. **Mahi Bajaj Sagar Length**: At **3,109 metres**, Mahi Bajaj Sagar Dam is the **longest dam in Rajasthan**.
16. **Panchana Dam Construction**: Panchana Dam in Karauli is Rajasthan's largest **earthen/mud dam (*मिट्टी का बांध*)**, fed by 5 rivulets (Ata, Machi, Bhadrawati, Barkheda, Bhainsawat).
17. **Sem Problem Cause**: *Sem* (waterlogging) in Hanumangarh/Bikaner is caused by an **impermeable subterranean gypsum/calcrete hardpan**, NOT just excessive water supply!
18. **Jhalra vs Baori**: A Baori collects direct rain and ground water; a **Jhalra does NOT collect direct rain runoff** — it collects subterranean seepage from an adjoining higher lake or tank!
19. **Khadin Inventor**: Khadins were engineered in the **15th century by Paliwal Brahmins of Jaisalmer**, NOT by Mughal or British engineers.
20. **Rejaani Paani Definition**: *Rejaani Paani* refers specifically to percolated rainwater trapped in the intermediate sand layer above the subterranean gypsum bed (*Khadia Patti*), tapped by Kuis.
21. **Modified PKC-ERCP Link Accord**: Signed on **28 January 2024** between Jal Shakti Ministry, Rajasthan, and Madhya Pradesh as a **National Project (90:10 funding ratio)**.
22. **Navnera Barrage Location**: Navnera Barrage (primary node of ERCP) is located on the **Kali Sindh River in Kota district** (Digod tehsil).
23. **Isarda Dam River**: Isarda Dam is built across the **Banas River** in Sawai Madhopur, downstream of Bisalpur Dam.
24. **Sei Diversion Tunnel**: Transfers water from the **Sei River (Sabarmati basin)** to the **Jawai Dam (Luni basin)** through Rajasthan's first 6.7-km water transfer tunnel.
25. **Largest Irrigation Source**: **Tube-wells (*नलकूप*)** are the largest single source of irrigation in Rajasthan (~48%), followed by open wells (~24%) and canals (~26%). Combined wells account for ~72%.

#### Q1. What is the *Sem Problem* in the IGNP command area?
**Model Answer**:  
Severe waterlogging and soil salinization caused by rising groundwater trapped above impermeable subterranean gypsum beds, sterilizing agricultural soils.

#### Q2. State the unique operational rule of the Narmada Canal Project.
**Model Answer**:  
First project in India where **100% pressurized drip and sprinkler (micro) irrigation is statutorily mandatory**; flood irrigation is prohibited.

#### Q3. Name the 7 Lift Canals of the Indira Gandhi Canal Project.
**Model Answer**:  
Chaudhary Kumbharam Arya, Kanwarsain, Panna Lal Barupal, Veer Teja Ji, Dr. Karni Singh, Guru Jambheshwar, and Jai Narayan Vyas.

#### Q4. Differentiate between *Palār Paani* and *Rejāṇi Paani*.
**Model Answer**:  
*Palār Paani* is direct surface rain runoff; *Rejāṇi Paani* is subterranean moisture trapped above an impervious gypsum bed, extracted via Kuis.

### 5-Marker Benchmark Responses (50 Words)

#### Q5. Evaluate the engineering architecture and agricultural significance of *Khadin*.
**Model Answer**:  
1. **Engineering**: Developed in 15th-century Jaisalmer by Paliwal Brahmins; an earthen bund (*Dhora*) is constructed across a rocky valley depression to impound monsoon runoff. Excess water discharges through sluice gates (*Khadia*) and spillways (*Chadar*).
2. **Agrarian Significance**: Standing water saturates the soil with nutrient-rich silt for 2–3 months. After drying in October, the retained capillary moisture allows high-yield winter Rabi crops (Wheat, Gram, Mustard) to mature **without any subsequent irrigation**.

#### Q6. Outline the objectives and core components of the Modified PKC-ERCP Link Project.
**Model Answer**:  
Signed as a **National Project (90:10 funding)** on **28 January 2024** by India, Rajasthan, and Madhya Pradesh:
1. **Objective**: Harvest surplus monsoonal runoff from Southern rivers (Chambal, Kalisindh, Parbati, Mej) at 75% dependability and divert it to deficit sub-basins (Banas, Morel, Banganga, Gambhir).
2. **Deliverables**: Solves drinking water crisis for **21 eastern districts** up to 2051, provides irrigation to **2.8 lakh hectares**, and recharges 1,487 rural tanks via hubs like **Navnera Barrage** (Kota).

### 10-Marker Analytical Essay (100 Words / 200 Words)

#### Q7. Critically evaluate the socio-economic and ecological transformation brought about by the Indira Gandhi Canal Project (IGNP) in Western Rajasthan. Examine the environmental hazards generated and recommend sustainable mitigation strategies.

**Model Answer Architecture**:

```text
                                  IGNP EVALUATION PARADIGM
                                             │
         ┌──────────────────┬────────────────┴────────────────┬──────────────────┐
         ▼                  ▼                                 ▼                  ▼
1. SOCIO-ECONOMIC BOOM  2. HYDROLOGIC MATRIX              3. ECOLOGICAL HAZARDS 4. SUSTAINABLE REMEDIES
   • Crop diversification  • Harike Barrage (649 km)        • Sem Waterlogging     • Bio-drainage (Eucalyptus)
   • Famine eradication    • 9 Branches + 7 Lift Canals     • Soil Alkalinity      • Subsurface tile drains
   • Agro-industries       • Stage I & II command           • Weed invasion        • Crop rationalization
```

1. **Socio-Economic & Agrarian Transformation**:
   - **Agricultural Green Revolution**: Transformed over 16 lakh hectares of hyper-arid sand dunes into fertile tracts. Bikaner, Sriganganagar, Hanumangarh, and Jaisalmer became hubs for cash crops: Long-staple American Cotton (*Narma*), Wheat, Mustard, Groundnut, and Kinnow citrus.
   - **Famine Eradication**: Decimated the recurring curse of *Trikal* (drought of grain, fodder, and drinking water). Ensured assured potable drinking water across desert districts via lift canals and feeder lines (e.g., Rajiv Gandhi Lift Canal to Jodhpur).
   - **Economic Spin-offs**: Spurred agro-processing industries, mandis, dairy modernization, livestock fodder security, and immigration into canal colonies.

2. **Severe Ecological & Environmental Pathologies**:
   - **The Sem Problem (Waterlogging & Salinization)**: Extensive seepage from unlined field distributaries coupled with an impermeable subterranean gypsum hardpan (*Gypsiferous stratum*) at 5–15 metres has caused the water table to rise rapidly (up to 1 metre/year) in Badopal, Rawatsar, and Suratgarh.
   - **Capillary Salinization**: Intense evaporation pulls saline subsoil water to the surface, creating barren, alkali-encrusted white sheets (*Reh/Kallar*), turning thousands of hectares of prime land into marshy wastelands.
   - **Ecosystem Degradation**: Proliferation of invasive xerophytes (*Vilayati Babul* - *Prosopis juliflora*) and aquatic weeds (*Typha*); surge in water-borne diseases and vector proliferation (malaria).

3. **Sustainable Policy Interventions & Remedial Measures**:
   - **Bio-drainage**: Extensive plantation of deep-rooting, high-transpiration trees like **Eucalyptus (*सफेदा*)** along canal banks to lower the water table naturally.
   - **Subsurface Drainage (SSD)**: Expanding Indo-Dutch project technology (underground perforated corrugated PVC pipes to drain perched water tables).
   - **Mandatory Micro-Irrigation**: Enforcing pressurized drip/sprinkler systems on the Narmada Canal model to eliminate wasteful flood irrigation (*Plev*).
   - **Promotion of Low Water-Intensive Crops**: Shifting cropping patterns from water-guzzling paddy and sugarcane towards drought-tolerant pulses, oilseeds, date palm (*Khajoor*), and olive orchards.

---

[Chapter 21 Complete ➔ Next: Rapid Revision Matrix 21: Water Infrastructure, Major Canals & Irrigation Projects]cf:T289b,Soil is the foundational pedological skin of Rajasthan's agricultural economy. Due to acute variations in geological parent rock, precipitation gradients (from $<10\text{ cm}$ in Jaisalmer to $>100\text{ cm}$ in Jhalawar), temperature extremes, and paleo-drainage history, Rajasthan exhibits a complex soil mosaic.

```text
                                PEDOLOGICAL PROFILE OF RAJASTHAN
                                                │
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                                             ▼
  MODERN USDA SOIL TAXONOMY                                                    ICAR TRADITIONAL SCHEME
  (वैज्ञानिक मृदा वर्गीकरण)                                                     (पारंपरिक क्षेत्रीय वर्गीकरण)
  • ENTISOLS (Most widespread; Desert sands)                                   • Sandy Desert Soil (~60% area)
  • ARIDISOLS (Arid soils with calcic horizon)                                 • Red-Loam Soil (Maize in Mewar)
  • ALFISOLS (Mature alluvium in Eastern Plains)                               • Black Regur Soil (Hadoti Vertisols)
  • INCEPTISOLS (Red-yellowish Aravalli soils)                                 • Alluvial Silt Soil (Eastern Plains)
  • VERTISOLS (Black shrink-swell clay in Hadoti)                              • Saline/Alkaline Soil (Reh/Kallar)
```

---

### A. Modern USDA Soil Taxonomy (Scientific Soil Orders)

In modern RPSC examinations, questions are predominantly framed using the **United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Soil Taxonomy Orders**. Rajasthan contains five distinct orders:

### B. Traditional & ICAR Soil Classification of Rajasthan

1. **Sandy Desert Soil (*रेतीली बलुई मृदा*)**:
   - Covers over **60% of the state's geographical area** (Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Barmer, Balotra, Phalodi, Jodhpur).
   - High porosity, high permeability, coarse sand grains ($>85\%$ quartz), severe nitrogen and humus deficiency, but possesses adequate levels of **phosphates and calcium**.
2. **Red-Loam Soil (*लाल दोमट मृदा*)**:
   - Found predominantly in **Dungarpur, Banswara, Udaipur, and Salumbar**.
   - Derived from the weathering of ancient Archaean granites and schists; rich in **iron oxide** (which imparts its vibrant red coloration); deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic matter.
   - Soil texture is light and moisture-retaining, making it the **ideal pedological medium for Maize (*मक्का*) and Paddy**.
3. **Deep Black Regur Soil (*काली मृदा*)**:
   - Confined to the **Hadoti Plateau (Kota, Bundi, Baran, Jhalawar)**.
   - Weathered from Cretaceous basaltic Deccan trap lava sheets; rich in potash, calcium, and iron; highly clayey.
   - Known as **"Self-Ploughing Soil" (*स्वतः जुताई वाली मृदा*)**: Expands and becomes sticky upon wetting; shrinks upon drying to form deep, gaping vertical cracks that naturally aerate the root zone.
4. **Alluvial / Loam Soil (*जलोढ़ / कछारी / दोमट मृदा*)**:
   - Formed by the depositional flood silt of the Chambal, Banas, and Banganga rivers across **Jaipur, Dausa, Alwar, Bharatpur, Dholpur, and Karauli**.
   - Most productive soil in Rajasthan; neutral pH (7.0 to 7.8); rich in potash and lime.
5. **Saline & Alkaline Soils (*लवणीय एवं क्षारीय मृदा — रेह, कल्लर, उसर*)**:
   - Extensive patches in **Sanchore, Balotra, Barmer, Nagaur, and Bikaner**.
   - Characterized by excessive accumulation of soluble sodium salts ($NaCl, Na_2SO_4$).
   - **Chemical Reclamation Invariants**:
     - **Alkaline Soils ($pH > 8.5$)**: Treated using **Gypsum (*जिप्सम — $CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O$*)**.
     - **Acidic Soils ($pH < 6.5$)**: Treated using **Lime / Limestone (*चूना — $CaCO_3$*)**.
     - **Saline Soils with high alkalinity**: Treated using **Rock Phosphate / Iron Pyrites**.

---

### C. Soil Erosion & Degradation Mechanisms
Soil erosion in Rajasthan is famously termed the **"Crawling Death of Agriculture" (*कृषि की रेंगती हुई मृत्यु*)**.
1. **Wind Erosion (*वायु अपरदन*)**:
   - Dominates the Western Sandy Plains (Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Barmer, Churu).
   - Hot summer westerly winds peel away dry, unvegetated topsoil, causing desertification and sand-dune migration (*Dhrian*).
2. **Water Erosion (*जल अपरदन*)**:
   - **Sheet Erosion (*चादरी अपरदन*)**: Sheet-wash occurs on the deforested, undulating mountain slopes of **Sirohi, Rajsamand, and Udaipur**, where monsoon rain washes away the fertile topsoil layer invisibly.
   - **Gully Erosion (*अवनालिका अपरदन*)**: Deep vertical channel incision caused by rapid surface runoff in the soft alluvial plains of the **Chambal Basin** (Sawai Madhopur, Karauli, Dholpur, and Kota), carving out the notorious **Beehad (*बीहड़*) and Utkhat Bhumi (Badlands)**.

---

### D. Soil Health Card Scheme (*मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड योजना*)
- **Historical Launch**: Officially launched on **19 February 2015** by Prime Minister Narendra Modi from **Suratgarh (Sriganganagar district, Rajasthan)**.
- **National Motto / Slogan**: *"स्वस्थ धरा, खेत हरा"* (Swasth Dhara, Khet Hara — Healthy Earth, Green Field).
- **The 12 Soil Health Parameters Tested**:
  1. **Primary Macro-nutrients (3)**: Nitrogen ($N$), Phosphorus ($P$), Potassium ($K$).
  2. **Secondary Macro-nutrients (1)**: Sulphur ($S$).
  3. **Micro-nutrients (5)**: Zinc ($Zn$), Iron ($Fe$), Copper ($Cu$), Manganese ($Mn$), Boron ($B$).
  4. **Physical Parameters (3)**: Soil Reaction ($pH$), Electrical Conductivity ($EC$ — measuring salinity), Organic Carbon ($OC$).

### A. Statutory & Policy Framework
- **National Forest Policy (1988)**: Mandates that at least **33% of total geographical area** (60% in mountainous zones and 20% in plains) must be maintained under forest cover.
- **Rajasthan State Forest Policy (2010)**:
  - Formulated in **February 2010**; Rajasthan was the **first state in India** to notify a standalone state forest policy aimed at raising forest cover to **20%**.
- **Updated Rajasthan Forest Policy 2023**:
  - Unveiled on **5 June 2023** (World Environment Day); reaffirms the target of achieving 20% green cover by 2040 through massive agro-forestry, community forestry, and eco-tourism promotion.

---

### B. Administrative (Legal) Forest Classification (State Forest Department)
The **Recorded Forest Area (RFA)** of Rajasthan stands at **32,863 sq km** (**9.60%** of total area), classified under the *Rajasthan Forest Act, 1953* into three legal categories:

```text
                         LEGAL FOREST CLASSIFICATION (RFA: 32,863 sq km)
                                                │
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                      ▼                                      ▼
  PROTECTED FORESTS                      RESERVED FORESTS                      UNCLASSED FORESTS
  (संरक्षित / रक्षित वन)                   (आरक्षित वन)                          (अवर्गीकृत वन)
      ~56.49%                                ~37.05%                                ~6.46%
   (18,564 sq km)                         (12,176 sq km)                         (2,123 sq km)
         │                                      │                                      │
• LARGEST LEGAL CATEGORY               • STRICTEST CATEGORY                   • LEAST RESTRICTIVE
• Grazing & felling allowed with       • Complete state monopoly; all         • No blanket ban on grazing
  strict permits & regulation.           grazing & tree felling prohibited.     or timber felling; nominal fees.
```

1. **Protected Forests (*संरक्षित / रक्षित वन*) — 56.49% (Largest Share)**:
   - Extent: Approximately **18,564 sq km**.
   - Legal status: Under government oversight, but local villagers are granted customary concessions for grazing livestock and collecting fallen fuel-wood under monitored permits.
2. **Reserved Forests (*आरक्षित वन*) — 37.05%**:
   - Extent: Approximately **12,176 sq km**.
   - Legal status: State property of absolute ecological conservation; **all human activities, livestock grazing, and wood felling are completely prohibited by law**.
3. **Unclassed Forests (*अवर्गीकृत वन*) — 6.46%**:
   - Extent: Approximately **2,123 sq km**.
   - Legal status: Forests not covered under the reserved or protected categories; tree felling and grazing are permitted upon payment of state royalties/fees.

The Forest Survey of India (FSI), Dehradun, assesses actual forest cover biennially via remote sensing (LISS-III sensors) based on **Canopy Density**:

| Canopy Class | Canopy Density Definition | Area in Rajasthan (sq km) | Share of State Area | Defining Geographic Reality |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Very Dense Forest (VDF)** | Canopy cover **$> 70\%$** | **78.15 sq km** | **0.02%** | Extremely sparse; confined to isolated pockets in Mount Abu, Sitamata, and Kumbhalgarh. |
| **Moderately Dense Forest (MDF)** | Canopy cover **40% to 70%** | **4,368.65 sq km** | **1.28%** | Found on upper Aravalli ridges and Hadoti valleys (Udaipur, Alwar, Chittorgarh). |
| **Open Forest (OF)** | Canopy cover **10% to 40%** | **12,208.16 sq km** | **3.57%** | **LARGEST component of Rajasthan's actual forest cover** (~73% of total forest cover). |
| **Total Actual Forest Cover** | Canopy cover **$> 10\%$** | **16,654.96 sq km** | **4.87%** | Absolute forest cover visible via satellite. |
| **Scrub (*झाड़ियां*)** | Canopy cover **$< 10\%$** | **4,808.51 sq km** | **1.41%** | Degraded thorny vegetation; not counted in official Forest Cover! |
